On the Friday before Thanksgiving,
[music] Marvin Kessler stood at his own
front door for two full minutes and
couldn't work the deadbolt. He'd turned
that lock every morning for 50 years.
[music]
What slowed his hands had gone down with
a glass of water 9 hours earlier.
You may know a milder version of that
morning. [music]
You wake up foggy, your fingers feel
thick, and the day takes an hour to
arrive. [music]
When CDC researchers counted emergency
hospital stays [music] caused by
reactions to medicines in Americans 65
and older, nearly half were people 80 or
older.
Marvin is in his 80s. [music]
If that's your decade or close to it,
this story is yours.
Five quiet changes come with the 80s.
Marvin met all five that week, one a
day, and every one of them has a fix.
We'll end at that front door with the
change people blame on everything except
their age.
Which change have you noticed most in
yourself? Your nose, your ears, or the
cold? Tell me in the comments. Just one
word. Nose, ears, or cold.
Right now, without getting up, name
every pill you swallowed in the last day
and what each one is for. Count the ones
from the drugstore shelf, too. Keep that
number for later.
Number five is a nose that stops warning
[music] you.
Marvin Kessler is 83, a retired butcher
in Dubuque, Iowa. For 41 years, [music]
he ran Kessler's Meats on Central
Avenue. Marvin could tell a tired pork
shoulder from across the walk-in [music]
cooler by smell alone.
On Monday morning, Marvin's neighbor let
herself in with a plate of coffee cake.
Dottie Brandt is 79, a retired
hairdresser from the yellow house next
[music] door.
Dottie stopped in the kitchen doorway
and said, "Marvin, I [music] smell gas."
The front knob on Marvin's stove sat
just past off. No flame, only a faint
hiss.
Marvin was 3 ft away with the newspaper,
and he smelled nothing at all.
Dottie didn't touch the knob or a light
switch because a spark is the danger.
She took Marvin by the sleeve, and they
went straight out the back door.
From her own kitchen, Dottie called the
gas company. A man in a gray truck
checked every room and aired out the
house.
Natural gas has no smell of its own. Gas
companies add a harmless chemical that
smells like rotten eggs, so a leak can
warn you. That warning only works if
your nose still does.
In a national health survey that tested
people's sense of smell, about four in
10 people 80 and older had a weakened
one.
Among people 70 and older, nearly one in
three couldn't pick out the smell of
natural gas.
Smell fades so slowly that most people
never notice it going. Food starts
tasting flat, and you reach for the salt
shaker. Coffee smells like less than it
used to. Marvin's nose had been the best
tool in his shop. He'd simply stopped
testing it.
You can test yours right now with
whatever is in reach.
Step one.
Pick up something with a smell you know
well, like coffee, a lemon, or a bar of
soap.
Step two.
Close your eyes and hold it a few inches
below your nose.
Step three.
Breathe in gently and ask yourself if
it's as strong as you remember.
If it seemed faint or took a second
sniff, you're in good company.
If your sense of smell has dropped
suddenly, or you smell things that
aren't there, mention it to your doctor.
Smell was never a perfect food test
anyway. Federal food safety advice says
food can make you very sick even when it
doesn't look, smell, or taste spoiled.
So, Marvin's fix didn't depend on his
nose. On Monday afternoon, he pressed
the test button on the smoke alarm in
the hall, and it shrieked. Then, Marvin
drove to the hardware store for a carbon
monoxide alarm. That gas has no smell
for anyone at any age.
Back home, Marvin stuck a roll of
masking tape and a marker to the fridge
door. Every leftover in Marvin's kitchen
now gets the day it was cooked written
in marker.
A weaker nose is common after 80, and
it's nobody's fault. A smoke alarm
doesn't care how old your nose is.
The people in today's stories are
illustrative examples. The changes they
live through are real.
Number four is the cold [music] you stop
feeling.
On Tuesday morning, Dottie Brandt came
back for her plate and kept her coat on.
Marvin's thermostat said 62. It had said
62 since his gas bill went up two
winters ago.
"Dottie, I worked 41 [music]
years in a walk-in cooler," Marvin said.
"62 is a heatwave."
Marvin truly felt fine,
but his hands were pale around the
coffee cup, and his fingertips [music]
were cold when Dottie took the mug from
him.
That's the change. The National
Institute on aging says the changes that
come with age can make it harder to
notice your body getting too cold. The
old nudge that sent you for a sweater
gets quieter.
And it doesn't take a frozen house. The
same institute says homes that are only
mildly cool, 60 to 65°, can lead to
hypothermia in older adults. Hypothermia
means the body's core temperature has
dropped below 95°.
The early signs are easy to wave off.
Cold hands and feet, a puffy face, pale
skin, shivering, slow or slurred speech,
feeling sleepy, grouchy, or confused.
Cold slows the brain, too.
So, the person it's happening to is
often the last one to notice. That's why
a body at 80 needs a thermostatic can
trust instead of a feeling it can't.
Marvin didn't think about any of that on
Tuesday. He thought about the bill. His
late wife had always paid it [music] and
Marvin still opened the envelope with
one eye shut.
So, Marvin did what a lot of people do
in a cool house.
He wore his cardigan buttoned to the top
and kept a blanket on his knees in the
recliner.
By supper, Marvin had stopped noticing
the cold at all.
In the shop, the cold had never fooled
him.
The walk-in had a big round thermometer
on the door and Marvin checked it every
morning before he unlocked the front. At
home, there was nothing on the wall but
a thermostat set to save money.
On Tuesday night, Marvin lay under two
blankets and couldn't get warm enough to
sleep. His feet felt like they belonged
to someone else.
Around midnight, he padded to the
bathroom cabinet.
Marvin took two small light blue caplets
from a box he'd bought for a sore back
in the spring.
He went back to bed and slept like a
stone.
On Wednesday morning, Dottie Brandt came
by with her own thermometer, the old
kind with a dial, and set it on Marvin's
kitchen table. It read 61.
Marvin looked at it for a long time.
Then Marvin turned the thermostat up to
68. That's the lowest setting the
National Institute on Aging suggests for
older adults in cold weather.
He did the rest himself.
Marvin dug his long underwear out of the
bottom dresser drawer to wear under his
pajamas. He rolled a bath towel along
the bottom of the back door where the
draft came in. And he found the old knit
cap he used to wear into the walk-in
cooler. Now it's his nightcap.
Extra covers help on cold nights, too.
And so do warm socks, slippers, and a
throw blanket in the daytime.
Marvin's son had once bought him a
little space heater for the den. Marvin
left it in the box, and that was fine.
The same guide warns that some space
heaters can be fire hazards or raise the
risk of carbon monoxide poisoning. If
you use one, follow its safety
directions and keep that carbon monoxide
alarm working.
In cold weather, it helps to have
someone check on you. So, Marvin and
Dottie made a deal. If the blind in
Marvin's kitchen window isn't up by 8:00
in the morning, Dottie comes over and
knocks.
If the bill is the reason your
thermostat is low, there's help for
that. A federal program called LIHEAP
helps households with lower incomes pay
heating bills. Your local area agency on
aging may know about it and about other
help near you.
If you said cold at the start, your body
is still sending the signal, so trust
it. It's the people who feel fine at 62
who most need a thermometer on the wall.
A house at 68° is good sense at 80, like
a coat in January.
By Wednesday afternoon, Marvin's kitchen
was warm enough for shirt sleeves. That
evening, he had somewhere to be for the
first time in a month.
Number three is the conversation you nod
through.
On Wednesday night, Marvin went back to
pinochle in the basement of the parish
hall. Four men at a folding table, a
radio playing in the corner, and
everyone talking at once.
Marvin laughed a beat late at the jokes.
He nodded at questions he hadn't quite
caught. Then he bid on a hand when
nobody had asked him to, and the table
went quiet.
Somebody asked Marvin, gently, whether
he was feeling all right. "I'm fine,"
Marvin said. "You all mumble." He drove
home early.
In the driveway, Marvin sat in his truck
for a while with the engine off.
The house was dark and the street was
quiet, and quiet was easy.
Then he went inside and took two the
blue caplets again before bed.
That's how hearing loss often looks from
across a card table.
Government health guides note that older
people who don't hear well are sometimes
mistaken for being confused. Marvin knew
exactly where he was. He was missing
every third word.
The signs are ordinary, so they're easy
to explain away.
You ask people to repeat themselves.
Voices seem to mumble. Talk with two or
more people gets hard to follow,
especially with noise in the room. And
the TV creeps up until someone
complains.
Dottie Brandt had been complaining for a
year. She could hear Marvin's Westerns
from her own kitchen through two walls
and a driveway.
On Thursday morning, Dottie came over
with the proof. She picked up Marvin's
remote and pointed at the little number
in the corner of the screen. 41.
"Same as your years in the shop," Dottie
said. "Mine sits at 18."
Marvin had an answer ready
>> [music]
>> about bad speakers on new televisions.
Then he noticed he'd had to ask Dottie
to say it twice.
High voices are often the first to go.
>> [music]
>> Children's voices and some women's
voices can blur into the background.
When Marvin's granddaughter called from
college on Sundays, he'd been saying,
"Uh-huh, that's great, honey," and
hoping [music] it fit.
More than half of Americans 75 and older
have hearing loss that gets in the way
of everyday life.
But among adults 70 and older who could
benefit from hearing aids, fewer than
one in three has ever used them.
The bigger cost shows up in the
calendar.
Researchers reviewed studies of older
adults with hearing loss. In most of
them, hearing loss was linked with more
loneliness and more social isolation.
That fit Marvin's month exactly. He
hadn't stopped liking pinochle. He'd
stopped being able to follow it, so he'd
stopped going. Two Wednesdays in
October, Marvin told the men his back
was acting up.
The hard part of hearing loss is that it
hides. Each conversation you miss feels
like the other person's fault. Only the
empty Wednesdays add up.
After Dottie left, Marvin called a
hearing clinic in town and booked a
hearing test for the Monday after
Thanksgiving. He wrote it on the kitchen
calendar in big block letters where he'd
have to look at it every morning.
Then he called one of the peanut men and
told him the truth.
"Thank God." the man said. "I thought
you were mad at us. Come back next week.
We'll turn off the radio."
That's one of the simplest things the
hearing guide suggest and it costs
nothing.
Tell people you have trouble hearing.
Ask them to face you when they talk and
sit away from the noise with the people
you want to hear in front of you.
If your hearing has been slipping, ask
your doctor about a hearing test.
Since 2022, hearing aids for mild to
moderate hearing loss have been sold
over the counter. You can buy them in
stores or online without a prescription
or an exam. A test first tells you how
much help your ears need and which kind.
One more thing belongs here because it
ties back to Monday.
If you can't hear the smoke alarm from
your bed, there are smoke alarms made
for people with hearing loss. They flash
a bright light or shake instead of only
beeping.
If you said ears at the start, you've
already done the hardest part, which is
saying it out loud.
Marvin's hearing was ordinary for 83.
Sitting home on Wednesday nights didn't
have to be.
That Thursday afternoon, Marvin needed a
ride to the pharmacy.
The pharmacy had one more change waiting
for him.
Number two [music] is an immune system
that answers more slowly.
On Thursday afternoon, Dottie Brant
drove Marvin to the pharmacy on Locust
Street to pick up his blood pressure
pills.
Taped to the counter was a hand-lettered
sign. Flu shots today.
"Haven't had the flu since Eisenhower."
Marvin said. He hadn't had a flu shot in
three winters, either.
Dotty raised one penciled eyebrow and
said nothing, which is how Dotty wins
most arguments.
Marvin's reasoning was simple. He'd
spent his whole working life in a cold
room with his hands in raw meat, and
he'd hardly missed a day. A man like
that doesn't need shots.
The pharmacist asked Marvin's age, then
she asked about two vaccines, not one.
Her question came from a real change.
The CDC says the body's immune defenses
change with increasing age, and
responses to vaccines may be lower in
older people. An immune system at 80
still works. It just answers a little
more slowly and a little less loudly.
That's the part Marvin's reasoning
missed. The man who never got sick in
the cooler was 50. The immune system
he'd counted on back then had aged right
along with the rest of him.
You can see it in the flu numbers. In
recent years, between 50%
of flu hospital stays have been in
people 65 and older.
That's also why the flu shots preferred
for people 65 and older are stronger
versions. Some are high-dose, and some
contain an added ingredient that boosts
the body's response. They're built for
an immune system that needs a louder
signal.
The second vaccine was for RSV, a common
virus that infects the lungs and
breathing passages.
The CDC recommends a single dose of RSV
vaccine for all adults 75 and older. It
isn't a yearly shot. Once you've had
that one dose, you're done for now.
While they waited, a young mother stood
in line ahead of them with a toddler who
coughed into everything.
In one week, Marvin would be at a
Thanksgiving table with a dozen
relatives. Two of them were under five,
and one was just home from a college
dorm.
Marvin had never heard of RSV, and
nobody had brought it up because Marvin
hadn't been asking.
Dottie had asked. She'd gotten her RSV
shot the year before, and she told
Marvin [music] so at a volume the whole
pharmacy could enjoy.
So, Marvin rolled up his left sleeve for
the flu shot and his right sleeve for
the RSV.
The pharmacist said both could be given
at the same visit. The whole thing took
less time than finding his reading
glasses.
On the way out, the pharmacist handed
Marvin a little card with both shots and
the date.
Marvin tucked it into his shirt pocket
next to his pen.
In the car, Marvin rubbed his shoulder.
He said [music] the flu shot hurt more
than the time he nicked his thumb on the
band saw.
Dottie said [music] that was a lie, and
Marvin admitted it was.
The vaccine list for 80 isn't quite the
list for 65, and the advice does change.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist which
vaccines you're due for. Pharmacies keep
a record, and so does your doctor's
office, so you don't have to remember it
all yourself.
Think of a vaccine as a wanted poster.
It shows your immune system what a germ
looks like before the germ ever arrives.
For a system that answers slowly, that
early look is a real help.
That getting ready takes time. The CDC
says it takes about 2 weeks after a flu
shot for the body to build its
protection. So, the earlier in the
season you ask, the better.
A slower immune system isn't a broken
one. A vaccine gives it a head start
before the germs show up at the door.
That night, Marvin's left arm was a
little sore.
He watched the news, took two of the
blue caplets for the third night in a
row, and went to bed at 10:00.
Number one is a pill that stays longer
than it used to.
Friday,
>> [music]
>> 7:00 in the morning.
Doddy Brandt stood on Marvin's porch
with his newspaper and watched him fight
the deadbolt through the glass.
Marvin got it open on the third try. His
head felt packed with wet sawdust and
his fingers were a step behind his
thoughts.
He knew what day it was and he knew
Doddy. He was just slow, the way he used
to feel the morning after a long
wedding.
Marvin's first thought was the gas,
but the new carbon monoxide alarm in the
hall glowed a quiet green and the stove
knobs were all straight up and off.
Doddy asked what he'd taken last night.
Marvin shuffled to the bathroom and came
back with the box. Tylenol PM.
Three nights in a row.
Tylenol PM is two medicines in one
caplet. One is acetaminophen, the pain
reliever in regular Tylenol. The other
is diphenhydramine, the same drug that's
in Benadryl. That's the part that makes
you sleepy.
Marvin had never thought of it as a
medicine. It came from the shelf next to
the cough drops.
Doddy fetched the magnifying glass from
the junk drawer and Marvin read the back
of the box out loud. In small print, it
said that when using this product,
drowsiness will occur. It said not to
drive. Marvin set the box down on the
kitchen table very gently, as if it
might go off.
This is what changed for Marvin after
80
Every pill you swallow has to leave your
body somehow, mostly through the liver
and the kidneys. With age, the kidneys
filter blood more slowly and the liver
and kidneys may not clear medicines the
way they once did.
In a small study in Canada, researchers
measured how fast people cleared
diphenhydramine from their blood.
In adults around 30, half of a dose was
gone in about 9 hours. In adults around
70, it took about 13 and a half hours.
Marvin is 83, older than the people in
that study. So, the two caplets he
swallowed at 10:00 could easily still be
at work at 7:00 in the morning, and a
little of each night's dose was still
there when the next one went down.
Think of the sink in the back of
Marvin's old shop. When the drain slows,
the water you poured in an hour ago is
still in the basin when you pour more.
Nothing's wrong with the water. The
drain is just older.
The federal government's own drug guide
is plain about it. Generally,
diphenhydramine shouldn't be used in
older adults, except for serious
allergic reactions, because other
medicines are safer and work better.
If you're 65 or older, the same guide
says to talk with your doctor about its
risks and benefits.
Marvin sat down hard on the bench by the
door.
"41 years," Marvin said, "I read every
label on every package of meat I sold. I
never read that one."
That CDC count from the start held a
hopeful finding, too.
Most of those emergency hospital stays
came from a handful of everyday
medicines, like blood thinners and
diabetes medicines, not rare ones.
The researchers wrote that better
management of those medicines could
reduce those hospital stays.
So, by 10:00, with the fog finally
lifting, Marvin went looking for a bag.
He found one of the old white paper bags
from the shop with Kessler's Meats
stamped on the side in red.
Into the bag went everything. Three
prescription bottles, a jar of fish oil,
the Tylenol PM, a tube of back cream
from the bathroom drawer, and a bottle
of leftover antibiotics from a bad cough
the year before that Marvin had kept
just in case.
At the start, you counted your pills.
Marvin would have said three. The bag
held seven.
That afternoon, Dottie drove him back to
the pharmacy on Locust Street, and
Marvin set the white paper bag on the
counter.
Healthcare quality experts have a name
for this. They call it a brown bag
medicine review, and they say every
patient should have one at least once a
year.
The guide for clinics even explains why.
A person with no prescriptions at all
could still be taking medicines or
supplements that nobody knows about. The
drugstore shelf counts, and so does the
bathroom drawer.
The pharmacist pulled up Marvin's record
on her screen. It listed three
medicines. She went through the other
four with him, asking when he took each
one and how. She set the old antibiotics
aside and offered to dispose of them for
him.
Marvin could name two of his three
prescriptions. He knew which one was for
his blood pressure and which was for his
cholesterol. The third one stumped him.
It had been prescribed by a doctor who'd
retired, and Marvin had kept refilling
it out of habit. The pharmacist wrote
that one down as a question for his
doctor.
When the pharmacist reached the blue
box, she stopped. She suggested Marvin
talk with his doctor about better ways
to sleep, and said she'd send a note to
his doctor's office, too.
Then the pharmacist wrote out a list of
everything Marvin takes, with the name,
the dose, and the reason for each.
Marvin folded it into his wallet behind
his old butcher's license.
Driving home, Marvin was quiet for a
while.
Then he told Dotty that for 41 years,
customers had trusted him to know what
was in the package. He figured it was
time somebody did the same for him.
On Friday night, the house was 68°.
Marvin wore his long johns and the knit
cap [music] from the cooler. The blue
box stayed in the white paper bag, and
he slept until [music] 6:00.
Marvin's body was doing what bodies do
at 83. It just needed his medicines
checked by someone who knew what 83 does
to them.
Marvin did one more thing that Friday.
Before lunch, he called his doctor's
office and told the nurse about the
morning at the door.
If a medicine leaves you groggy or dizzy
the next morning, call your doctor or
pharmacist that same day. Don't stop a
prescription on your own before you ask.
And if the hearing in one ear drops
suddenly, see a doctor right away.
Call 911 for sudden confusion or sudden
trouble speaking or understanding. Call
it for sudden numbness or weakness in
the face, an arm or a leg, especially on
one side. Call it for someone who is
very cold, sleepy, and slurring words.
If you smell gas, don't touch a light
switch or the stove. Leave the house
first, then call the gas company from a
neighbor's. If the carbon monoxide alarm
goes off, get outside into fresh air
first. Then call 911.
None of this is a diagnosis. Your own
doctor and pharmacist know your
medicines best.
The next Thursday, [music]
Marvin carved the Thanksgiving turkey at
his daughter's table, the way he has
since his own kids were small. He cut it
against the grain in thin, even slices,
and nobody else was allowed near the
knife.
The TV was off, and Marvin sat where he
could see every face.
When his granddaughter told a long story
about her college roommate, Marvin
laughed in all the right places. Dottie
Brant, at the far end of the table, gave
him a small nod.
Afterward, Dottie wrapped the leftover
turkey in foil.
Marvin pulled the masking tape and the
marker from [music] his coat pocket,
tore off a strip, and wrote one word on
it.
Tonight, open your bathroom cabinet and
look for any box that says PM,
nighttime, or sleep on the front. Set
those boxes with your pill bottles so
they go along on your next pharmacy
[music] trip.
And now that you've had Marvin's week,
nose, ears, or cold, [music] would you
change your first answer? Tell me in the
comments. Just one word. And send this
to the friend [music] who swears by a
little something for sleep.
In Marvin's front hall, the carbon
monoxide alarm glows [music] green. On
the foil in his fridge, in square
butcher's capitals, one word. Thursday.

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
If you're over 70 and feel healthy right now, a sudden decline doesn't always come out of nowhere. It can start with one quiet trigger, weeks before anyone notices. This video counts down five of them: weight you lose without trying, a world that quietly gets smaller, the fall that didn't happen, a few days in a hospital bed, and the one that often doesn't look like what it is, so it gets blamed on age.

Keep count of how many are in your life right now. At the end, your number tells you whether this is just getting older or something you can start turning around this week. Researchers at Yale who followed 754 people over 70 found that when someone lost the ability to bathe, dress or walk on their own, eight in ten got it back within a year.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — Why healthy 70-year-olds suddenly decline
1:29 — Trigger 5: Weight you lose without trying
5:59 — Trigger 4: A world that gets smaller
10:18 — Trigger 3: The fall that didn't happen
15:03 — Trigger 2: A few days in a hospital bed
19:50 — Trigger 1: The one that gets blamed on age
24:38 — What your number means

If this helped, a like and a subscribe help the next video reach more people.

The people in this video are illustrative examples. This channel shares general health education from published research, narrated with an AI voice. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

list to your next checkup.
Four or five? Don't wait for your yearly
visit. Call your doctor's office this
week.
And whatever your count, if you or the
person you live with becomes confused
over a few hours or a day, the way Helen
did, don't wait for it to pass. Call the
doctor's office that same day. If you
can't reach anyone, go to the emergency
room.
Some signs can't wait for a call back.
Call 911 right away if any of these come
on suddenly. Numbness or weakness in the
face, arm, or leg, especially on one
side. Confusion or trouble speaking or
understanding. Trouble seeing. Trouble
walking, dizziness, or loss of balance.
Or a severe headache with no known
cause. If you're not sure, call.
Helen did one more thing that week. She
called Kate back and asked for a
promise.
If she ever sounds confused on the
phone, even a little, Kate won't wait
for it to pass. She'll call her mother's
doctor that same day.
On the second Thursday in December,
Helen parks on Fountain Square. She's
gained back two of the 9 lb.
Her physical therapist came for the
first time on Monday and left her a page
of exercises for every morning.
Helen stands at the bottom of the cafe's
three concrete steps and takes hold of
the skinny iron railing.
Then she climbs them, one at a time.
Inside, two friends are already waving
from the corner table. Helen's coffee is
poured and there's a slice of pie at her
place that she didn't order.
Tonight, call one person who would
notice if you didn't sound like yourself
>> [music]
>> and ask them for Kate's promise. And
think back to your one word from the
start. Fall, hospital, or alone. Now
that you've walked Helen's line back,
which of those three words [music] would
you pick today? Tell me in the comments.
Just one word. And send this to the
friend who blames every slowdown on
getting older.
In Helen's [music] kitchen in Bowling
Green, the calendar turns to February.
Every Thursday in January is written in
pen and not one of them is crossed
[music] out.

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
Flu season after 70 plays by harder rules. The CDC estimates that in recent seasons, 70 to 85 percent of seasonal flu deaths happened in people 65 and older.

On a December night on Birch Lane, Leon, seventy-seven, asks Ansel what day it is — twice in ten minutes. His flu season started back in October at the pharmacy counter. Follow Leon through six everyday mistakes: skipping the flu shot over an old myth, thinking it's the only shot you need (RSV, pneumonia, COVID), letting germs come to the holiday table, riding it out instead of calling early for an antiviral, treating the first good day as the finish line, and waiting for morning when the flu sends an emergency sign.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — Leon's question on a December night
1:46 — Mistake 6: Putting off the flu shot
6:06 — Mistake 5: Thinking it's the only shot you need
9:32 — Mistake 4: Germs at the holiday table
13:03 — Mistake 3: Riding it out instead of calling early
17:03 — Mistake 2: The first good day isn't the finish line
20:06 — Mistake 1: Waiting for morning on an emergency sign
24:54 — January on the ice

If you enjoyed this story from Birch Lane, please like this video and subscribe to Ansel Senior Health so you never miss an episode with Ansel and Marion.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Ansel, Marion and their neighbors are illustrated characters. This channel shares general health education from published research, narrated with an AI voice. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

subtitles.plaintext:
On the first Friday night in December,
>> [music]
>> Leon, 77, sat in his recliner on Birch
Lane and asked Ansel what day it was.
10 minutes later, Leon asked again.
[music]
Between the questions, he was breathing
like a man who had just carried a canoe
up from the lake. [music]
The day before, Leon had felt so much
better that [music] he'd decided his flu
was over.
If you're over 70, you know the moment.
A chill runs across your shoulders, your
bones [music] start to ache, and you
tell yourself you'll sleep it off.
After 65, the flu plays by harder rules.
The CDC estimates that in recent years,
>> [music]
>> between 70 and 85% of seasonal flu
deaths happen in people 65 and older.
Six everyday mistakes tilt those odds
the wrong way, and Leon made all six in
one season.
The last one matters most, the signs
Marion spotted that Friday night. The
ones that mean you don't wait for
morning.
Right now, say out loud the month of
your last flu shot.
Then try your last pneumonia shot.
If the second one stumps you, you're in
good company, and number five is for
you.
When the flu comes on, what do you do
first? Call or wait?
Tell me in one word in the comments.
We'll come back to your answer at number
three.
Leon is Ansel's fishing buddy, a retired
high school football coach with a gray
goatee, a booming laugh, and a maroon
coach's windbreaker.
Leon has lived with type 2 diabetes for
years. His flu season started in October
at the pharmacy counter on Main Street.
Number six [music] is putting off the
flu shot because of something you once
heard.
On a gray [music] Tuesday in
mid-October, Marion rolled up the sleeve
of her coral cardigan at the drugstore
on Main [music] Street. Ansel sat in the
next chair, his mustard yellow tie
tucked inside his navy sweater. Marion
and Ansel both had their flu shots in
under 10 minutes.
Leon had come along to pick up his
diabetes prescription.
Leon stood by the greeting cards with
his arms crossed over his windbreaker.
"Not me." Leon said. "The last time I
got that shot, it gave me the flu. Three
days in bed."
That's one of the most common reasons
people skip the shot, and the CDC
answers it directly.
A flu vaccine cannot cause flu. The
shots are made from killed virus, or
from a protein taken from the virus. So,
there's nothing in the needle [music]
that can infect you.
What a shot can do is make you feel off
for a day or so.
A sore arm, a headache, a low fever,
achy muscles.
Those side effects are usually mild and
short-lasting, especially compared with
the flu itself.
There's a second explanation for Leon's
three days in bed years ago.
It takes about two weeks after the shot
for your body to build its protection.
If a flu virus reaches you before then,
you can still get sick, and the shot
gets the blame.
Marion didn't argue at the pharmacy
counter.
Back home, Marion wrote Leon flu shot in
red ink on the kitchen calendar on every
Monday until Thanksgiving.
Leon pretended not to see it every time
he came over for coffee.
Why does Marion bother?
Partly because your immune defenses
change as you age.
That's part of the reason people 65 and
older are at higher risk of serious flu
complications.
So, older arms get their own shots.
For people 65 and older, the CDC prefers
three kinds of flu vaccine over the
standard dose.
One is a high-dose shot. One is a
recombinant shot, and one is an
adjuvanted shot made with an added
ingredient that helps create a stronger
immune response.
If the names won't stick, just ask the
preferred flu shot for people 65 and
older. And if none of the three is on
the shelf that day, get a regular flu
shot instead of walking out without one.
Timing matters, too.
September and October are generally good
months, and ideally you're vaccinated by
the end of October.
People 65 and older should generally not
get it early, in July or August, because
protection may fade over time.
But late still beats never.
Getting the shot after October can still
help protect you.
And it has to be every year.
Flu viruses keep changing, so the
vaccine is updated each season. And the
protection from last year's shot fades
with time.
The shot may still help, even when it
doesn't keep the flu away.
Researchers who pooled studies of adults
in the hospital with flu found a
difference.
Vaccinated patients had about 26% lower
odds of landing in intensive care. And
their risk of dying was 31% lower than
for un-vaccinated patients.
Leon held out for 5 more weeks.
Every Monday, Leon saw the red ink, and
every Monday, he changed the subject to
walleye. On the Monday before
Thanksgiving, with Marion's red calendar
staring at him across the Brooks kitchen
table, Leon finally gave in. "Fine,"
Leon said, "but if I get sick, I'm
blaming your calendar."
So, Leon rolled up his sleeve at the
drugstore that afternoon.
Remember those 2 weeks?
Leon's shot went in 3 days before
Thanksgiving dinner.
Your own shot doesn't need 5 weeks of
red ink. One call to your pharmacy can
set the day, and Medicare and most
private insurance plans cover it. The
shot isn't perfect, but it lowers your
chance of getting the flu, and of
getting seriously ill if you do.
At that same counter, the pharmacist
asked Leon two more questions.
Leon answered both of them with a no.
Number five is thinking the flu shot is
the only one you need.
The pharmacist, a young woman with a
clipboard, asked Leon his age.
"77," Leon said.
Then she asked whether Leon had ever had
an RSV vaccine or a pneumonia shot.
"One needle a day," Leon said, with that
booming laugh that turned heads in the
cough drop aisle.
"That's my limit."
RSV is a respiratory virus that usually
gives adults mild, cold-like symptoms.
But some adults who get it develop
pneumonia, an infection in the lungs,
and the risk of severe RSV illness rises
with age.
The CDC recommends an RSV vaccine for
everyone 75 and older.
Between 50 and 74, it's recommended for
adults at increased risk of severe RSV.
That includes people with chronic heart
or lung disease, a weakened immune
system, or certain other medical
conditions, and people living in a
nursing home.
So Leon, at 77, qualified on his age
alone.
Ansel, at 74, leaned over the counter
and asked about himself.
The pharmacist told Ansel it depends on
his health and to check with his doctor.
Ansel wrote "RSV?" on the back of his
receipt. Marion filed the receipt.
The RSV shot differs from the flu shot
in one big way.
It isn't a yearly shot. It's a single
dose, and if you've already had one,
even last year, you shouldn't get
another one at this time.
Then there's the pneumonia shot, which
your pharmacist may call the
pneumococcal vaccine.
It's recommended for all adults 50 and
older.
That shot is tied straight to the flu.
Having flu increases your risk of
pneumococcal disease, and pneumococcal
pneumonia is a serious flu complication
that can cause death.
You can get the pneumococcal vaccine
your provider recommends at the same
visit as your flu shot.
There's also this season's COVID
vaccine, the 2026 to 2027 version.
Current guidance recommends it for all
adults. It also asks each person to talk
over the benefits and risks with their
provider and make a personal decision.
That's four different shots with four
different rules. Nobody expects you to
keep all of that in your head. That's
what the person with your records is
for.
That night, Marion carried her accordion
file to the kitchen table, the one where
she keeps every receipt and every shot
record since the 1990s.
Ansel had been sure he'd never had a
pneumonia shot. Marion found the record
in about 2 minutes, from the year he
turned 65.
Ansel studied it for a long time and
said nothing, which in the Brookes house
counts as an apology.
Marion's own list had one blank, and she
circled it in pencil for her next
checkup.
Leon's list, if he'd made one, would
have been mostly blanks.
Yours doesn't need an accordion file,
just the shots you remember and the
years, so your pharmacist can tell you
which you're due. And if one is missing,
it usually takes one short visit to fix.
Leon walked out of the drugstore that
day with a single bandage on his arm.
3 days later, Leon walked into the
church fellowship hall for Thanksgiving
dinner.
Number four is letting the germs come to
the table with you.
Every Thanksgiving, the little white
church on Lake Street sets up long
folding tables in the fellowship hall.
Paper tablecloths, a buffet of roasters,
and about 80 people from all over town.
Ansel, Marion, and Leon have eaten there
together [music] for years.
Before dinner, Marion stopped in the
church kitchen [music] and washed her
hands at the big steel sink.
Ansel washed his, too,
mostly because Marion was watching.
Leon went straight for the buffet.
Leon shook a dozen hands on his way
across the hall.
Then he used the same stuffing spoon
everybody else had used.
Leon sat down across from a family with
a little boy who coughed into his hand
all through the meal.
Between the turkey and the pumpkin pie,
Leon rubbed his eyes and buttered a roll
with that same hand.
Flu mostly spreads through droplets in
the air when people with flu cough,
sneeze, or talk. It can spread from up
to 6 ft away.
Less often, you pick it up from a
surface, like a serving spoon or a
doorknob, and then touch your mouth,
your nose, or your eyes.
Two more facts change how you see a
holiday table.
People with flu can spread it starting
about a day before they feel sick.
And young children can stay contagious
longer than adults.
So, the cough across the table is only
part of it.
The warm handshake from someone who
feels perfectly fine can carry it, too.
Marion's habit at the church sink is the
textbook one.
Wet your hands, lather the backs,
between your fingers and under your
nails, and scrub for at least 20
seconds.
That's humming Happy Birthday twice,
start to finish. Then rinse, and dry
with a clean towel.
When you cough or sneeze, use a tissue
or your sleeve, not your hand, and throw
the tissue away.
That keeps your own germs off the next
serving spoon.
On the way out at the coat rack by the
fellowship hall door, Marion held out
her little bottle of hand sanitizer.
Leon looked at it, laughed his booming
laugh, and zipped up his windbreaker.
"Coach's hands," Leon said. "40 years of
sweaty footballs. Nothing gets through
these." Marion tucked the bottle back
into her purse without a word. Ansel
held the door, and the three of them
walked out into the cold.
When there's no sink nearby, use a hand
sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol. The
label tells you.
Then keep your hands away from your
eyes, nose, and mouth because that's the
doorway the virus uses.
And if your grandkids are coming for the
holidays and one of them wakes up with a
fever and a cough, you're allowed to
change the plan.
Avoiding close contact with people who
are sick is one of the simplest ways to
stay well.
A video call this week and a big hug
next week is still a holiday.
Tonight, put a small bottle of hand
sanitizer in your coat pocket and
another one by your front door. Before
you eat with a crowd, wash at the sink
and keep your hands off your face until
the dishes are cleared. You don't have
to skip the holidays to do any of this.
20 seconds at a sink still leaves plenty
of time for pie.
Leon didn't wash his hands once that
afternoon.
Two days later, the chill arrived.
Number three is riding it out at home
instead of calling early.
On Saturday afternoon, Leon was in his
garage putting new line on his ice
fishing reels.
The chill hit Leon like a bucket of lake
water.
Within an hour, [music] he had a fever,
aches in every muscle, and a dry cough.
Flu symptoms [music] usually come on
suddenly, and Leon's came on right on
schedule, about two days after that
dinner.
Leon thought he knew exactly what to do.
He pulled his maroon windbreaker on over
two sweatshirts, sank into his recliner,
and decided to sweat it out.
On Sunday, Ansel knocked on Leon's door
with a jar of Marian's chicken soup.
Leon took the jar through a crack in the
door.
"Don't come in," Leon said. "I'll be
fine by Tuesday." From then on, Ansel
called Leon every evening at 6:00.
If you said wait at the beginning,
you're in Leon's company, and plenty of
people would agree with you. Most people
with flu have a mild illness and don't
need medical care.
But the CDC draws a clear line at 65.
People 65 and older should call their
health care provider right away if they
get flu symptoms.
The reason is a group of prescription
medicines called antivirals.
They fight the flu virus itself.
Antibiotics don't because antibiotics
treat bacteria, not viruses. And flu
antivirals aren't sold over the counter,
so the only way to get one is through a
call or a visit.
The CDC's own words on timing are short.
Antiviral drugs work best when started
within 1 to 2 days after flu symptoms
begin.
They can lessen symptoms and shorten the
time you're sick by about a day.
A day shorter may not sound like much.
The bigger reason is that starting early
can also help reduce some flu
complications.
When you call, remind your doctor that
you're in a higher risk group for flu.
Your age counts. So does diabetes, heart
disease, lung disease like asthma, or a
past stroke.
Think back to the last time you were
really sick.
How many days went by before you picked
up the phone? Keep that number in mind
for a moment.
Leon's number was four.
Leon waited through Sunday, Monday, and
Tuesday, coughing in his recliner while
the soup jar sat on the counter.
Every evening at 6:00, Ansel asked
whether Leon had called the clinic.
Every evening, Leon had a new reason.
They'll just tell me to rest.
I don't want to bother anybody on a
Sunday. It's only the flu, Ansel. On
Tuesday night, Marion stood on Leon's
porch with her phone in her hand and the
clinic's number already dialed. Leon
opened the door crack, blinking at the
porch light. Marion didn't argue.
She just held out the phone until he
took it.
On Wednesday morning, Ansel drove Leon
to the clinic, both of them in masks.
Leon didn't say a word the whole way.
A nurse swabbed Leon's nose. The test
came back positive for flu.
The doctor's first question was when the
symptoms started.
Leon had to count backward on his
fingers, and he still wasn't sure
whether it was Saturday or Friday.
By then, it was almost 4 days since
Leon's first chill, well past that best
window.
His doctor prescribed an antiviral
anyway.
Starting later can still help,
especially for people at higher risk of
serious flu complications.
Not everyone with flu runs a fever, so
don't let a normal thermometer talk you
out of calling.
Most people who catch the flu get better
at home.
The early call simply keeps your options
open while they work best.
By Thursday morning, Leon felt better.
That's where his next mistake began.
Number two is treating the first good
day as the finish line.
On Thursday morning, Leon woke up
without the chills.
Leon took a fever reducer from the
bathroom cabinet and swallowed it with a
cup of coffee.
That coffee was about the only thing
Leon had drunk since Wednesday.
By 10:00, Leon felt like himself. So,
Leon drove downtown to the bait shop to
buy a new blade for his ice auger. Leon
chatted at the counter for half an hour,
>> [music]
>> shook the owner's hand, and coughed
twice into his fist while he paid.
Two things were wrong with that trip.
The first was the pill.
A fever reducer can hide a fever.
That's why the CDC's rule for getting
back to your normal activities has two
parts.
First, your symptoms are getting better
overall.
Second, you've had no fever, and you
haven't taken anything to bring a fever
down.
Both have to be true for at least 24
hours.
By that rule, Leon's good day counted
for zero hours.
His fever hadn't gone away.
It was just sitting under the pill.
Even after you meet that rule, take
extra care around other people for the
next 5 days.
That can mean a well-fitted mask, more
hand washing, and a little distance.
You can still spread the virus while you
feel better. And if the fever comes back
after you've gone out, the clock starts
over. Back home and away from others.
The second problem was the coffee. Many
people with flu don't feel like eating
and Leon had stopped drinking much of
anything else. The advice for anyone
sick with flu is plain. Rest and drink
plenty of fluids like juice and water,
but not alcohol.
Rest isn't laziness, either. Your body
is busy fighting off the flu. The fever
usually goes away in 3 to 4 days, but
other flu symptoms get better over 7 to
14 days. The cough and the tired feeling
can hang on for weeks.
And sometimes the fever comes back.
That sentence is the one to remember.
A fever or a cough that comes back after
it seemed to leave isn't just a slow
recovery. It sits on the emergency list.
And it's waiting at number one.
Leon got home from the bait shop around
noon.
Leon sat down in his recliner, still in
his windbreaker, and didn't get up again
until dark. His water glass on the side
table stayed empty. If a good morning
ever fools you like Leon's did, give it
the full 24 hours, no fever and no fever
reducer, before you go out. The first
good day really is a good sign. It just
isn't the last day.
On Friday evening at 6:00, Ansel made
his usual call.
This time, the phone rang eight times.
Ansel stood in the Brooks kitchen and
counted every ring. By the fifth, Marion
had set down her dish towel.
Number one is waiting for morning when
the flu sends an emergency sign.
When Leon finally answered, his voice
was thin.
Leon stopped every few words to cough.
Ansel didn't like the sound of it and
Marion was already reaching for her
coat. Ansel and Marion walked down Birch
Lane in the dark, past the first real
snow banks of the winter.
Leon opened his front door leaning on
the wall.
Then Leon lowered himself back [music]
into his recliner, breathing hard after
12 steps.
Leon's cough was deeper than Saturday's.
The fever was back,
>> [music]
>> and Leon's forehead felt hot under
Marion's hand.
That's when Leon asked Ansel what day it
was. 10 minutes later, Leon asked again.
Marion asked one more question.
When had Leon last used the bathroom?
Leon thought about it for a long moment.
This morning, Leon said.
I think.
Ansel, Marion said, call 911.
Leon waved his big hand toward the dark
window.
It's night time, Marion. I'll call the
clinic in the morning. In flu season,
that may be the most dangerous sentence
a person can say.
Marion knew what she was looking at,
because she'd taped the list inside her
kitchen cabinet in October.
The CDC lists emergency warning signs of
flu complications.
People with these signs should get
medical care right away.
Here's that list for adults in plain
words. Trouble breathing or shortness of
breath. Pain or pressure in the chest or
belly that won't go away. Dizziness that
won't go away. Confusion or being hard
to wake up. Seizures. Not urinating.
The list goes on.
Severe muscle pain. Severe weakness or
being unsteady on your feet. A fever or
cough that gets better,
then comes back or gets worse.
And any long-term condition you have,
like diabetes or heart disease, getting
worse.
That night, Leon had four of those signs
at once.
Any one of them is enough.
For any of these signs, the place to go
is the emergency room. With Leon short
of breath and confused, Marion wanted a
crew with oxygen, not a ride in the
backseat.
That pattern of better then worse has a
reason behind it.
While your body fights the flu, you can
pick up a second infection such as
pneumonia. A fever or cough that goes
away and then comes back may be a sign
of exactly that.
There's one more sign on that list that
deserves its own minute.
Pain or pressure in your chest.
In a study from Ontario, Canada, the
risk of a heart attack was about six
times higher in the week after a
confirmed flu infection.
The link was strongest in older adults.
So, in the week after the flu, take
chest pressure or squeezing seriously
and pain in your jaw, neck, back, or
arms.
The same goes for sudden shortness of
breath, feeling faint, or breaking into
a cold sweat.
For any sign of a heart attack, the
instruction is to call 911 immediately.
Ansel made the call from Leon's kitchen
phone, reading Leon's house number off
the mail on the counter.
Marion sat on the arm of the recliner
and held Leon's hand.
Red lights flashed across the snowbanks
on Birch Lane.
The ambulance crew put an oxygen mask
over Leon's goatee right there in his
recliner.
Ansel rode along. Marion packed Leon's
reading glasses, his pill bottles, and
his phone charger into a grocery bag and
followed in the car.
At the hospital, a chest x-ray showed
pneumonia. Leon spent five nights there
with oxygen, fluids, and medicine for
the infection. By the third night, Leon
was complaining about the gelatin, which
the nurses took as a very good sign.
On the fourth day, Ansel sat by Leon's
hospital bed with two cups of coffee.
Leon was quiet for a while. Then Leon
said, "Saturday. I should have called
Saturday."
Ansel didn't say a word. He just handed
Leon his coffee.
On his last morning in the hospital,
Leon asked a nurse for a pen.
Leon copied the warning signs himself in
big block letters, the way he used to
draw up plays on a locker room
chalkboard. He pressed so hard the
letters came through on the next page.
Ansel watched him underline the words
comes back twice.
By the middle of January, the ice was
thick enough for fishing houses.
Once Leon had fully recovered, he went
back to the drugstore counter on Main
Street and asked for the two shots he'd
turned down. "77,"
Leon told the pharmacist before she
could ask. Ansel took his receipt with
"RSVP" on it to his own checkup, and his
doctor answered it in 2 minutes.
Then Leon and Ansel spent a Saturday in
Leon's ice house with a thermos of
coffee and a jug of water.
They caught nothing at all, and Leon
laughed about it the whole way home.
If you're 65 or older and flu symptoms
start, call your doctor right away, that
same day, and ask whether an antiviral
is right for you. Go to the emergency
room or call 911 for trouble breathing,
chest pain or pressure, or new
confusion. The same goes for not
urinating, severe weakness, or a fever
or cough that comes back worse. Day or
night, don't wait for morning.
None of this replaces your own doctor,
who knows your lungs, your heart, and
your list of pills.
Bring your shot list to your next visit
and let your doctor fill in the blanks.
Tonight, copy that emergency list in big
letters and tape it inside a kitchen
cabinet door. Then tell me in the
comments, now that you've seen Leon's
week, call or wait? And send this to the
friend who always says they'll just
sweat it out.
On Birch Lane, Leon's maroon windbreaker
hangs by his front door.
Inside his kitchen [music] cabinet,
taped next to his coffee mugs, is a list
in big block letters.

Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

records.text:
Do your calves ache when you walk after 70, then ease when you stop? That can be peripheral artery disease (PAD), not just age. The CDC says about 6.5 million Americans 40 and older have it, and six everyday mistakes make it worse.

On Birch Lane, Leon, seventy-seven, lays down his cribbage cards at Ansel and Marion's kitchen table on a July night: his right foot has gone cold, pale and numb. That night really started six months earlier, on a long winter drive to Duluth. Through Leon's year, this story covers long trips and blood clots, checking your feet, the painless ankle test, why supervised walking is a first treatment for leg pain, why "just a few" cigarettes still count, and the two leg emergencies you should never wait out.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — Leon's foot goes cold
1:51 — Mistake 6: Sitting still for hours on a long trip
4:45 — Mistake 5: Never looking at your feet
8:03 — Mistake 4: Calling it just age
13:43 — Mistake 3: Stopping walking because it hurts
18:01 — Mistake 2: The "just a few" cigarettes
21:05 — Mistake 1: Waiting when a leg turns cold, or swells up hot

If you found Leon, Ansel, and Marion's story helpful, please like this video and subscribe to Ansel Senior Health so you never miss an episode from Birch Lane.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Ansel, Marion and their neighbors are illustrated characters. This channel shares general health education from published research, narrated with an AI voice. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

subtitles.plaintext:
At 20 to 10 on a Friday night in July,
Leon, 77, laid down his cribbage [music]
cards at Ansel and Marion's kitchen
table.
His right foot had gone cold and pale,
and Leon couldn't move his toes.
If you're over 70, your legs may [music]
know a quieter version. Halfway up the
block, a calf tightens, so you stop
[music] and pretend to admire something
until it lets go.
That ache can have a name, peripheral
artery disease, or PAD.
The CDC says about 6 and 1/2 million
Americans 40 and [music] older have it.
Six everyday mistakes make it worse
after 70.
The last one plays out in minutes, not
years. What to do when a leg suddenly
turns cold, and what Marion did next.
Right now, slip off your socks and lay
the back of a hand on top of each foot.
Does one feel colder than the other?
Compare the color of your toes, too. A
colder foot can be one sign of PAD.
When your legs ache on a walk, what do
you do? Push on or sit down?
Tell me in one word in the comments.
We'll come back to your answer at number
three.
Leon is Ansel's fishing buddy, a retired
high school football coach who lives at
the end of Birch Lane in a small
Minnesota lake town. Leon has a gray
goatee, a booming laugh, and a maroon
coach's windbreaker he wears in every
month of the year, January included.
Ansel, 74, is a retired railroad
signalman who still wears a tie every
day.
Marion, 72, keeps the calendar and every
receipt.
That July night really started 6 months
earlier in the back seat of Ansel's car.
Number six is sitting still [music] for
hours on a long trip.
In January, Ansel drove Marion and Leon
up to Duluth [music] to see the railroad
museum.
It's about 4 and 1/2 hours each way.
Leon rode in the backseat with his broad
shoulders wedged against the door and
his maroon windbreaker zipped to the
chin.
At the first rest area, Leon wouldn't
get out.
"I'm fine." Leon said.
"Wake me up in Duluth."
Your calf muscles help push blood back
up out of your legs.
When you sit still for hours, that help
mostly stops.
The blood in your leg veins moves more
slowly.
The CDC says anyone traveling more than
4 hours, whether by car, bus, train, or
plane, can be at risk for blood clots.
Most people who get one have other
risks, too, like older age, recent
surgery, a previous clot, or diabetes.
Clots in the deep leg veins are most
common in adults over 60.
Leon has type 2 diabetes.
He's had it for 11 years and he carries
his glucose meter in his windbreaker
pocket.
Marion had read up on long trips before
they left because Marion reads
everything before a trip. So, at the
second rest area, Marion didn't ask. She
opened Leon's door and held it.
Leon walked across the parking lot
toward the vending machines.
Halfway there, Leon stopped and studied
the big highway map on the wall for a
long time.
He rubbed the back of his right calf,
then walked on. Marion noticed and filed
it away with her receipts.
Back in the car, Marion taught the
simplest move there is. Stretch your
legs out as far as the seat allows, then
flex your ankles, pulling your toes up
toward you, and let them relax.
Leon did his ankle flexes for 20 miles,
mostly so Marion would stop watching him
in the mirror.
Ansel, behind the wheel, was excused.
On the drive home, Leon got out at every
stop without being asked.
At the last gas station, Leon walked one
slow lap around the pumps, then stopped
by the ice machine and rubbed that same
calf again.
Marion wrote the date on the back of a
gas receipt.
Tonight, if a long drive or a flight is
coming up, plan the stops before you
leave. On any trip over 4 hours, move
your legs often, flex your ankles while
you sit, and take breaks to stretch your
legs.
Even on a long trip, the risk of a blood
clot is generally very small. These
moves cost nothing and take about a
minute.
What a clot in the leg actually looks
like, and what to do about it, comes in
number one.
Number five is never looking at your
feet.
In late [music] February, Leon bought
new insulated work boots at the farm
supply store on Main Street. They were
stiff [music] as cardboard.
Leon wore them to shovel his driveway
that same afternoon.
By evening, the back of Leon's right
heel had a blister the size of a dime.
Leon didn't feel much, and he didn't
look.
Leon found it 4 days later when his sock
stuck to his heel.
2 weeks after that, Leon was still
limping a little when he came over for
coffee.
Marion noticed.
In the Brooks mudroom, Leon finally
pulled off his sock and showed them.
The blister had opened into a raw pink
sore, and it hadn't closed at all.
Then Marion looked closer and saw more.
Leon's right foot was paler than his
left and cooler under her hand.
The skin on his right shin was smooth
and shiny with hardly a hair on it. His
right big toenail looked like it hadn't
grown since Christmas.
Each of those can be a sign of poor
blood flow.
One foot colder than the other. A foot
or leg turning pale or blue. Toenails
and leg hair that stopped growing.
Smooth, shiny skin.
And sores on the legs or feet that don't
heal.
The sore was the part that worried
Marion most.
When not enough blood reaches your legs
and feet, a sore or an infection has a
hard time healing.
With nerve damage from diabetes, you may
not even feel a blister forming.
Federal diabetes guide set a clear line.
Call your healthcare provider right away
if a cut, blister, or bruise on your
foot doesn't start to heal after a few
days. Leon's heel was 2 weeks past that
line.
Ansel walked railroad track in every
kind of weather for 40 years. On the
signal crew, the rule was simple.
You check your feet at the end of every
shift because a blister you find tonight
is one you can still fix.
The same habit works for anyone. Check
your feet each evening when you take off
your shoes and check between your toes.
If bending over is hard, use a mirror or
ask someone else to look. You're looking
for cuts, sores, red spots, swelling,
blisters, and warm spots.
And never go barefoot. Wear shoes and
socks or slippers even inside the house.
There's a doctor's half of the habit,
too.
Ask to have your feet checked at every
visit with your primary care provider.
If you have PAD and diabetes, your
doctor should examine your feet twice a
year.
Leon called the clinic first thing the
next morning from the Brooks kitchen
phone with Marion standing right beside
it.
Tonight, when you take off your shoes,
look at both feet in good light, soles
and between the toes included.
Then lay a hand on each foot and
compare.
Most nights you'll find nothing at all,
and that's the point. A 2-minute look is
how a small sore gets caught while it's
still small.
What Leon said at that appointment and
what he almost didn't say is number
four.
Number four [music] is calling it just
age.
Go back to early February. Most
mornings, Ansel and Leon walked the path
around [music] the lake to the bait shop
and back.
That winter, Leon started stopping.
Every few blocks, Leon would halt and
admire the ice fishing houses out on the
lake.
After a couple of minutes, he walked on
as if nothing had happened.
"It's my calf," Leon finally admitted,
rubbing the back of his right leg.
"It cramps up, then it goes away. That's
just 77, Ansel."
In 35 years of coaching, Leon benched
more than one player for hiding a sore
leg.
His rule was famous at the high school.
"You tell me, or you sit."
Ansel reminded him of it right there on
the lake path. Leon let out that booming
laugh and changed the subject to
walleye.
Doctors have a name for Leon's walk.
Pain, aching, heaviness, or cramping in
your legs that comes when walking or
climbing stairs and goes away after rest
is called intermittent claudication.
It's the most common symptom of PAD.
The pain is often in the calf.
It can also be in the buttock, the
thigh, or the foot. At first, it may
show up only when you walk uphill, walk
faster, or walk farther. Over time, it
comes sooner with less walking.
Leon understood the reasoning coaching
terms. For 35 years, he watered the
practice field with a garden hose. Step
on that hose halfway, and a trickle
still gets through. Ask for a full
spray, and the pinch won't let it
through. So, the far end of the field
stays dry.
Your leg arteries can narrow in a
similar way.
A waxy plaque made of fat, cholesterol,
and other material builds up on their
inner lining.
Sitting still, your calf gets enough
blood through the narrowed artery. When
you walk, the muscle asks for more. The
artery can't deliver it, and the muscle
aches until you rest.
That's also why this ache quits so
neatly.
PAD pain is often brought on by leg
exercise and quickly relieved by rest
with no need to change position.
Then came the March appointment, the one
about the heel.
Leon planned to talk about the blister
and nothing else.
In the truck, Ansel said,
"Tell her about the walks." Leon looked
out the window.
"It's age, Ansel."
In the exam room, Leon took off both
boots and both socks before anyone
asked.
Marian had told him to. "Bare feet in
the exam room, remind your care team to
check them."
His doctor cleaned and dressed the heel.
Then she pressed two fingers on top of
each of Leon's feet and behind each
ankle feeling for a pulse. On the left
foot, she found it right away. On the
right, she had to search.
That's when Leon, studying the ceiling,
mentioned his calf.
"It's probably just age," Leon said. His
doctor didn't think so. She ordered an
ankle test for that same afternoon.
It's called the ankle-brachial index. A
nurse wrapped blood pressure cuffs
around both of Leon's arms and both
ankles while he lay on the exam table.
She used a small ultrasound device to
pick up the blood flow. The test is
painless.
It compares the blood pressure in your
ankle with the blood pressure in your
arm.
A normal reading is one or a little
above. .9 or below is abnormal. Leon's
left leg came back normal. His right leg
came back at .7.
You may have heard that this test isn't
recommended. The National Screening
Panels' words are narrower than that.
The USPSTF
Preventive Services Task Force concludes
that the current evidence is
insufficient to assess the balance of
benefits and harms of screening for PAD
with this test. That conclusion covers
adults without symptoms.
For people 65 and older with no
symptoms, the national heart guidelines
are a little warmer and call screening
with the test reasonable.
With no symptoms, it's a fair question
to talk over with your doctor.
Symptoms change the picture. Leon had an
ache on every walk, a weak pulse, and a
sore that wouldn't heal. For someone
with symptoms like his, the resting
ankle test is the recommended way to
make the diagnosis.
So, Leon had PAD. The next fact made
Leon sit up straight.
If you have PAD, you probably have
plaque build-up in your other arteries,
too, including the arteries in your
heart and brain.
His doctor talked with Leon about
medicines to protect those arteries.
If you've been told you have PAD, ask
your doctor or pharmacist whether any
medicine for your heart and arteries
fits you.
Think back to your last real walk. How
far did you get before your legs wanted
you to stop? If a number of blocks came
to mind, keep it there because number
three is about that number.
Tonight, write three things on a card
where the ache is, how far you walk
before it starts, and how long you rest
before it goes.
At your next visit, say it in one plain
sentence. My calf hurts when I walk and
it stops when I rest. Not every sore leg
is PAD and this test is quick and
painless. Saying it out loud is how you
find out which kind of ache you have.
Number three is stopping [music] walking
because it hurts.
Leon's first plan after the diagnosis
was simple.
If walking hurt his leg, he'd quit
walking.
Leon parked himself in the recliner by
his front window. For 3 weeks, Ansel
walked to the bait shop alone.
If you said sit down at the start,
you're in good company.
It feels like the careful choice.
The research points the other way.
In 2024, the American Heart Association
and the American College of Cardiology
published new national guidelines for
PAD, written with vascular surgeons and
other specialists. For people with leg
symptoms, supervised exercise therapy is
recommended to improve walking, daily
function, and quality of life. For calf
pain that limits you, it or a structured
program like it should be offered as a
first treatment.
The surprising part is how it works.
The evidence is strong that walking on
and off into mild or moderate pain is
what improves walking the most.
And plain advice to go out and walk
hasn't been shown to work on its own.
Supervised means a real program. It
takes place in a hospital or outpatient
clinic, often in the cardiac rehab room
with trained staff watching.
Each hour-long session holds at least 30
to 45 minutes of training. Sessions come
at least three times a week for at least
12 weeks.
On a treadmill, you walk until the calf
pain gets moderate.
Then you rest until it eases and you
walk again.
Each week, the staff asks a little more
of your legs.
Two more facts matter.
Medicare and most commercial insurance
companies now cover this therapy for
people with claudication.
Yet in the United States, only about 2%
of patients get referred.
Leon's doctor wrote him that referral.
The program ran in the cardiac rehab
room at the hospital in the next town,
Monday, Wednesday, and Friday mornings.
Ansel drove him every time, the way you
drive a man whose excuses you know by
heart.
On the first morning, a young exercise
specialist set Leon's treadmill at a
slow pace.
About 4 minutes in, his right calf began
to burn.
"Keep going until it's a five out of
10," she said. "Then sit."
So Leon walked, sat, and walked again.
To a coach who'd spent a lifetime
telling players to rest a sore leg, it
felt backward.
Marion kept score. On the red calendar
in the Brooks' kitchen, she wrote down
how many minutes Leon walked before his
first rest, every session.
The first week said four, four, and
five. Leon pretended not to care and
checked the calendar every time he came
over for coffee.
By the last week of May, the numbers in
Marion's neat handwriting said 11, 12,
and 12.
By week six, Leon was walking longer
before the ache arrived.
By week 12, in June, Leon walked the
lake path to the bait shop with Ansel.
He stopped only once to actually look at
a loon.
Remember the number of blocks from a
minute ago?
In a program like this, that's the
number the staff works to push up, a
little at a time.
Not everyone lives near a hospital
program. Structured programs at home or
in the community work, too, planned by a
health professional, often with a coach
or an activity monitor.
Home sessions usually last 30 to 50
minutes, working up to at least 30
minutes of continuous walking.
For people screened for other heart
problems first, supervised exercise has
an excellent safety record.
Tonight, if your calves ache on walks,
write one question for your next visit.
Is a supervised exercise program for my
legs right for me, and is it covered?
Don't start pushing into leg pain on
your own before your doctor has checked
you. For this kind of ache, the first
treatment is walking, done the right
way.
Number two [music] is the just a few
cigarettes.
Leon started smoking at 17 [music]
on his first summer job.
Over 60 years, he'd cut down to four a
day on his front porch, never in the
house.
Leon figured four barely counted.
Ansel knows the habit. He smoked for 6
years on the railroad, and he still
remembers how hard quitting was.
Smoking is the main risk factor of PAD.
It damages your blood vessels, raises
your blood pressure, and causes
unhealthy cholesterol levels.
The nicotine also makes your blood
vessels tighten and reduces blood flow
in your legs.
Leon put it in coaching terms.
"So, my hose is already pinched," Leon
said. "And every cigarette stands on it
a little harder."
Smoking also makes PAD symptoms worse,
and Leon could feel that part on the
treadmill.
Those four cigarettes on the porch were
walking with him to the bait shop every
morning.
Cutting down feels like progress, but
researchers who pulled 141 studies
looked at heart disease and stroke in
light smokers. About one cigarette a day
carried roughly half the extra risk of a
full pack a day.
The bottom line is blunt. No safe level
of smoking exists for the heart and
blood vessels.
Aim to quit, not to cut down.
Doctors are supposed to bring it up at
every visit, and Leon's doctor did
exactly that.
Leon said it was like a referee who
throws the same flag on every play.
People with PAD who smoke should get
help building a plan to quit.
That plan includes medicines, along with
counseling or a quit program.
So, Leon made a plan.
He talked with his doctor and his
pharmacist about which medicine could
help him.
He called the National Quitline,
1-800-QUIT-NOW,
and Leon picked his quit day.
The fishing opener in May, when his
hands would be busy with a rod.
Leon kept his house and his truck
smoke-free, too. With PAD, it pays to
avoid secondhand smoke in every indoor
space, cars included.
On opening morning, Leon handed his
porch ashtray to Marion. She planted
marigolds in it.
The first week was the hardest.
Leon sat on his porch each morning with
his coffee and nothing for his other
hand.
He got grumpy around 10:00 every
morning, right when the second cigarette
used to come. Ansel brought over a bag
of sunflower seeds, and the two of them
sat there spitting shells into the
flower bed like a pair of teenagers.
Tonight, if you smoke, even a few, write
the quit line number on your calendar,
1-800-QUIT-NOW,
and call it tomorrow.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist whether a
medicine or nicotine replacement could
help you quit.
Quitting lowers the risk of PAD getting
worse, even after it's been found. It
isn't too late in your 70s.
Number one is waiting when a leg
suddenly turns cold or swells up hot.
Back to that Friday night in July.
Leon had been off cigarettes for 2
months.
He'd finished his 12 weeks, and he was
beating Ansel at cribbage.
Then his right foot went numb under the
Brooks' kitchen table.
At first, Leon laughed, that booming
laugh of his.
"Fell asleep," Leon said, and stamped
his foot on the floor.
It didn't wake up. Within a few minutes,
the numbness turned into a deep, hard
ache.
Leon tried to wiggle his toes, and they
wouldn't move.
"Give it 10 minutes," Leon said.
That was the mistake on the table.
Marion was already kneeling on the
kitchen floor.
She pulled off Leon's right shoe and
sock, then his left, and laid a hand on
each foot.
The left foot was warm. The right foot
was cold and nearly white.
Marion had read about this exact picture
back in March, on the government's heart
institute page. A sudden drop in blood
flow to your leg is called acute limb
ischemia, and it's a serious medical
emergency.
The instruction is plain.
Call 911 right away, because every
minute matters.
When these signs come on suddenly, get
help if any one of them occurs. You
can't feel or move your foot. Your leg
or foot hurts or feels like pins and
needles while you're resting. Or one
foot is paler or colder than the other.
Quick treatment may save your limb.
"Ansel, call 911." Marion said. Ansel
already had the kitchen phone in his
hand.
Doctors call it one of the most
treatable forms of PAD and one of the
most dangerous.
Recognizing a cold, painful, or numb leg
in time is crucial. And the person needs
to be seen on an emergency basis.
For a sudden blockage in a leg artery,
the answer is the emergency room or 911.
Don't wait to see if it passes.
The ambulance came down Birch Lane 11
minutes later.
Ansel rode along and Marion followed in
the car with Leon's maroon windbreaker
on the seat beside her.
At the hospital, the team started a
blood thinner through an IV right away.
That treatment is meant to start as soon
as this emergency is diagnosed.
That same night, a vascular surgeon
opened the blocked artery in Leon's
right leg.
Leon kept his leg. He spent 4 days in a
hospital bed complaining about the
coffee and asking who was winning the
cribbage game.
On his first morning in the hospital, a
nurse had Leon flex his ankles in bed
pulling his toes toward him. It was the
same move Marion had made him do in the
backseat in January. Lying in bed for a
long time raises the risk of a clot in
the veins the same way a long car ride
does.
That vein clot is the second leg
emergency and it looks almost like the
opposite of Leon's.
A cold, pale leg points to an artery. A
swollen, warm, red leg can point to a
vein. It's called deep vein thrombosis
or DVT.
It mainly affects the lower leg and
thigh, most often on one side of the
body.
The CDC lists the signs, swelling of
your leg or arm, pain or tenderness you
can't explain,
skin that's warm to the touch, redness
or discoloration of the skin. If you
have any of these, contact your doctor
as soon as possible.
The bigger danger is a piece of that
clot traveling to the lungs.
Some signs can't wait. If you have DVT
and develop chest pain, trouble
breathing, coughing up blood, or
fainting, call 911 or go to the
emergency room.
Before Leon went home, the vascular team
went over the warning signs with him
again and booked his first follow-up
visit.
Leon's first question was whether he
could keep walking.
They told him to get back to his program
once his doctors cleared him, and Leon
wrote that down himself.
That week, Marion wrote two lines on the
back of the hospital parking receipt.
Cold, pale, numb leg, call 911.
Swollen, warm, red leg, call the doctor
right away. And with chest pain or
trouble breathing, call 911.
Tonight, read those two lines out loud
and put them by your phone.
The word that matters is sudden.
A foot that has always felt a bit cooler
is worth bringing up with your doctor
soon. A leg that turns cold, pale, and
numb within minutes, or swells up hot
and red, can't wait for morning.
You'll probably never need those two
lines. If you ever do, they save the
minutes that matter most.
If you said push on at the start, Leon
would have agreed with you in January,
and sit down was his answer in March.
By June, he'd learned the third answer.
Walk to a moderate ache, rest, and go
again with a program behind you.
In August, Leon walked the lake path to
the bait shop with Ansel. Maroon
windbreaker on, nothing in its pocket
but the glucose meter. He stopped once
to watch a loon dive and then walked on.
If your calves ache on walks and ease
with rest, make an appointment soon.
Call right away if a sore on your foot
doesn't start to heal after a few days
or if one leg turns swollen, painful,
warm, or red. Call 911 for a leg that
suddenly turns cold, pale, or numb or
for chest pain or trouble [music]
breathing.
A video can't feel the pulse in your
feet.
Your own doctor [music] can and every
step here is worth taking to that
appointment.
Tonight, take off your socks,
>> [music]
>> compare your feet in good light, and put
Marion's two lines by your phone.
Then answer one question in the
comments.
The next time your calf [music] aches on
a walk, will you push on, sit down, or
ask about a program?
Share this with a friend who stops
[music] on every walk to admire the
scenery.
At the end of Birch Lane, marigolds grow
in Leon's old porch ashtray, [music]
and by the kitchen phone hangs a parking
receipt with two lines on it in Marion's
handwriting.

Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.
