Stool stuck and won't come out after 70? A hard, breath-held push can make you faint, and a sudden watery leak after days of constipation can be a sign of stuck stool that needs a same-day call.

One national study counted about 700,000 U.S. emergency room visits for constipation in a single year — and after 70, the urge gets quieter, so hard stool can sit low in the rectum longer than you think. Through the mornings of Lloyd Pruitt, a 78-year-old retired school bus driver, we walk through six things that keep stool stuck after 70: the morning timing, the way you sit, the breath you hold, the slowdown you can't feel, the home rescue that backfires, and the leak that looks like good news.

⏱ CHAPTERS

1:26 — #6: The morning bus your colon missed
5:39 — #5: Why sitting straight blocks the exit
9:28 — #4: Pushing hard vs. the soup breath
12:55 — #3: The quiet thirst slowdown after 70
17:00 — #2: The home rescue that backfires
20:55 — #1: The leak that looks like good news
24:42 — Lloyd's two-week morning reset in Erie
25:05 — Red flags: when to call the same day

If plain-spoken chalkboard guides like this help you stay independent at home, tap Like and Subscribe to Body After 70 so you never miss an episode.

subtitles.plaintext:
On the fifth morning, Lloyd Pruitt
thought his [music] trouble was over
because something was finally coming
out. It was a little brown water on his
pajamas. It was the [music] most
dangerous sign of his whole week.
Lloyd is 78, a retired school [music]
bus driver in Erie, Pennsylvania. For
four days, something hard had sat
[music] right at the exit, and it
wouldn't budge.
You may know that feeling. You sit, you
feel it [music] right there, low and
heavy, and you push until your ears
ring. That's stool stuck in the [music]
rectum, the last inches of the bowel.
If you're anywhere near Lloyd's age,
it's more common than people admit. One
national study counted about 700,000
emergency room visits for constipation
in a single year.
Six things keep stool stuck after 70.
We'll count down to that brown water
because it's the sign that means home
care stops today.
Try this in your chair. Sit up straight,
then lean forward and rest your elbows
on your knees. Feel your belly soften
and your bottom ease a little? Hold on
to that. It's number five.
When you're stuck, what's the first
thing you do? Push, wait, or reach for
something? Tell me in the comments. Just
one word, and keep your answer because
Lloyd tried all three.
Number six [music] is the bus your body
stopped catching.
For 31 years, Lloyd Pruitt drove the
same school bus route through the east
side [music] of Erie. His mornings ran
like a timetable. Up at 5:15, coffee at
5:30, the bathroom at 5:40, the bus out
of the lot at 10 after 6.
In all those years, Lloyd almost never
had trouble in the bathroom. He thought
that was luck. It was the timetable.
Then Lloyd retired, and the timetable
went with him. Now he sleeps until 9:00,
some days even later. He eats toast in
his recliner around 10:00 with the
morning game shows on. Nobody needs him
anywhere, and for the first time in his
life, his body has no idea what time it
is.
Your colon keeps a timetable, too.
Researchers who recorded the colon of
healthy volunteers around the clock
found it nearly still during sleep. It
woke up after meals, and it woke up
after getting up in the morning.
The big pushes, the ones that actually
carry stool down to the exit, came only
about four times a day. Most of them
came after waking up. Think of them as
the express buses. Miss one, and the
next may not come until after lunch.
Eating is what calls the next bus. When
food reaches your stomach, it sends a
signal down the line, and the colon
answers with a push. That's why
breakfast matters more than lunch or
supper. It lands on top of the morning
wave.
The people in today's stories are
illustrative examples. [music]
What happens inside them is real, and it
happens to a lot of us.
That Monday, an express bus pulled in
for Lloyd at about 20 to [music] 10:00.
He felt a faint nudge low down in the
middle of a game show. It was so faint
that he finished the show first. By the
commercial, the nudge was gone.
That faint nudge is the other half of
number six. When stool arrives in the
rectum, it stretches the wall, and the
stretch sends the message that it's time
to go. With age, that message gets
quieter.
In one small study, healthy people in
their 80s needed about half again as
much pressure inside the rectum as young
adults before they felt the urge. So, by
the time a man of 78 feels it clearly,
the stool has often been waiting a
while.
Lloyd's bus driving years had hidden
that change from him. He went at 5:40
because the clock said so, not because
his body shouted. Once the clock was
gone, the whisper was all he had, and a
game show was louder.
And waiting stool doesn't stay soft. The
bowel keeps pulling water out of it.
Every hour it sits, it gets drier and
harder. By Tuesday morning, the thing
sitting low in Lloyd was firmer than
anything he'd passed in years.
So, the fix for number six is to stop
waiting for a loud signal. Go when the
express bus runs. Get up at the same
time each day and eat breakfast at the
table, not in the recliner. Then sit on
the toilet soon after, whether you feel
much or not.
A warm drink can help set that scene. In
one lab test, a cup of regular coffee
woke up the colon about as strongly as a
full meal. Decaf and warm water did
less.
If coffee doesn't agree with you, a warm
cup can still become the first step of a
morning your body learns to expect.
Give it five quiet minutes, not 40.
If nothing happens, get up and go about
your day. A body takes a couple of weeks
to learn a new schedule, so a quiet
morning isn't a failure.
If you said wait at the start, number
six is yours.
Waiting worked when a clock did the
deciding. If your own mornings drifted
after you stopped working, the clock
that ran your body is gone, and you can
put a small one back.
Lloyd didn't know any of that yet. On
Monday, he missed the bus. On Tuesday,
he went looking for it the hard way.
Number five is sitting on the toilet the
way you sit at a steering wheel.
On Tuesday morning, Lloyd sat on the
toilet bolt upright. Back straight,
hands on his knees, eyes front. It's how
he'd sat for 31 years behind the wheel
with 40 kids behind him. He sat that way
for 20 minutes, and nothing moved.
There's a reason sitting tall works
against you.
Low in your pelvis, a sling of muscle
loops around the end of the bowel, like
a hand around a garden hose. When you
stand or sit up straight, that hand
keeps the hose bent.
That bend is useful. It's part of what
keeps you from leaking while you walk
around all day. But to empty, the hose
has to straighten out.
Squatting straightens it best. A modern
toilet seat puts your hips and knees
about level, so the bend stays partly
closed. You end up pushing stool around
a corner.
Surgeons at the Cleveland Clinic in
Florida watched this happen on X-ray.
They took 22 people who couldn't empty
during the test while sitting upright.
Then they asked them to lean forward,
like the famous statue called The
Thinker.
Leaning forward opened the bend wider.
And 11 of the 22, half of them, emptied
completely in that position.
It was a small study in people who
already had trouble, but the idea costs
nothing to try.
Bev Pruitt, Lloyd's wife, already knew
most of this. [music]
Bev is 75.
After her hip replacement 2 years ago, a
physical therapist taught her how to sit
on the toilet.
So, on Tuesday night, [music] Bev went
to the pantry. She came back with the
little wooden step stool she uses to
reach the [music] turkey platter, and
she set it down in front of Lloyd's
toilet.
Bev's therapist had taught her a simple
setup. A sturdy, low footstool, wide
enough for both feet that won't slide.
Feet about hip width apart on top of it,
so your knees come up a little higher
than your hips.
Then lean forward with a straight back
and rest your elbows on your knees, the
way you did in your chair a few minutes
ago.
Keep your heels down on the footstool,
not up on your toes. Lifting your heels
tightens the very muscles you're trying
to relax.
If you've had a hip replaced, like Bev,
ask your surgeon or your therapist how
high is safe for you. Bev's own
footstool is lower than most on her
therapist's advice.
One more thing. If you use a raised
toilet seat, the tall white kind with
handles that many people get after a
surgery, it lifts your hips even higher
above your knees, so the bend gets
tighter.
A raised seat is often exactly right for
getting up safely. A footstool under
your feet gives you back the knees up
shape while you sit. If your raised seat
is there because of a new hip, ask your
surgeon or therapist before you add one.
You don't need anything fancy. Bev's
stepstool cost $9 20 years ago. What
matters is that it's steady, it's wide,
and it stays put when you shift your
weight.
Lloyd tried it that night. Feet on the
stepstool, elbows on his knees.
He felt the difference right away.
Something shifted, lower and closer, but
nothing came.
That's the honest limit of a footstool.
It makes it easier to empty a stool
that's ready. It can't soften one that's
been drying out since Monday.
For most people, a footstool and a lean
make most mornings easier, and that's
worth a lot. But Lloyd was past most
mornings. So, on Wednesday, he did what
almost everybody does next.
Number four is holding your breath and
pushing.
On Wednesday morning, Lloyd gripped
[music] the edge of the seat. He took a
big breath, clamped his mouth shut, and
bore down hard. It's how he used to lift
a spare tire off the rack at the bus
garage.
Lloyd's face went dark red. A vein stood
out on his forehead. Then the edges of
the bathroom went gray, and he grabbed
the towel bar. It came halfway off the
wall. In the kitchen, Bev heard the
screws pop.
What happened to Lloyd has a name.
Pushing hard with your breath held is
called a Valsalva. It squeezes your
chest so hard that less blood gets back
to your heart for a few seconds.
Your blood pressure can dip while that's
happening. In some people, it can bring
on fainting or a heartbeat that goes out
of rhythm. And a faint in a small
bathroom can end with a fall onto a tile
floor.
There's a second problem with bearing
down. You need that sling of muscle to
let go, and a hard breath-held push is
the opposite of letting go.
Pelvic floor therapists, who train these
muscles for a living, say to avoid
straining and holding your breath.
They teach a slow breath out instead.
Bev learned it after her hip surgery,
and on Wednesday afternoon, she taught
it to Lloyd at the kitchen table.
Breathe in through your nose and let
your belly fill like a balloon. Then
breathe out slowly through pursed lips,
as if you're cooling a spoonful of soup.
As you breathe out, let your belly ease
gently forward. Don't squeeze down.
Lloyd laughed the first time.
"I drove a bus for 31 years," Lloyd
said, "and now I'm cooling soup on the
toilet." Bev made him do it twice more
until he stopped laughing.
You can try it right where you are. One
slow breath in, belly out. Now a long,
slow breath out through pursed lips.
Notice that your shoulders drop and your
lower belly softens instead of
clenching.
That soft, open feeling is exactly what
you want on the toilet.
A few slow breaths and a few minutes are
enough.
If nothing comes, stand up slowly with
one hand on the sink or a grab bar. Then
walk a lap of the house. Moving your
legs helps move your bowel, and another
wave will come along later.
Lloyd tried it that way on Wednesday
after lunch. Feet on the step stool,
elbows on his knees, three long soup
breaths.
He passed a few small, hard pieces, like
pebbles. It was the first thing in 3
days. It wasn't the whole thing, and
Lloyd could feel that, too.
Those pebbles are worth knowing about.
Small, hard pieces with the feeling that
you're not done can mean a bigger stool
is still sitting behind them. Keep that
in mind because it comes back at number
one.
That afternoon, Bev put the towel bar
back up with longer screws. Some fixes
are simple.
If you said push at the start, you're in
good company. Lloyd pushed. Almost
everybody does. The soup breath takes
the danger out of the hardest minute of
the morning.
Wednesday evening brought the next clue,
and Bev found it sitting on the kitchen
table.
Number three is the slow down you can't
feel.
Lloyd's water glass from lunch was still
full.
Bev looked at it, then at him.
Since October, Lloyd had been cutting
back on drinking after noon so he
wouldn't have to get up so often at
night.
And since his left knee started acting
up, Lloyd had quit his morning walk to
the corner store for the paper.
Now the paper came to the porch.
Lloyd went from the bed to the recliner
to the table and back again.
Neither change felt like anything at
all. That's what makes number three
sneaky. After 70, the thirst signal gets
quieter, too. Researchers who study
aging find that older adults feel
thirsty later and drink less to catch
up.
So, Lloyd wasn't ignoring his thirst. He
barely had one. And when your body runs
a little short of water, it holds on to
what it has. Less goes into the stool,
and the stool comes out harder and
drier.
Sitting still adds its own slow down.
Walking jostles the bowel and helps it
keep things moving.
Health guides for older adults list two
little activity as a cause of
constipation, and a daily walk as one of
the simplest fixes.
There was one more quiet change in
Lloyd's life. At his checkup in October,
he'd started a new pill.
Lloyd never connected it with the
bathroom at all.
Many common medicines, prescription and
over-the-counter, can slow the bowel.
You don't need to memorize which ones.
Ask your pharmacist whether any of your
medicines slow the bowel. Don't stop or
change any of them on your own. That
decision belongs to your doctor.
Bring the bottles or a list the next
time you pick up a refill.
Pharmacists answer that question all day
long, and it costs nothing to ask.
Think back to yesterday for a moment.
How many glasses did you drink before
supper?
Most people guess higher than the truth.
Keep that number in your head for a
minute.
Lloyd's fix came from Bev in a plastic
pitcher.
Now she fills it every morning and sets
it on the kitchen counter. Lloyd pours a
glass with breakfast, one mid-morning,
one with lunch, and one in the middle of
the afternoon.
Most of the pitcher is gone before
supper. So Lloyd's nights stay quiet,
and his days have enough water in them
to keep things soft.
It doesn't all have to be plain water.
Health guides for older adults count
water, juice, and other fluids. Lloyd's
morning coffee counts.
So does the soup Bev makes on Thursdays.
What doesn't work is waiting until you
feel thirsty, because at 78, that signal
comes late.
If your doctor has given you a fluid
limit for your heart or your kidneys,
that limit comes first. Ask how to
spread it across the day.
A glass, by the way, means about 8 oz,
roughly what a regular coffee mug holds.
Lloyd's rule is simple. If the pitcher
isn't half empty by lunch, he's behind.
The corner store got Lloyd back, too,
slowly.
10 minutes after lunch, just to the end
of the block and back at first, with his
cane on bad knee days.
On cold, eerie afternoons, he walks laps
of the upstairs hallway instead.
The walk isn't exercise in the gym
sense. Nobody's timing him. It's legs
moving after a meal when the colon is
already awake. Some days his knee
complains and Lloyd goes anyway, a
little slower.
If yesterday's number was low, move most
of your drinking earlier in the day and
add one short walk after a meal. Neither
one will soften a stool that's already
stuck. They make the next one softer and
that's how you stay out of Lloyd's week.
But on Wednesday night, the next stool
wasn't Lloyd's problem. The one already
stuck was. And on Thursday, he decided
to get it out himself.
Number two is the rescue that backfires.
By Thursday, Lloyd had had enough. He
hadn't passed anything real since
Sunday. His belly felt tight and sitting
down hurt. So, Lloyd did something a lot
of people do and never mention.
He put on a rubber glove from under the
sink and he tried to dig it out with his
finger.
It didn't work and it hurt. The skin and
lining just inside the opening are thin.
A fingertip or a fingernail can scratch
or tear them. When Lloyd looked at the
tissue, there was a streak of blood.
Then Lloyd remembered an old squeeze
bottle enema under the bathroom sink
left over from a test years ago. He used
it.
20 minutes later, a little water came
back out and nothing else.
So, Lloyd went looking for a second one.
His logic made sense to him. If one
didn't do it, the stool must need more.
That logic is exactly what makes this
rescue dangerous.
Bev found Lloyd in the hallway reading
the back of the box. It said not to use
more than one in 24 hours. Bev read that
line out loud twice.
That box was the salt type kind with
sodium phosphate on the label. The FDA
has warned that more than one dose of
these in 24 hours can seriously harm the
kidneys and the heart and can even be
fatal.
The FDA was clear on one more point.
Even if nothing has come out after a
single dose, don't use another one
within 24 hours. That's exactly the
moment Lloyd was standing in.
Doctors who reviewed constipation in
older adults add a warning about enemas
in general. Salt type and soap suds
enemas can throw off the body's salts
and damage the lining of the rectum.
When a doctor does use one, plain warm
water is usually the safest.
You may have seen videos telling you to
give yourself an enema whenever you're
stuck. That advice skips the most
important step, which is asking first.
Which kind, if any, and how often is a
question for your doctor or pharmacist?
The same goes for the strong laxatives
that make the bowels squeeze, the
stimulant kind. Health guides say those
are for severe constipation or for when
other treatments haven't worked. Ask
your doctor or pharmacist before the
first dose, not after the third.
If your answer at the start was reach
for something, this is your number.
When you're stuck and nothing is
working, the safest next step is a phone
call, not a stronger product.
But glove matters, too, in a different
way.
Needing a finger to help stool out is
one of the signs doctors use to
recognize a real bowel problem. That's
not something to keep doing quietly.
It's something to tell your doctor.
Most people never say it out loud, and
Lloyd was no different. He'd rather have
told Bev he'd backed the bus into the
principal's car.
But doctors hear this every week. The
words can be plain. Sometimes I have to
use my finger to get it out. That one
sentence tells your doctor more than 10
minutes of describing your diet.
Bev called the pharmacist, the one who
has known them for 20 years. The
pharmacist said what you'd hope, no
second enema, nothing stacked on top.
Call the doctor's office in the morning
if nothing changes.
Then the pharmacist added the part Bev
wrote on the back of an envelope. Call
right away if his belly swells up hard,
if he throws up, or if he can't pass
gas.
A stuck stool is common and very
treatable. The treatment just works best
in the right hands. And on Friday
morning, Lloyd's body sent the signal
that it was time for those hands.
Number one is the leak that looks like
good news.
On Friday, the fifth morning, Lloyd woke
up to a damp spot on his pajamas, a
little brown water. Then a little more
in the bathroom with cramps that came
and went.
Lloyd almost laughed with relief. "It's
finally moving." Lloyd called to Bev
through the door. "Now I've got the
runs." He had his grandson's basketball
game that night, and he figured a pad
and a seat near the exit would do.
Bev didn't laugh. Five days of nothing
and now water?
Bev had read about this on Thursday
night after she talked to the
pharmacist.
What was happening inside Lloyd was the
opposite of moving. The hard plug was
still sitting low, wedged in place.
Behind it, looser stool from higher up
was building. And some of that liquid
was seeping around the plug the way
water leaks around a cork.
Doctors call it overflow. It looks
exactly like diarrhea, so people treat
it like diarrhea. Doctors at the Mayo
Clinic wrote that it's often
misdiagnosed at first or made worse with
anti-diarrhea medicine.
Health references describe it the same
way. Liquid stool leaking or sudden
watery diarrhea in someone who's been
constipated can be the sign of a stuck
mass of stool behind it.
That's why the pad and the seat near the
exit were the wrong plan. A pad would
have hidden the leak. A dose of
anti-diarrhea medicine would have slowed
the bowel above the plug even more.
Either way, Lloyd would have spent
another weekend getting worse while
looking better.
So, Bev picked up the phone at 1 minute
past 8:00. Bev told the nurse three
things. Five days with no real bowel
movement, a hard-feeling low down, and
now liquid leaking around it.
The nurse said to bring Lloyd in that
day.
The nurse asked two more questions. Was
his belly swollen hard? Was he throwing
up? Bev looked at Lloyd. His belly was
sore, but soft, and he hadn't thrown up.
"If either answer had been yes," the
nurse said, "they'd have been talking
about an ambulance."
That afternoon, a gloved exam found it
in seconds. A large, hard mass of stool
stuck low in the rectum. Doctors call it
a fecal impaction.
The clinic staff cleared it the way it's
usually done, with warm water enemas and
careful work by hand, by people who do
this every week. Lloyd went home before
supper, sore and tired, and lighter in
the place that mattered.
Before Lloyd left, his doctor went over
a plan to keep it from coming back. The
timing, the water, the walking, and
which product to use, how much and for
how long.
Most people who've had an impaction need
a plan like that, and Lloyd's fit on one
page.
In the car, Lloyd was quiet for a long
time.
Then he said the thing a lot of people
feel.
"I almost didn't let you call," he told
Bev. "I didn't want to bother anybody
with something like this." Bev kept her
eyes on the road. "That's what they're
there for," she said.
He missed his grandson's game.
That night the phone rang, and Lloyd
heard about all 11 points, one basket at
a time.
That leak is number one because it's the
moment a bad week turns into a medical
problem. Left alone, an impaction can
block the bowel. In rare cases, it can
wear a sore into the bowel wall or even
tear it.
And it fools people for one simple
reason. It looks like the one thing
you've been waiting for.
Two weeks later, Lloyd's old bus alarm
goes off at 7:00. Coffee and oatmeal at
the kitchen table. Then the step stool,
his elbows on his knees, and the soup
breath.
Bev's pitcher waits on the counter, and
his cane hangs by the door for the walk
to the corner store. The step stool
never went back to the pantry. Bev
bought a new one for the turkey platter.
If stool has been hard to pass for
weeks, or you often have to strain, or
you've needed a finger to help, call
your doctor's office this week.
Call the same day for liquid stool
leaking after days of constipation. Call
the same day for blood in or on your
stool. And call the same day if you or
the person you live with turns suddenly
confused during a bad spell of
constipation.
If you suddenly can't pass stool or gas,
don't take a laxative. Call right away.
And call 911 if your belly is swollen
and painful, you can't [music] pass
stool or gas, and you're throwing up.
None of this is a diagnosis. Your own
doctor is the one to examine you and
[music] decide what's right for you.
Tonight, find a sturdy low footstool and
set it in [music] front of your toilet.
And now that you've met Lloyd, push,
wait, or reach for something.
Would you change your first answer?
Tell me in the comments. Just [music]
one word. And send this to the friend
who keeps an old enema box under the
sink, just in case.
In the Pruitt's bathroom in Erie, a
little wooden stepstool sits [music] in
front of the toilet. Above it, the towel
bar holds with longer screws. [music]

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
Stiff every morning after 70? Most morning stiffness is ordinary wear-and-tear arthritis that loosens in a few minutes. But new stiffness in both shoulders or both hips that lasts an hour or more can be a different condition, and it can travel with a warning sign for your eyesight. CDC survey data found that just over 47% of Americans 65 and older have been diagnosed with arthritis.

On Birch Lane, Ansel and Marion wake up with familiar rusty knees, while their neighbor Hector, seventy, suddenly can't lift his arms to put on his straw fedora. This story walks through six everyday morning-stiffness mistakes, from jumping out of bed to guessing about your medicines, and shows how to tell ordinary stiffness from the kind that needs your doctor. The last one is polymyalgia rheumatica, and the four signs (headache, scalp, jaw, eyes) of giant cell arteritis that should never wait.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — Hector can't lift his hat
1:32 — Mistake 6: Jumping straight out of bed
5:23 — Mistake 5: Resting all day because it hurts
9:10 — Mistake 4: Never timing your stiffness
12:27 — Mistake 3: Calling every ache "just age"
16:14 — Mistake 2: Guessing about your medicines
20:10 — Mistake 1: New stiffness in both shoulders or hips
26:00 — The wreath, and when to call

If you found Ansel, Marion, and Hector's story helpful, please like this video and subscribe to Ansel Senior Health so you can share the next Birch Lane episode with someone you care about.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Ansel, Marion and their neighbors are illustrated characters. This channel shares general health education from published research, narrated with an AI voice. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

subtitles.plaintext:
On a Monday morning in November, Hector,
[music] 70, couldn't lift his arms high
enough to put on his own straw fedora.
[music]
Hector blamed his birthday.
The real cause can travel with a threat
to your eyesight.
If you're over 70, you know the first
steps of the [music] morning, rusty
knees, a back like a plank, and a
bathroom that seems a mile away.
CDC survey data from 2019 through
[music] 2021 found that just over 47% of
Americans 65 and [music] older had been
diagnosed with arthritis.
Six everyday mistakes make [music]
morning stiffness worse or hide the kind
that isn't ordinary.
The last one [music] is Hector's, and it
matters most because of what it can do
to your eyesight.
Try this in your chair.
Lift both arms slowly up over your head
as if you're reaching for the top shelf.
Did both shoulders go up freely? Hold on
to that.
And this morning, how long did it take
before you moved easily? Minutes or
hours?
Tell me in the comments with one word.
Ansel Brooks, 74, and Marion, 72, live
on Birch Lane in a small Minnesota lake
town.
Hector lives across the street. He fixed
furnaces for 40 years, and he still
wears his straw fedora in November.
That November, all three of them woke up
stiff.
Only one of them needed a doctor.
Number six [music] is jumping straight
out of bed the second the alarm goes
off.
Ansel's alarm clock rings at 6:15,
[music]
and for 40 years he's answered it the
same way.
The railroad taught him that.
Ansel throws back the quilt, plants both
feet on the cold bedroom floor, and
stands up in one motion.
That November, his knees answered back.
Ansel walked down the hall to the
kitchen like a signal arm frozen in
sleet, one stiff jerk at a time.
Marion watched him from the coffee maker
and said he sounded like the back porch
steps.
Ansel's doctor told him years ago that
his knees have ordinary wear and tear
arthritis, the most common kind.
40 years of climbing signal ladders will
do that.
Joints like Ansel's stiffen when they
sit still for a while, and 8 hours in
bed is the longest you sit still all
day.
Heat increases blood flow, flexibility,
and how much pain you can tolerate.
Gentle movement does the rest.
So, the fix starts under the quilt.
The Arthritis Foundation suggests a few
small moves in bed before you get up.
Reach your arms above your head. Point
your toes, then flex them back. Roll
your ankles in slow circles, and gently
turn your head side to side.
You repeat those until you feel less
stiff.
It takes a few minutes, and nobody has
to see you do it.
Ansel tried it the next morning lying on
his back while the furnace kicked on.
Ansel pointed his toes, rolled his
ankles, and reached for the headboard
like a man stretching after a long
freight run.
Then he sat up, waited a breath, and
stood.
Marion tried the moves, too, on her side
of the bed.
Marion said rolling her ankles under the
quilt was like warming up the choir
before the first hymn. Nothing fancy,
just getting everybody in tune.
Warmth helps before the day really
starts, too.
A warm shower helps. So does an idea
Marion loved. Toss your clothes in the
dryer for a few minutes before you get
dressed.
So, Marion tossed Ansel's pale blue
shirt in the dryer while he showered.
Ansel came into the kitchen warm from
the collar down, and he admitted his
knees felt about 10 years younger.
One caution on that shower.
Keep the water from getting too hot,
particularly if you have heart problems.
Warm is the goal. You're loosening a
joint, not cooking it.
One more trick made Ansel laugh out
loud. Do the fiddly jobs the night
before. Lay out your clothes and pre-tie
your necktie. So, in the morning, you
can just slip it over your head.
Ansel has worn a tie every day since
1974
Stiff fingers at 6:15 had been turning
his mustard yellow knot into a 10-minute
job. So, that night, Ansel tied it
loosely at the kitchen table and hung
it, still knotted, on the bedpost. The
next morning, Ansel slipped the knot
over his head, snugged it up, and was at
the kitchen table before the coffee
finished.
Tonight, before you turn out the light,
pick your three moves for the morning.
Toes, ankles, and arms.
Lay out tomorrow's clothes where you can
warm them up.
Ordinary morning stiffness is common,
and a few slow minutes under the quilt
is often all it asks for.
Across the street, at 7:00 that same
morning, Ansel saw Hector out in the
driveway scraping frost off his truck.
Hector was scraping with his elbows
pinned to his sides in short, careful
strokes.
When Ansel waved, Hector waved back from
the hip, not over his head. Ansel
figured he'd slept wrong.
Number five [music] is resting all day
because it hurts.
The second week of November brought the
first real cold snap.
Marion's [music] knees and hips ached in
the mornings, the way they do every year
when the lake starts to freeze.
Most mornings, Marion walks with Joyce,
her walking partner, a loop
[clears throat] around the lake.
That week, Marion texted Joyce on Monday
that it was too cold.
Marion texted again on Tuesday and on
Wednesday, too.
Marion spent those three days in the
armchair by the front window with a
crossword and a heating pad. Resting
felt like the kind thing to do for sore
knees.
By Thursday, Marion was stiffer than
she'd been on Monday.
Getting out of that armchair took two
tries and a hand on the windowsill.
Joints need movement the way a furnace
needs air. The CDC says physical
activity is safe for people with
arthritis.
Activity can help reduce joint pain and
improve function and mood. So, be as
active as you can and try not to let
whole days go by without moving.
You don't have to do it all at once,
either.
Even 5 or 10 minutes at a time is
beneficial. Over a week, the goal for
most adults, including people with
arthritis, is at least 150 minutes of
moderate activity.
Joint-friendly choices include brisk
walking, cycling, light gardening,
dancing, tai chi, swimming, and water
exercise.
Add muscle-strengthening activity at
least two days a week. For older adults,
balance activities belong in the mix,
too.
On Thursday afternoon, Joyce knocked on
the Brooks' front door in her teal
windbreaker and white sun visor.
"If it's too cold for the lake," Joyce
said,
"it isn't too cold for the mall."
So, Marion and Joyce drove to the mall
in the next town and walked two slow
laps past the stores that hadn't opened
yet.
Marion's knees complained for the first
lap and went quiet on the second. That
night, Marion got out of the armchair on
the first try.
Friday morning was a different story.
Marion woke up with her knees sorer than
they'd been all week, and she told Ansel
the mall had been a mistake.
That's an honest part of starting.
When you start or increase physical
activity, it's normal to have some pain,
stiffness, or swelling.
Over time, that should get better. If it
doesn't, contact your health care
provider. Start slowly and pay attention
to how your body feels.
So, Marion went back to the mall on
Saturday, slower, for one lap instead of
two.
By the next Thursday, Marion and Joyce
were doing three laps and arguing about
which store had the best pretzels.
Joyce talked her into the Tuesday Tai
Chi class at the community center, too.
Ansel went along to the first class,
mostly to tease.
Ansel spent the hour moving slower than
he ever had in his life.
On the drive home, he admitted his knees
felt better than they had all week.
Think back over the last 7 days.
On how many of them did you walk for at
least 10 minutes?
Keep that number in mind.
Tonight, choose a 10-minute walk for
tomorrow, and pick a backup for a bad
weather day, like a hallway, a mall, or
a store with wide aisles.
Then do it at an easy pace.
Moving is how a stiff morning loosens
its grip.
But a few days later, it was Marion who
asked the question that changed Hector's
November.
And she had Ansel's kitchen timer to
thank for it.
Number [music] four is never timing your
stiffness.
Ansel spent his working life with
timers.
A railroad signal [music] has to change
on time, every time, or trains stop.
So, when Marion said his stiffness was
better, Ansel wanted proof.
On Friday morning, Ansel set the white
kitchen timer on the nightstand.
Ansel pressed start when his feet
touched the floor. He pressed stop when
he could walk down the hall without
touching the wall. The timer said 12
minutes.
That number means something.
Federal arthritis experts describe wear
and tear arthritis, called
osteoarthritis,
with joint stiffness that usually lasts
less than 30 minutes in the morning or
after resting.
Rheumatoid arthritis is different.
It's an autoimmune disease, where immune
cells inflame the inner lining of the
joints. Its stiffness lasts longer than
30 minutes, typically after waking in
the morning. The symptoms often happen
on both sides of the body with joints
that can be tender, swollen, and warm.
So, the clock gives your doctor a real
clue.
12 minutes points one way, 2 hours
points another.
You'll need your own finish line. So,
pick one simple thing.
Walking to the mailbox without a hitch.
Buttoning your shirt. Opening the coffee
can.
Stop the clock when that thing feels
easy.
Ansel timed himself all week and wrote
the minutes on a notepad stuck to the
refrigerator.
9 14 11 12.
Not once did his knees go past 15
minutes.
Later that month, Marion borrowed the
timer, too.
During that cold snap in her armchair,
her stiffness had taken about 20 minutes
to ease.
After a week of mall laps, Marion's
number was under 10.
On Saturday, Hector came over to bleed
the radiator in Ansel's den, the way he
does every fall.
Marion poured him coffee and asked, half
joking, how long Hector's stiffness
lasted in the mornings.
Hector took off his straw fedora and set
it on the kitchen table.
"Till lunch," Hector said.
Then Hector had to kneel at the
radiator.
He got down slowly, holding the edge of
the desk, and getting back up took him a
long time.
Ansel noticed that Hector didn't reach
up once to adjust his hat.
When Hector left, Marion stood at the
front window and watched him cross Birch
Lane.
Hector walked to his door like a man
carrying two full buckets of water,
shoulders low and stiff.
That answer, "Till lunch," bothered
Marion all weekend.
It should bother you a little, too,
until you hear number one.
Tomorrow morning, put a clock or a
kitchen timer by your bed. Start it when
your feet touch the floor and stop it at
your finish line.
Do it for a week and write the minutes
on a notepad on the refrigerator. If the
number runs past 30 most mornings,
especially with swollen joints, take
that notepad to your doctor. For most
people, the answer is short, and that's
good news you can actually measure.
Number three [music] is calling every
ache just age.
By the third week of November, Hector
had a list [music] of things he couldn't
do.
Hector couldn't comb the back of his
hair.
He couldn't reach the coffee cups on the
second shelf. Getting out of his
recliner took a rocking start.
Marion saw it first at the grocery store
on Main Street. Hector stood in the
cereal aisle staring at a box of oatmeal
on the top shelf.
Then Hector asked Marion, who was barely
5 ft tall, to reach it for him.
What bothered Marion most was how fast
it had come.
Just before the stiffness started,
Hector had carried the storm windows up
a ladder all by himself.
Then, over a few days, both shoulders
seized up, and then both hips.
Hector had an explanation for all of it.
"I'm 70," Hector told Ansel across the
fence.
"This is what 70 feels like."
This is a man who drove out at midnight
in January for any neighbor whose
furnace quit.
Hector never once told a customer that a
cold house was just what old furnaces
do.
But for his own body,
that was exactly his answer.
Ansel didn't believe it.
The National Institute on Aging says
some people put off going to the doctor
because they think pain is part of aging
and nothing can help. Its answer is
blunt. That's not true.
It's important to see a doctor if you
have a new pain.
And finding a way to manage pain is
often easier if it's addressed early.
Hector's pain was new.
His stiffness was new.
But Hector thought a doctor would only
shrug and tell him what he'd already
told himself.
So Ansel spoke Hector's language. For 40
years, Hector never fixed a furnace
without a service ticket. "Where's the
noise? When did it start? Does it come
and go?
What makes it worse?" "Write one for
yourself," Ansel said.
"That's a good way to get ready for any
visit.
Think about where it hurts and when the
pain started.
Ask yourself whether it comes and goes
and what it feels like. Notice when you
feel it, in the morning or the evening,
and what makes it better or worse. And
list what you've already tried,
including over-the-counter medicines, a
heating pad or an ice pack, and whether
any of it helped."
Your doctor may also ask you to rate
your pain from 0 to 10.
0 is no pain and 10 is the worst you can
imagine.
Some doctors ask you to keep a daily
diary of when the pain comes and what
kind it is.
That night, Hector sat at his kitchen
table and filled out a service ticket on
the back of an old work order.
Both shoulders, both hips. Started about
2 weeks ago over a few days. Worst when
he wakes up and it lasts till lunch.
Tried a heating pad and long hot showers
and neither helped much. Pain level, a
six.
Then Hector looked at what he'd written.
Hector had seen thousands of service
tickets. He knew this one didn't
describe a furnace that was just getting
old.
Tonight, write your own service ticket
for any ache that's new or that has
changed.
Where it is, when it started, how long
it lasts in the morning, and the number
from 0 to 10.
Most new aches have simple causes. A
clear ticket helps your doctor find the
simple ones fast and catch the others
early.
But Hector still didn't call his doctor.
He had a new theory and it was sitting
in his medicine cabinet.
Number two is guessing about your
medicines instead of asking.
Hector takes a cholesterol pill, a
statin, every night at bedtime.
On Sunday, his nephew sent him an
article saying statins cause muscle
aches.
Hector read it twice at the kitchen
table with his reading glasses pushed up
under the brim of his fedora.
On Monday, Hector told Ansel and Marion
he'd solved it. He was going to quit the
pill.
Hector had already set the bottle on his
window sill, apart from the others, like
a part pulled off a furnace for the
scrap bin.
Marion put down her coffee cup.
Ansel said,
"Hector, you wouldn't pull a part out of
a furnace because a customer read about
it online."
They had a point.
The government's drug guide for the
statin atorvastatin lists muscle pain,
tenderness, or weakness among its
uncommon but serious side effects.
Those mean call your doctor or get
emergency help immediately. And don't
stop taking it without talking to your
doctor.
There's a second half to that story.
Researchers pulled 23 large trials of
statins with about 155,000
people in them.
In the trials comparing a statin with a
dummy pill, about 27 in every 100 people
on a statin reported muscle pain or
weakness. On the dummy pill,
it was nearly as many.
So, more than 90% of those muscle
complaints weren't caused by the statin.
The small extra risk showed up mostly in
the first year of treatment.
Age matters here, too.
If you're older than 75, your provider
may prescribe a lower dose of a statin
to help lessen possible side effects.
That's a decision for you and your
doctor, made together.
Hector had taken the same pill for 6
years.
That didn't rule it out, but it made the
article a lot less convincing.
If Hector had started the pill last
month, it would have been a different
conversation.
So, on Tuesday, Ansel drove Hector to
the pharmacy on Main Street.
Hector stood at the counter with his
service ticket in one hand and the pill
bottle in the other.
Hector asked one question, "Could this
pill be doing this to my shoulders?"
The pharmacist read the ticket, then
read it again.
She asked Hector how long he'd been on
the pill, and he said 6 years.
Then she asked how long the stiffness
lasted each morning, and she frowned at
the answer.
"Don't stop the pill," the pharmacist
told Hector.
"Call your doctor today.
Both shoulders and both hips, that long
every morning, needs a look."
You can do what Hector did.
Bring your pill bottles to the pharmacy
counter or to your next visit and ask
whether any of them could be causing
your aches.
Pharmacists know side effects the way
Hector knows furnaces.
That evening, Marion lined up the
Brooks' own pill bottles on the kitchen
counter and wrote down when each one
started. Nothing on Ansel's side was
new. Marion's newest bottle was 3 years
old.
Tonight, line up your pill bottles on
the kitchen counter. On a sheet of
paper, write each medicine's name and
roughly when you started it.
If an ache began within a few months of
a new medicine, ask your doctor or
pharmacist about that one. Never stop a
medicine on your own. Most aches turn
out to have another cause, and asking is
how you find out which.
Out in the pharmacy parking lot, Hector
sat in Ansel's truck for a long minute
with the ticket on his knee.
"6 years on that pill," Hector said.
"I was ready to blame it because it was
easier than calling."
Then Hector called his clinic, right
there from the truck.
They gave him an appointment for
Thursday morning.
Number one is brushing off new stiffness
in both shoulders or both hips that
[music] lasts a long time every morning.
On Thursday, Ansel drove Hector to the
clinic because Hector couldn't turn far
enough to check his mirrors.
Ansel waited in the lobby and counted
ceiling tiles.
In the exam room, Hector handed his
doctor the service ticket.
His doctor read it, then asked Hector to
raise both arms over his head.
Hector's arms stopped just above his
shoulders.
That's the same move you made in your
chair at the start of this video.
The doctor had Hector's blood drawn for
two tests that measure inflammation in
the body.
The results came back the next day.
Both were high.
Hector had polymyalgia rheumatica.
The name sounds long, but it's an
inflammatory condition that causes
aching and stiffness in the shoulders,
upper arms, and hips, and sometimes the
neck.
Federal arthritis experts say it occurs
almost exclusively in people older than
50, typically in their late 60s and 70s.
Women get it more often than men.
Its stiffness is usually worse on
waking, and it usually lasts an hour or
more.
Hector's story fit the rest of their
description, too. It's typical to have
trouble raising your arms above your
shoulders. Getting up from bed or a
chair can be hard, and so can dressing
and brushing your hair. The symptoms can
come on quickly, usually over a few
days.
Some people also get flu-like symptoms,
like a low fever, weakness, a poor
appetite, or weight loss. Hector had
been skipping breakfast for a week and
hadn't mentioned it to anyone.
Without treatment, this condition
doesn't get better,
but a low dose of a steroid medicine
called prednisone can markedly ease the
symptoms, often within a day or two.
Treatment usually goes on for a year or
two, with the dose lowered slowly.
Hector took his first dose on Friday
morning.
By Sunday, Hector was combing the back
of his hair again.
On Monday, Hector stood in his front
hall and put on his straw fedora with
both hands.
That week, Hector borrowed Ansel's white
kitchen timer.
The first morning, his stiffness lasted
about 20 minutes. By Friday, it was
under 10. Hector taped each number
inside a kitchen cabinet, like readings
on a furnace he'd just repaired.
His doctor was honest about the rest.
Steroids can bring side effects like
weight gain, diabetes, or thinner bones.
So, the doctor would keep a close eye on
all three. And it's common for symptoms
to come back when the dose is lowered or
stopped. That's why every change in the
dose goes through the doctor.
But, the most important part of that
first visit was a warning.
And it's the reason this mistake is
number one.
About 10% of people with polymyalgia
rheumatica also have a related condition
called giant cell arteritis.
It's inflammation in arteries,
especially the ones on each side of the
head and scalp.
These are the signs Hector's doctor went
through, one by one.
A new headache, often around the
temples.
A scalp that's tender to the touch,
sometimes even before the headache
starts. Pain in the jaw, especially when
chewing.
And any change in vision, like double
vision or losing sight in one or both
eyes.
That list matters because of the eyes.
Federal experts say visual symptoms, if
left untreated, can lead to permanent
vision loss within hours or days.
With prompt treatment, that loss can
often be prevented.
For giant cell arteritis, steroid
medicines are often started even before
a biopsy is done.
When eyesight is at stake, doctors don't
wait for every test result.
Hector asked the question everyone asks.
What if one of those shows up at 2:00 in
the morning?
His doctor didn't hesitate. A new
headache, a sore scalp, or jaw pain
means call the clinic that same day, or
go to urgent care if you can't reach
anyone.
Any sudden change in your sight means
call 911.
That evening, Hector repeated the four
signs to Ansel and Marion over coffee at
the Brooks kitchen table.
Ansel said them back like a signal code,
and Marion made them both say them
twice.
Hector had none of those signs, but
Hector went home and did what he did on
every job for 40 years.
Hector took a roll of masking tape and a
marker, and he labeled the inside of his
medicine cabinet door. Headache, scalp,
jaw, call the same day. Eyes, call 911.
Hector's strip of tape is the most
useful thing on this list.
Polymyalgia rheumatica generally
responds well to treatment.
The real danger for Hector was the weeks
he spent calling it age, while a warning
sign could have been on its way.
If both your arms went up freely at the
start, good.
If you said minutes, that fits ordinary
stiffness.
If you said hours, that's worth a call
to your doctor, especially if it's new,
and especially in both shoulders or both
hips. And that number of walking days
from earlier?
Whatever it was, tomorrow can add one.
Tonight, learn Hector's four words.
Headache, scalp, jaw, eyes. If you're
over 50 and new stiffness in both
shoulders or hips lasts an hour or more
each morning, call your doctor this
week. Most morning stiffness is the
ordinary kind. Knowing the difference is
what keeps it that way.
Two weeks later, Hector stood on his
front step and hung a pine wreath high
on his door, while Ansel held the box of
hooks.
Hector reached both arms over his head
to hang it, then tipped his straw fedora
to Marion across the street.
At his checkup in December, his doctor
began lowering the dose slowly. Hector
told Ansel across the fence that 70 felt
fine after all.
Call your doctor this week for new
stiffness in both shoulders or hips that
lasts an hour or more each morning or
stiffness with swollen warm joints.
If you're over 50, call the same day for
a new headache, a tender scalp, or jaw
pain [music] when you chew. Call 911 for
any sudden trouble seeing.
None of this is a diagnosis. [music]
Your own doctor and pharmacist know your
joints and your medicines and every
[music] step here belongs in that
conversation.
Tonight, pick your three moves for under
the quilt [music] and set a timer by the
bed.
Then tell me in the comments
tomorrow morning, how many minutes did
[music] your stiffness last? And send
this to the friend who says every ache
is just age.
On Birch Lane, a pine wreath [music]
hangs high on the door across the
street.
Inside Hector's medicine cabinet, a
strip of masking tape waits for the
morning he might need it.

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
Over 70, your kidneys rarely give you a warning. The CDC estimates about 9 in 10 adults with chronic kidney disease don't know they have it.

On a gray January morning on Birch Lane, Agnes, eighty-one, asks Marion when her husband will be home. Two days of a stomach bug had slowed her kidneys almost to a stop, and nobody saw it. Ansel and Marion trace six everyday mistakes: a new supplement with hidden licorice root, trusting a good blood pressure reading, never asking for the two kidney tests (GFR and the urine albumin test, UACR), taking Advil or Aleve every day without asking, keeping your kidney number to yourself, and waiting it out at home when you're sick and barely peeing.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — Agnes's question in January
1:26 — Mistake 6: The supplement nobody saw
5:01 — Mistake 5: "My numbers are good"
9:01 — Mistake 4: Never asking for the two kidney tests
13:30 — Mistake 3: A pain reliever every day
16:56 — Mistake 2: Keeping your kidney number to yourself
20:27 — Mistake 1: Waiting it out when you're sick
25:46 — March on Birch Lane

If this story helped you or someone you love, please like this video and subscribe to Ansel Senior Health so you never miss our next episode on Birch Lane.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Ansel, Marion and their neighbors are illustrated characters. This channel shares general health education from published research, narrated with an AI voice. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

subtitles.plaintext:
On a gray Monday morning in January,
Agnes, 81, sat in her kitchen on Birch
Lane and asked Marion when her husband
would be home.
Agnes' husband died 6 years ago.
Over 2 days of a stomach bug, her
kidneys had slowed almost to a stop, and
nobody saw it.
If you're over 70, your kidneys have
probably never said a word to you.
You take something for your stiff hands,
you drink your coffee, and you feel
fine.
That silence is the trouble.
The CDC estimates that about 9 in 10
adults with chronic kidney disease don't
know they have it.
Six everyday mistakes put your kidneys
at risk after 70.
The last one is what happened in Agnes'
kitchen, along with the signs that can't
wait for morning.
Right now, try to say your own kidney
number out loud.
It's called your GFR.
If nothing comes to mind, you're like
most people, and number four shows you
how to get it.
And when your hands or knees ache, what
do you reach for first? Advil, Aleve, or
Tylenol?
Tell me in one word in the comments.
We'll come back to your answer at number
three.
Agnes is the widow two doors down from
Ansel and Marion Brooks in a small
Minnesota lake town. Her story starts
back in October with a package in
Ansel's mailbox.
Number six is starting a supplement
without showing anyone the bottle.
In the last week of October, the maples
on Birch Lane were nearly bare.
Ansel, 74, a retired railroad signal man
who still wears a tie every day, carried
a small cardboard box in from the
mailbox.
He opened it at the kitchen table with
his pocketknife.
Inside was a bottle of herbal joint
capsules.
Ansel had ordered them from an ad in the
back of his railroad retirees magazine.
The ad promised "knee comfort from
nature"
and it had a picture of a man about
Ansel's age hiking up a mountain.
Ansel's knees have ached for years, ever
since 40 years of climbing signal
ladders. So, Ansel swallowed the first
two capsules with his morning coffee and
called it progress.
Marion, 72, keeps the calendar and every
receipt in the house.
Marion picked up the bottle and put on
her reading glasses.
The label listed 14 herbs in print so
small it looked like a railroad
timetable. One of them was licorice
root.
Marion took a picture of the label with
her phone, the way she photographs every
receipt.
"What do these do to your kidneys?"
Marion asked.
"My kidneys are fine." Ansel said.
"How do you know?" Marion said. Ansel
opened his mouth, closed it, and drank
some coffee. He didn't know his kidney
number, either.
Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs,
each about the size of a fist.
In a single day, they filter about 150
quarts of blood.
Each kidney holds about a million tiny
filtering units. Many of the pills and
capsules you swallow leave your body
through those filters.
The National Kidney Foundation warns
that the government doesn't regulate
herbal supplements for dose, content, or
pureness.
Some herbal products can contain
ingredients known to cause kidney
damage. Licorice root and St. John's
Wort are two herbs considered high risk
for people with kidney disease.
Those last words, "people with kidney
disease", matter more than they sound.
Most of the people who have it,
remember, don't know they're in that
group.
In the first week of November, Ansel and
Marion stopped at the drugstore on Main
Street.
At the pharmacy counter, Marion held up
her phone and showed the pharmacist the
photo of Ansel's label.
One of a pharmacist's most important
jobs is to review all your medicines.
That includes the over-the-counter ones
and the supplements to catch unsafe
combinations and side effects. The
pharmacist read the list twice. She
suggested Ansel talk it over with his
doctor before he took any more.
Ansel put the bottle on the top shelf of
the kitchen cupboard behind the gravy
boat to wait for his checkup. He
grumbled that it had cost him $39.
Marion had the receipt, of course.
Tonight, gather every supplement,
vitamin, and herbal tea in the house
into one grocery bag.
Take that bag or a photo of each label
to your next visit or to your
pharmacist.
Much of what's in that bag may turn out
to be fine for you. The point is that
someone who knows your kidneys reads the
label before your kidneys do.
Marion's question,
"How do you know?" followed them across
the drugstore.
In the blood pressure chair by the
greeting cards sat Agnes with a cuff on
her arm.
Number five is thinking that good
numbers today mean healthy kidneys.
Agnes is tiny with white hair in a bun,
thick round glasses, and a lavender
quilted vest.
That afternoon, Agnes wore her wool coat
over the vest and her cookie tin rode
along in a tote bag.
The machine beeped. 126 over 74.
"See?" Agnes said, tapping the screen.
"Fine. So, my kidneys are fine, too."
Agnes has had high blood pressure for 22
years. She takes a blood pressure pill
every morning, and last spring her
doctor added a small water pill.
Her readings have been good for a long
time, and Agnes is proud of them.
Marion was proud of them, too.
But on the walk home, past the frosted
lawns, Marion kept thinking about those
22 years.
"Agnes, when did anyone last check your
kidneys?"
Marion asked at the corner.
Agnes thought about it for half a block.
"They take blood every year," Agnes
said.
"Nobody's ever said a word, so I suppose
they're fine."
The National Institutes of Health's
Kidney Institute is plain about it.
The most common causes of chronic kidney
disease in adults are diabetes and high
blood pressure.
And the longer you've had either one,
the more likely you are to develop it.
High blood pressure can damage blood
vessels and other parts of the filtering
system in the kidneys.
Diabetes does its harm through sugar.
High blood sugar can damage the kidneys'
filters.
Agnes understood it best in baking
terms. Each tiny filter works like the
fine screen in Agnes's flour sifter.
Water and waste pass through. The big
things, like protein and blood cells,
stay in the blood.
Years of hard pressure can damage that
screen.
Then some protein starts slipping
through into the urine.
The sifter lets through what it should
hold back.
The CDC's newest estimate puts numbers
on it. About one in three to have
chronic kidney disease. So do about two
in 10 adults with high blood pressure.
For adults with diabetes, it's about
four in 10.
So why don't people notice? Most people
in the early stages have no symptoms at
all. The signs you can see on your body
tend to come later as kidney function
goes down. Swelling in the legs, feet,
or ankles.
Itchy skin. Muscle cramps. Poor sleep.
Trouble focusing.
That's the honest problem with signs you
can see. By the time you can see them,
the kidneys have often been struggling
for a long time.
Agnes's reading at the drugstore told
her about her blood pressure that
afternoon.
It couldn't tell her a thing about the
screen in her sifter.
For many people, the only way to know is
a blood test and a urine test.
That evening, Agnes dug her last
printout out of the cookie tin where she
keeps her papers. She spread it on her
kitchen table under the lamp and ran her
finger down the columns.
It had a GFR line. It didn't have the
urine test at all.
Tonight, find your most recent blood
test printout or log into your patient
portal.
Look for a line that says GFR or eGFR.
It's often listed near a line called
creatinine. Write the number and the
date on your calendar.
If your blood pressure is in range,
that's real good news. And keeping it
there is one of the best ways to protect
your kidneys.
A good reading just can't stand in for
the tests.
Agnes slid the printout back into her
cookie tin.
The next morning, Marion wrote Agnes's
checkup on the red kitchen calendar in
the square for November 17th and
underlined it twice.
Number four is never asking for the two
kidney tests.
The week before Thanksgiving, the first
real snow came down on Birch Lane.
Marion drove Agnes to her yearly checkup
with the wipers going and Agnes's cookie
tin on her lap for the front desk.
In the waiting room, Marion wrote two
lines on an index card.
Blood test, GFR.
Urine test, albumin, the one called
UACR. Marion handed the card to Agnes
and Agnes held it the way she used to
hold a hymn number.
The list of who should be checked is
short. If you have diabetes, high blood
pressure, heart disease, or kidney
failure in your family, get checked for
kidney disease. With diabetes, get
checked every year.
For the others, ask your doctor how
often.
The blood test, GFR, estimates how well
your kidneys filter your blood. It's
often worked out from the routine blood
panel, so many people already have it
without knowing.
The urine test looks for albumin, the
protein that slips through a damaged
screen. It's one cup of urine.
It shows a different kind of damage than
the blood test does, which is why the
two belong together.
The cup is the one that gets skipped.
Researchers who pulled the records of
more than 2 million adults with high
blood pressure looked at a 2-year
stretch.
Only about four in 100 had the urine
albumin test. For people with diabetes,
it was about one in three.
Ansel had a saying for that from 40
years on the railroad.
You never wait for a signal to fail. You
test it on schedule while the trains are
still running fine.
So, Agnes asked,
in the exam room, she read the card to
her doctor word for word. Her doctor
ordered the urine test that same
morning. Agnes filled the little cup in
the clinic bathroom and handed it
through the window with a molasses
cookie.
You can say it the same way.
Has my kidney function been checked with
both the blood test and the urine
albumin test?
If the urine test hasn't been done, can
we do it today?
And if someone tells you your blood work
was normal, ask one more question.
Did that include the urine albumin test?
It's a fair question and a good office
won't mind it.
3 days later, Agnes's doctor called her
back in to go over the results. Marion
drove again.
Agnes's GFR was 51. Her urine albumin
was 70.
A GFR of less than 60 may mean kidney
disease.
A urine albumin above 30 may be a sign
of it, too. Agnes had both.
Her doctor didn't jump to a final
answer.
One test can be off, so she wanted both
repeated in about 3 months to be sure.
Marion wrote the date in her pocket
calendar right there in the exam room.
Her doctor also went over her blood
pressure pill. Its name ends in pril.
Two families of blood pressure medicine,
the ones ending in pril or sartan, may
slow kidney disease. If your tests show
kidney changes, ask your doctor whether
one of those fits you.
Then her doctor asked one more question.
"Are you taking anything for pain?"
Agnes said no. She was only thinking of
prescriptions.
"I don't feel a thing." Agnes told
Marion in the car afterward.
Marion patted the cookie tin on Agnes's
lap.
That was exactly why the cup had been
worth asking for.
That night, Ansel asked Marion for an
index card of his own.
His checkup was in February, and he
copied her two lines onto it in his
square railroad printing.
Then he taped the card to the cupboard
door, right in front of the joint
capsules.
Tonight, copy Marion's two lines onto a
card and clip it to your calendar for
your next visit. Blood test, GFR, urine
test, albumin. Both tests are ordinary.
One tube of blood and one cup of urine.
And the sooner you know you have kidney
disease, the sooner you can get
treatment to help protect your kidneys.
Think back right now.
When did you last fill a cup at a
checkup?
If you can't remember the season, keep
that in mind. By number two, that cup's
number has a job to do.
Number three is a pain reliever every
day without asking.
Thanksgiving week, Agnes's kitchen
smelled like cinnamon and lard.
Agnes was rolling out eight pie crusts
for the church supper, and her knuckles
ached with every pass of the rolling
pin.
Since August, Agnes had taken two Aleve
every morning with her coffee from the
big bottle she buys at the grocery
store.
She never thought to mention it to
anyone. To Agnes, it wasn't a real
medicine.
Marion came over to crimp crusts and saw
the bottle by the sugar canister.
Marion turned it around in her flowery
hand and read the back.
If you answered Advil or Aleve at the
start, you're reaching for the same
family of medicine as Agnes.
Ibuprofen in Advil and Motrin and
Naproxen in Aleve are called NSAIDs.
The Kidney Institute's warning is
direct. NSAIDs include popular pain
relievers and cold medicines that can
damage your kidneys if you take them for
a long time. They can also lead to
sudden kidney injury if you take them
when you're dehydrated or your blood
pressure is low.
Think of that sifter again. NSAIDs lower
the amount of blood that flows through
your kidneys. For a screen that's
already worn, less flow leaves less room
for error.
For Agnes, with a GFR of 51, the next
line is the one that counts. The
National Kidney Foundation says people
with chronic kidney disease should avoid
NSAIDs, especially if their GFR is lower
than 60. People with kidney disease
should talk with a health care
professional before taking them on their
own.
Agnes had passed another line, too.
The federal drug guide for
over-the-counter Naproxen says to stop
taking it and call your doctor if your
pain lasts more than 10 days.
Agnes was more than 100 days in.
If you answered Tylenol, that's a
different kind of medicine called
acetaminophen.
In general, acetaminophen is safe for
the kidneys at recommended doses.
But it's easy to take too much by
accident if you don't read labels, so it
still deserves a word with your
pharmacist.
The Monday after Thanksgiving, Agnes
called her doctor's office from her
kitchen phone. Marion sat beside her and
the Aleve bottle sat on the table
between them.
Agnes said it plainly,
"I've taken two Aleve every morning
since August and I didn't tell you." Her
doctor asked her to stop the daily Aleve
and come in to talk about her hands.
At that visit, Agnes brought the bottle
and one question in Marion's
handwriting.
"What can I take or do to relieve the
pain in my hands?"
Her doctor looked at her kidney numbers,
her blood pressure pills, and her baking
schedule. They worked out a different
plan together.
Tonight, line up every pain reliever in
your house on the kitchen counter.
Turn each one over and find the active
ingredient.
If it says ibuprofen or naproxen, and
you take it most days, ask your doctor
or pharmacist whether it's safe for your
kidneys. An occasional dose for a short
time isn't the worry here.
Day after day, for months, without
anyone checking your kidneys, is.
Agnes's hands felt better by Christmas.
Her next mistake came in a box marked
cold and sinus.
Number two is keeping your kidney number
to yourself.
In the second week of December, Birch
Lane had Christmas lights on every porch
and a foot of snow along the curbs.
Agnes caught a head cold at choir
practice. Her nose ran, and her head
pounded.
At the drugstore, Agnes picked a box of
cold and sinus tablets off the shelf. It
had a picture of a red, sore nose on the
front. Marion took the box from her and
turned it over.
On the back, under active ingredients,
was ibuprofen.
Pain relievers hide inside many cold
medicines, and NSAIDs are sold under
many different brand names.
That's why the name on the front tells
you so little.
So, Agnes carried the box to the
pharmacy counter.
This time, she said the sentence out
loud.
"My kidney number is 51."
The pharmacist pulled up Agnes's record.
Agnes fills every prescription at that
one drugstore, so all her medicines were
right there on the screen.
The pharmacist set the cold tablets
aside and suggested something else for
the stuffy nose. Then she checked the
doses of everything else Agnes takes.
That one sentence matters because of
what your kidneys do with medicine.
When your kidneys don't filter as well
as they used to, some medicines can
build up to unsafe levels in your blood.
Your doctor may tell you to take a
medicine less often or take a smaller
dose.
Doctors are supposed to consider your
kidney number when they dose medicines
that leave through the kidneys.
They can only do that if they know it.
The eye doctor, the dentist, the urgent
care clinic, and the hospital may each
see only part of your record.
The same goes for scans.
Iodine-based contrast dye, the kind used
for many CT scans, is one of the known
risk factors for sudden kidney injury.
If anyone schedules you a scan with dye,
mention your kidney number then, too.
That evening, Marion sat at Agnes's
dining table and made her a wallet card
in her choir director handwriting.
Every medicine and supplement Agnes
takes, with doses, her GFR, 51, and the
date. The name of her one pharmacy.
Ansel covered the card in clear packing
tape front and back, the way he used to
protect paperwork in a signal box.
"That'll outlast both of us," Ansel
said. Agnes slid it into her purse
behind her library card.
A week before Christmas, Agnes used it
for the first time.
At the dentist's office, the hygienist
asked if anything had changed with her
health.
Agnes didn't say nothing. She handed
over the card.
"Remember that cup you tried to place a
minute ago?
The number it gives you belongs on a
card like this one, right under your
GFR.
Tonight, make your own wallet card. List
your medicines and supplements, your
latest kidney number and its date, and
your pharmacy. Keep it in your wallet
and bring it, or all your pill bottles,
to every visit. A kidney number on a
card doesn't take your medicines away
from you.
It lets the people who prescribe them
get the dose right."
Agnes's wallet card was in her purse on
that January morning in her kitchen.
It helped.
But the mistake that put her there
happened two days earlier.
Number one is waiting it out at home
when you're sick and barely peeing.
By the middle of January, the lake was
frozen hard and ice fishing houses
dotted it like a little village.
A stomach bug went through the church
choir.
On Saturday, it reached Agnes.
Agnes threw up most of Saturday and the
diarrhea lasted into the night. She
couldn't keep down more than a few sips
of water.
Agnes stayed in bed under two quilts
with her lavender vest over her
nightgown.
On Sunday morning, Agnes did what she
always does.
She took her blood pressure pill and her
water pill right on schedule because
Agnes hasn't missed a dose in 22 years.
Mary Ann called on Sunday afternoon.
"Just a bug, dear." Agnes said.
"Don't come over. You'll catch it."
Agnes' voice sounded thin, but Agnes
always sounds cheerful on the phone.
The Kidney Institute explains what was
happening inside her.
When you get sick with something like
the flu or diarrhea, the blood pressure
in your body may decrease.
The same goes when you have trouble
drinking enough fluids. If you keep
taking your blood pressure medicines
when you're dehydrated or your pressure
is low, your kidneys might have a hard
time protecting themselves. And taking
NSAIDs when you're sick and dehydrated
can cause kidney injury.
Agnes had no plan for a day like that
Sunday. Nobody had ever talked with her
about what to do with her pills when she
couldn't keep water down.
So, she did the only thing she knew,
which was to keep going exactly as
usual.
Back to the sifter one last time.
Less fluid in your body means less flow
reaching the screen. The pills meant to
lower your pressure lower it further.
The screen still works, but almost
nothing is pouring through it.
On Sunday evening, Agnes noticed she'd
hardly gone to the bathroom all day. She
decided it made sense. Less water in,
less water out. She went to bed early
and slept badly.
That was one of the signs.
The National Kidney Foundation lists the
signs of sudden kidney injury, making
less urine than usual or none,
swelling in your legs, ankles, or feet,
tiredness, shortness of breath,
confusion, nausea, chest pain or
pressure.
This kind of injury can develop over a
few hours or a few days. For most
people, it comes on within 48 hours.
Monday morning, Marion called at 8:00,
the way she'd promised.
No answer. She called again at 8:15.
Then Marion pulled on her boots and took
the spare key off the hook by her back
door. She walked two doors down through
the snow.
Marion found Agnes in the kitchen in her
nightgown and lavender vest with the
cookie tin open in front of her.
Agnes smiled and asked when her husband
would be home for lunch.
Marion knew the rule for this.
A sudden change in mental status, like
confusion, is a medical emergency.
So are breathing problems, chest pain
lasting 2 minutes or more, and fainting.
You call 911 and you don't wait to see
if it passes.
Ansel, call 911,
Marion said into her phone.
Ansel made the call from their own
kitchen, then hurried two doors down in
his slippers and his tie.
Marion held Agnes's hand the whole time.
The ambulance came down Birch Lane 9
minutes later. Marion handed the crew
Agnes's wallet card. In 10 seconds, they
had every medicine Agnes takes and her
kidney number.
At the hospital, the team called it
acute kidney injury, the sudden kind.
They gave Agnes fluids through her
veins, stopped the medicines that might
be making it worse for a while, and
watched her kidneys for several days.
By Wednesday, Agnes knew exactly where
she was.
Marion and Ansel visited with the cookie
tin, and Agnes asked who'd taken over
her spot in the alto section.
A sudden injury like this can also leave
lasting damage, so a follow-up visit
matters.
Agnes' doctor booked her kidney tests
for March, within 3 months of the
hospital stay.
Before Agnes went home, her doctor sat
down with her and wrote a plan for the
next time she got sick.
The questions on it are ones anyone can
ask before a bug arrives.
If I get sick, are there medicines I
shouldn't take while I'm sick? If I need
to stop a medicine when I'm sick, when
do I start it again? If I have diarrhea
or I'm vomiting, do I need to change how
or when I take my blood pressure
medicine?
Agnes and Marion added one rule of their
own.
Whenever either of them is sick, there's
a phone call by 9:00 every morning. No
answer means the other one comes over
with the spare key.
Tonight, write those three questions on
a card and take them to your next visit.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist which of
your medicines, if any, change when
you're sick. You may never need that
card, but a plan made while you're well
is the one you can actually follow when
you're sick.
In March, the ice on the lake turned
gray and began pulling away from the
shore.
Agnes' repeat tests confirmed early
kidney disease, and her numbers had come
back to about where they were in
November. Agnes came to Sunday dinner at
the Brooks house with her cookie tin.
Taped inside the lid were two cards, her
wallet list, and her sick day questions.
Ansel had his own two tests in February.
Both came back normal. The joint
capsules are still behind the gravy
boat, and Ansel says they can stay
there.
If you're on that short list from number
four, ask for both kidney tests at your
next visit. Call your doctor the same
day if your urine slows way down or
stops.
Call the same day, too, if new swelling
shows up in your legs, ankles, or feet.
Call 911 for confusion, trouble
breathing, chest pain, or fainting.
A video can't measure your kidneys. Your
own doctor can with one tube of blood
and one cup of urine.
Tonight, find your last kidney number
and write the two test names on your
calendar.
Then tell me in the comments,
do you know your kidney number? Yes or
no.
And send this to the friend who takes
something for aches every morning and
says their kidneys are fine.
Two doors down from the Brooks, a cookie
tin sits by Agnes's phone with two cards
taped inside the lid.

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.
