head full of wet [music] sand, and she
loses the thread of a recipe halfway
through.
Her friend from church told her [music]
she is just catching up on 40 years of
lost sleep.
She has started leaving the oven on
because she forgot [music] she was
baking. She reads the same page of her
novel three nights running.
When her son calls on Sunday, she is
still in her robe at 11:00.
She tells him retirement [music]
is wonderful, and part of her believes
it. That is the belief.
Here is what the pooled research shows.
Researchers combined nine separate
studies covering almost 63,000 people.
The risk of mild cognitive impairment
and dementia did not keep falling as
sleep got longer.
It bottomed out around 7 hours and then
rose again as the hours stretched past
nine.
Joan is on the right arm of the U, and
the extra hours are not paying her back
the way she was told. If anything, each
extra hour in bed is leaving her a
little foggier than the hour before.
So, go back to the number you gave me a
minute ago.
If you said six or five and a half, you
were standing where Leona is standing.
If you said nine, nine and a half, 10,
you were where Joan is. If you said
seven or seven and a half or eight, you
were in the bottom of the curve.
The job is to protect it. Each arm of
the curve feels different from the
inside. The short arm feels like being
wide awake at four and dull by two.
The long arm feels like never quite
waking up at all.
The bottom of the curve feels like
nothing in particular, and that is what
you are after. You get up, [music] and
the day is simply there.
Either way, you need to understand what
the 7 hours [music] are for.
Once you do, the fixes stop feeling like
nagging and start feeling like plumbing.
Your brain is [music] about 3 lb of the
most metabolically active tissue in your
body, and all day long it produces
waste. Protein [music] fragments,
chemical byproducts, the exhaust of
thinking.
Think of a kitchen [music] after a big
holiday dinner. The cooking is the
thinking.
The pile [music] in the sink is what
thinking leaves behind.
Somebody has to run the water, and the
brain cannot [music] do it while it is
still cooking. Everywhere else in your
body, the lymphatic system carries waste
away.
Your brain does not have ordinary lymph
vessels running through it. For a long
time, nobody could explain how it took
out its own garbage. Then researchers
working with rodents found the answer,
and a later review of that work laid it
out. There is a rinse cycle. Clear
fluid, the same cerebrospinal fluid that
cushions your brain, is pushed along the
outside of your blood vessels.
It flows in through tiny water channels
in the brain support cells called
aquaporin 4. It washes through the
tissue and drains back out carrying the
waste with it. It is called the
glymphatic system, glial plus lymphatic.
And it runs mostly while you are asleep.
That is a large part of why sleep is not
optional for a brain.
It is not only rest. It is the
dishwasher cycle.
Picture the cable that runs from the
wall to your television. The copper wire
in the middle is the artery. The plastic
sheath around it is the space the rinse
water travels through. All day, with the
brain busy, that sheath is narrow and
the flow is a trickle.
When you fall into deep sleep, the brain
cells actually shrink a little. The
sheath widens, and the trickle becomes a
flush. It is a drain that only opens at
night. And it opens widest in one
specific stage, stage three sleep, the
slow-wave sleep.
It is the stage that older adults get
less and less of as the decades pass.
At 20, you got a thick slab of it every
night without trying. At 70, you may get
half of that, and the half you get is
fragile. A barking dog, a full bladder,
a sore hip, and the door swings shut.
You cannot buy more slow-wave sleep. You
can only stop interrupting the sleep you
already have.
What is in the wastewater matters.
Two proteins in particular,
beta-amyloid, the sticky fragment that
clumps into the plaques found in
Alzheimer's brains, and tau, the protein
that tangles inside dying neurons.
Reviews of the clearance system describe
it plainly.
When the overnight rinse works, these
proteins are swept out. When it falters,
they pile up. And that pile up is one of
the earliest steps toward Alzheimer's
disease, years before any memory slips
show.
That timeline is the hopeful part, not
the scary part. The pile up is slow. It
takes years to matter, which means the
nights you fix this year still count.
Now look at Leon again, with that drain
in mind.
Leon falls asleep at 10:30 and gets his
first and deepest slow-wave sleep by
midnight. Good. But deep sleep is
heaviest in the first half of the night.
Leon's 1:30 bathroom trip, which you
will hear about shortly, lands right on
top of it.
Then the 4:40 wake up means there is no
second half of the night to make up what
the trip broke. Leon's eyes snap open at
4:40, and whatever was scheduled for the
last 90 minutes simply does not happen.
Three years of nights where the drain
closes before the sink is empty.
A little more amyloid left behind each
morning than was there the morning
before. Notice how Leon feels at 4:40.
He feels sharp.
The brain that wakes early often wakes
alert, and one likely reason is that the
body's morning stress hormone is already
rising. That alertness is the trap.
It feels like proof that he is finished
sleeping. That same alertness is the
reason the fog arrives at 2:00 in the
afternoon, when the hormone wears off.
You might wonder whether one or two
short nights could really matter.
A 2018 study in the Proceedings of the
National Academy of Sciences took 20
healthy adults and put them through a
PET scan after a full night of sleep and
again after a single night of being kept
awake. After one night, the amyloid
signal in the hippocampus, the memory
center, and in the thalamus, the brain's
relay station, was measurably higher.
One night.
The study did not follow them to see how
fast it cleared, and no one should read
one scan as lasting damage. But it tells
you the machinery is [music] not
theoretical and that it is counting
every night, including the ones you are
shrugging [music] off. You already know
what one short night feels like.
The name on the tip of your [music]
tongue that will not come. The keys in
the refrigerator. The reason you walked
into the room gone before you got there.
Those are not signs of damage. They are
the brain running on a sink that did not
get [music] fully emptied.
The point is that every one of those
nights is a turn of the same handle.
Think back right now.
When was the last night you slept
straight through? No bathroom trip, no
2:00 a.m. ceiling, and woke to the clock
instead of before it?
If you have to reach back months or you
honestly cannot remember, hold on to
that. It is going to matter again in a
few minutes.
Jones saw that the U works differently,
and it is worth being careful here. The
long sleepers get frightened by this
part, and they should not be.
10 hours in bed does not mean the drain
ran for 10 hours. In many long sleepers,
the sleep is shallow and broken, and the
slow-wave stage is thin. One likely
explanation is that the body stretches
the hours out trying to make up in
quantity what it is missing in depth.
The extra hours are a symptom of a rinse
that is not working well, not the cause
of it. You can usually feel the
difference. Deep sleep leaves you heavy
and sure of where you are when you wake.
Shallow sleep leaves you groggy and
surprised by the clock. Joan wakes at
8:00 feeling as though she has only just
closed her eyes.
That is 10 hours of light dozing, not 10
hours of rinsing.
There is a second possibility that
researchers studying the genes that set
a person's natural sleep length have
raised, and it is the serious one. In
some older adults, sleep that quietly
lengthens over a year or two may be an
early sign of a brain that is already
changing, rather than a habit that
caused the change.
We will come back to that because it
decides whether Joan's problem is a
bedroom problem or a doctor's office
problem.
So, the target is about 7 hours of
actual sleep with as much of it unbroken
as you can manage.
One thing that cheers people up,
the National Institute on Aging is plain
that getting older does not mean you
need less sleep. The need does not
shrink. What shrinks is the ease of
getting it, and ease can be rebuilt. You
are not trying to become a different
sleeper. You are trying to remove the
things that have been shoving your sleep
off course.
Most of them turn out to be small.
Before anything else, measure.
Tonight, when you turn out the lamp,
glance at [music] the alarm clock and
remember the time.
When you wake for good in the morning,
glance again. Subtract the stretches you
know you were awake, the bathroom trip,
the hour you spent staring at the dark.
That number, not the number of hours you
were lying down, is your real sleep. Be
honest about the stretches. If you
turned over and saw the the
you were awake.
If you remember the furnace ticking, you
were awake. Round the awake, time up,
not down. Keep a pencil in the back of
an envelope on the nightstand and write
the two times before you forget them. It
takes 10 seconds. Do it for 7 nights and
you will know which arm of the you you
live on. That is more than most doctors
ever get to find out in a 15-minute
visit.
Then there are the five things that push
older adults out of the 7-hour window
and what to do about each. It ends with
the one that needs a professional.
Number five is the makeup sleep. The
Saturday sleep-in, the 10 hours after a
bad Thursday, the 90-minute nap at 2:00
in the afternoon.
This is Joan's entire routine and it
feels like kindness to yourself. What it
actually does is pull slow-wave sleep
out of the night and spread it thin
across the day.
So the one stretch when the drain should
run full is the stretch where you were
tossing.
You have felt this. The long Sunday
morning and then Sunday night you were
staring at the ceiling at midnight.
Monday is wrecked, so Monday night you
go to bed early.
And now the week is a seesaw. The body
does not catch up on sleep the way a
bank account catches up on deposits. It
runs on a clock and every morning you
sleep in moves the clock. The fix is a
single fixed wake time, 7 days a week,
chosen by you.
>> [music]
>> It is never moved more than 30 minutes,
even after a terrible night.
The terrible night [music] is the hard
part. The alarm goes at 7:00. You slept
4 hours and every part of you says
[music] stay down. Get up anyway. Open
the curtains. The tiredness you carry
[music] that day is the price of a good
night that night. It is a fair trade.
The nap stays if you love it, but it
moves before 2:00 and it ends at 20
minutes with a timer.
For Joan, that means an alarm at 7:00
every morning, including Sunday, and no
lying there afterwards. Within 2 weeks,
her body starts delivering the deep
sleep at night where it belongs.
It is no longer being allowed to deliver
it at 2:00 in the afternoon.
The first few days, she will feel worse.
Tell yourself that in advance, so it
does not frighten you into quitting.
Number four is the light.
Your brain decides when to release
melatonin, the hormone that opens the
door to sleep, by reading the light
hitting the back of your eye.
After 60, the lens of the eye yellows
and lets less of that light through. Two
things follow.
In the evening, there are the overhead
kitchen lights and the television and
the phone in bed.
They keep telling an already dim-sighted
brain that it is still afternoon. In the
morning, you are not getting enough
bright light to tell it the day has
started.
You will notice this as a brain that is
foggy at 9:00 in the morning and oddly
alert at 10:00 at night.
That second wind is not energy. It is a
clock that has lost track of noon.
The fix is a trade. After 8:00 in the
evening, lamps instead of ceiling
lights, and the phone charges in the
kitchen, not on the nightstand. If you
read in bed, use a small bedside lamp
and a paper book.
If the television is your company in the
evening, move to a lamp-lit room and sit
farther [music] from the screen.
Dim is the goal, not dark. And within an
hour of your fixed wake time, you get
outside [music] for 15 minutes of
daylight, even an overcast one.
That can be just standing [music] on the
porch with your coffee.
Morning light is the strongest sleep
medication most people over 60 have
never taken. Glasses and a window do not
count. If the weather is bad, s- stand
in the open doorway.
Within a week, most people notice they
are sleepy earlier in the evening
without trying to be.
Number three is pain.
The hip that complains when you roll
over, the knee,
the low back that sends you to the edge
of the bed at 2:40 to stretch it out.
Pain fragments sleep in a particular
way.
It does not always wake you fully.
It lifts you out of deep sleep into
light sleep over and over. So, you can
spend 8 hours in bed and get almost no
slow wave rinse at all. You will notice
it is a night that felt long and a
morning that feels bruised. You do not
remember waking. You just know [music]
you did not rest.
Two things to do. First, talk to your
doctor about timing. If you take
acetaminophen or another pain
medication, try [music] taking it an
hour before bed instead of at dinner.
That can shift the coverage to the hours
you needed. A pillow between the knees
for [music] side sleepers and under the
knees for back sleepers takes the twist
out of the hip and low back.
Second, and this is the rule that
changes everything [music] for people
lying awake in pain or in worry.
If you are awake [music] in bed for what
feels like 20 minutes, get up.
Go to a dim room, sit in a chair, read
something [music] dull, and go back only
when you are sleepy. Sleepy, not tired.
Sleepy is the heavy eyelid.
Tired is the wish that you could sleep.
Keep a chair and a boring book ready in
the next room, so you are not deciding
this at 2:00 in the morning.
The first few nights you may get up
three times. By the second week, it is
usually once. Lying in bed awake teaches
your brain that the bed is a place to be
awake.
This is the core of a structured program
called cognitive behavioral therapy for
insomnia, CBT-I for short.
It is the first thing to ask your doctor
about if the awake stretches have been
going on for 3 months or more. Many
sleep specialists now recommend trying
it before sleeping pills for older
adults.
Partly that is because it does not leave
you foggy or unsteady at 3:00 in the
morning.
Number two is the bathroom.
This is Leon's real problem and he does
not know it yet.
He wakes at 4:40 because his bladder
wakes him.
He has decided that since he is up
anyway, he might as well stay up.
He also goes once around 1:30 and does
not count it because he falls back
asleep.
If you asked him how many times he gets
up, he would say once.
The 1:30 trip has become invisible to
him.
That is true of most people,
which is why the log matters more than
memory.
This is why I asked you a few minutes
ago when you last slept straight through
to the alarm. If you had to reach back
months, think about a trip like this
one. The one you do not count.
There is a good chance it is what has
been cutting your nights in two.
Researchers put sleep monitors on the
wrists of nearly 1,100 older adults.
They found that each additional
nighttime trip to the bathroom tracked
with measurably worse sleep.
More time awake, more fragmentation,
less of the deep sleep where the rinse
runs. The trip itself costs 5 minutes.
The climb back down into deep sleep
afterwards can take far longer than the
trip did.
After the second trip, the night is
often too short to get there at all.
What to do? Start by moving your fluids
earlier. Most of your water and all of
your coffee and tea before 6:00 in the
evening. After that, a small sip, not a
glass.
That means the big glass of water with
dinner moves to lunch.
The evening tea becomes a cup at 4:00.
If you take pills at bedtime, take them
with the smallest swallow that gets them
down.
If your ankles swell during the day,
that fluid is pooling in your legs. Your
kidneys only get to it when you lie
flat. So, it arrives in your bladder at
1:30. Put your feet up above your heart
for 30 minutes around 4:00 in the
afternoon. Then the kidneys handle it
before bedtime instead of after. Lie on
the couch with your feet on the arm or
on the bed with two pillows under your
calves.
The 4:00 news is a good timer.
Compression socks during the day help
the same way. And if you take a water
pill, a diuretic, ask your doctor
whether it can move to the morning or
early afternoon.
Many people over 60 are taking it at
dinner on a schedule set years ago.
That single timing change can erase the
1:30 trip. Do not move it on your own.
The same pill at the wrong hour can
leave you dizzy, and your doctor needs
to know the schedule.
If you are still up twice or more a
night after 3 weeks of this, talk to
your doctor. A prostate, a bladder, or a
heart that is not moving fluid well can
all look like a small bladder. Each one
has its own fix.
Number one is for Joan.
The most serious reason an older adult
drifts out of the window is not
something they chose. Sleep that
lengthens on its own. Not the sleeping
in you decided on.
The nights that quietly went from 7
hours to 8 to 9 to 9 and 1/2.
That drift happened over a year or two,
along with naps you did not used to
need. And a morning fog that coffee does
not touch.
Here is what to watch for.
You start sitting down after breakfast
and losing an hour. You cancel the
morning walk because you are not up for
it. Someone has to call twice to get you
to the phone. Your family says you seem
slower, and you say you are just tired.
For some people, this is not a habit
affecting the brain.
It is the brain affecting the habit. The
slow wave stage thins, the REM sleep
falters, amyloid and tau accumulate. One
of the earliest outward signs can be a
person who needs more and more sleep and
feels less rested by it.
In other people, the same picture comes
from an underactive thyroid, from
depression, from a breathing problem
during sleep, or from a medication.
Every one of those is treatable. You
cannot tell those apart from your bed.
A doctor can.
And every treatable cause gets easier to
treat the sooner it is found. Waiting to
see if it passes is the one choice that
costs something.
So, the action for number one is not a
bedroom change. It is an appointment.
Take the 7-night log you started, the
real hours of sleep, and walk in with
it. Say exactly this. My sleep has
gotten longer over the last year, and I
am more tired, not less.
That one sentence puts the right
questions in your doctor's head about
thyroid, about mood, about breathing,
about memory. It is the sentence Joan
has not said to anyone because her
friend told her she was catching up.
Bring the log and bring someone who
lives with you if you can.
They have noticed things you have not.
Ask what should be checked and write the
answer down before you leave.
Leon does [music] the measuring first, 7
nights, real hours.
The number is 5 [music] hours and 50
minutes once the 1:30 trip is counted.
Not the six [music] and change he had
been guessing.
With his doctor's blessing, he moves his
water pill to breakfast. He puts his
feet up during the 4:00 news. He stops
drinking anything after supper.
Inside a month, the 1:30 trip is gone.
The 4:40 wake-up slides to 5:30, then to
6:00. He is sleeping through the last
rinse cycle for the first time in 3
years. Joan keeps her appointment. Her
doctor finds a thyroid running low,
which is a pill and a recheck, not a
sentence. Once it is treated, her sleep
comes back toward 8 hours on its own.
The wet sand in the morning lifts.
If you sleep under six or over nine and
feel fine, bring your seven-night log to
your next routine visit. If you are up
twice or more a night, or lying awake 20
minutes most nights, make that visit
this week. If sleep has lengthened on
its own with daytime confusion or
drowsiness, or someone has noticed you
repeating yourself, call and ask to
[music] be seen now.
None of this is a diagnosis. Your log is
a starting [music] point for your own
doctor, who knows the rest of your
history.
Tonight, glance at the clock [music]
when the lamp goes off, and again when
you wake for good.
Write the two times on that envelope
before you forget them.
Then come back to the number [music] you
gave me at the start. Now that you know
where seven sits, is yours on the short
arm, [music] the long arm, or the bottom
of the curve?
Tell me in the comments, and send this
to [music] the one person in your family
who brags about getting by on 5 hours.
Tonight, count the hours, [music]
and let the clock be the one that wakes
you.

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
Tired all the time after 65? Sometimes it is just age — but researchers who asked 515 women about their heart attacks found that about 7 in 10 had felt unusually tired more than a month before.

Halfway around the frozen lake on Birch Lane, Joyce, sixty-eight, sits down hard on a bench and tells Marion she's just tired. Her season of fatigue started back in October. This story follows six everyday mistakes: calling it "just getting older," never asking for the simple blood tests, never asking whether a medicine is adding to it, sitting more because you're tired, missing the low mood that looks like tiredness, and waiting it out when the tiredness comes with other warning signs.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — The bench on the lake path
1:12 — Mistake 6: Calling it "just getting older"
5:38 — Mistake 5: Never asking for the blood tests
9:56 — Mistake 4: The medicine that adds to it
13:56 — Mistake 3: Sitting more because you're tired
17:18 — Mistake 2: The low mood that looks like tiredness
21:19 — Mistake 1: Tiredness with warning signs
25:20 — Back on the lake loop

If you know someone who keeps saying their exhaustion is just their age, share this episode with them and subscribe to follow Ansel and Marion's next story on Birch Lane.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Ansel, Marion and their neighbors are illustrated characters. This channel shares general health education from published research, narrated with an AI voice. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

"Then what does 72 feel like?" Marion
asked. "Because I've been standing here
waiting for you
all through October." It kept up. Twice,
Joyce turned back at the bench and
walked home.
One afternoon at 4:00, Marion found
Joyce asleep in her armchair by the
front window, a library book open on her
chest. Joyce left her leaves unraked for
the first time in years.
That night, Marion told her husband
Ansel about the bench over supper.
Ansel, 74, is a retired railroad
signalman who still wears a tie every
day.
He meets the walkers at the end of the
loop with a thermos of coffee. Ansel set
down his fork and held his hands apart
the way he does when he's measuring
something.
"I was tired at 68, too." Ansel said.
"Everybody slows down."
"Slowing down takes years." Marion said.
"Joyce changed in a couple of months.
That's the difference worth noticing.
Not how tired you are, but how fast it
changed."
The National Institute on Aging is
careful with this.
Everyone feels tired now and then.
But sometimes, fatigue can be the first
sign that something is wrong in your
body.
Fatigue isn't quite the same as feeling
sleepy.
Drowsiness is feeling the need to sleep.
Fatigue is a lack of energy and
motivation.
The list of things that can add to
fatigue is long. Anemia, thyroid
disease, diabetes, heart disease, and
kidney disease, sleep apnea, certain
medicines, grief, stress, and
depression.
Getting older isn't on that list. And
when a health problem is behind the
tiredness, treating it may help reduce
the tiredness, too.
There's a line in time, too. If you've
been tired or low on energy for several
weeks with no relief, call your health
care provider.
If you answered weeks or months at the
start, that line is yours.
Joyce was at 4 weeks and counting.
Marion didn't argue any further.
The next morning, she took a small
spiral notebook from her desk drawer,
the kind she uses for choir attendance.
Marion handed it to Joyce at the halfway
bench.
What she was handing over has a name, a
fatigue diary.
It can help you find patterns in the day
when you feel more or less tired.
Marion drew three lines on the first
page, morning, afternoon, and evening.
Joyce wrote in it every day for 2 weeks
in her neat librarian printing.
How tired she felt from 1 to 5,
what she had just done, eaten, or taken.
Every afternoon line said four or five.
You could start the same notepad tonight
with Joyce's three lines.
Fatigue is a common symptom, and most of
the time it isn't caused by a serious
disease.
2 weeks of honest lines just turn
I'm tired into something a doctor can
work with.
At the end of those 2 weeks, Marion read
the notebook at the bench and handed it
back.
"Take this to your doctor," Marion said.
"And take the bench with you."
Number five [music] is never asking for
the simple blood tests.
In the middle of November, [music]
the first real snow came down on Birch
Lane. Marion drove Joyce [music] to the
clinic on Main Street with the wipers
going and the spiral notebook on Joyce's
lap.
In the exam room, Joyce did what you did
at the start of this video.
She named one thing she could do a year
ago that she couldn't do now.
"Last fall, I walked the whole lake loop
and waited for Marion," Joyce said. "Now
I turn back at the bench."
That one sentence told her doctor more
than I'm tired ever could. It has a
when, a where, and a before and after.
For tiredness that lasts, your provider
will ask about your sleep, your daily
activities, your appetite, and your
exercise.
Then usually a physical exam and lab
tests.
Among the blood tests a doctor may order
for fatigue are three ordinary ones, a
complete blood count, which checks for
anemia, a thyroid test, and sometimes a
vitamin B12 level.
Start with the blood count. Red blood
cells carry oxygen from your lungs to
every part of your body.
When you don't have enough healthy red
blood cells, that's anemia, and the lack
of oxygen can make you feel tired or
weak.
Ansel puts it in railroad terms with his
hands.
Red blood cells are the boxcars and
oxygen is the freight.
Fewer boxcars means less freight and
everything down the line runs slow.
Anemia isn't rare at this age.
In one national survey, about one in 10
Americans 65 and older had anemia.
After 85, it was more than one in five.
Most of those cases were mild, which is
exactly why they're easy to miss.
Then the thyroid, the small
butterfly-shaped gland at the front of
your neck.
Its hormones control how every cell in
your body uses energy.
When it runs low, the body slows down.
You may feel cold, tired, constipated,
or down,
and you may forget things.
Thyroid specialists say an underactive
thyroid is very common after 60 and
grows more common with age.
In older people, memory trouble that
gets blamed on age can be the only sign.
And other problems cause the same
symptoms, so a blood test is the only
way to know for sure.
Last, vitamin B12.
Your body needs it to make red blood
cells.
Older adults are more likely to have
stomach and digestive problems that make
B12 harder to absorb.
Low B12 can bring fatigue and
light-headedness when you stand.
Over time, it can also bring numbness
and tingling in the hands and feet and
trouble with balance.
That's when Joyce remembered her toes.
For a month, they'd tingled on the
walks.
Joyce had blamed her old winter boots.
Her doctor ordered the blood work that
morning.
Joyce rolled up the sleeve of her teal
windbreaker in the lab down the hall,
and Marion held the notebook.
3 days later, the clinic called.
Joyce's blood count showed anemia. Her
B12 level was low.
Her thyroid test was normal.
Joyce took the call in her kitchen with
Marion sitting beside her.
Joyce set the phone down and laughed, a
little shakily.
"Since September," Joyce said, "I
thought I was just getting old, and it
was my blood."
A normal result is a real answer, too.
It crossed one cause off Joyce's list,
so her doctor could look harder at the
other two.
And her doctor didn't want to wait.
Nerve damage from low B12 may become
permanent if treatment doesn't start
promptly. People with this kind of
anemia often do well once it's treated.
If you've been tired for weeks, it's
fair to ask whether those same three
blood tests make sense for you.
Back in the exam room that first day,
her doctor had asked one more question.
"What do you take every morning?"
Number four is [music] never asking
whether a medicine is adding to it.
Joyce had to think. "Just a little
heartburn pill," [music] Joyce said.
Every morning for about 9 years. And an
allergy pill at bedtime from drugstore
because the furnace air made her sneeze
all winter.
Joyce hadn't mentioned either one in
years.
To Joyce, they weren't real medicines.
They were just part of breakfast and
bedtime.
Federal health guides name this
connection plainly. Some medicines can
make it harder for your body to absorb
vitamin B12 over time. Among them are
some heartburn medicines and metformin,
a diabetes medicine.
That doesn't make heartburn pills bad.
For plenty of people, they're the right
medicine.
It means that after years on one, it's
fair to ask what else it might be doing.
Ansel's boxcars need building.
Your body makes red blood cells in the
soft marrow inside your bones, and it
needs B12 for the job. To pull B12 out
of your food, your stomach releases a
special protein that helps you absorb
it. Changes in the stomach or years of
certain medicines can leave the marrow
short of material.
When the results came back, her doctor
didn't take Joyce off anything on the
spot. They would look together at
whether she still needed the heartburn
pill and at what dose. For the low B12,
her doctor prescribed shots at the
clinic, a few close together at first,
then about once a month.
That treatment came from Joyce's own
blood test and her doctor's judgment.
It's the kind of decision that belongs
in the exam room.
Then there was the bedtime allergy pill.
Some medicines can cause drowsiness or
fatigue, too.
The list includes antihistamines for
allergies, blood pressure medicines,
sleeping pills, steroids, and water
pills. Medicines for nausea and pain and
some antidepressants can add to it, too.
The next afternoon, Joyce stood at the
pharmacy counter of the drugstore on
Main Street with her allergy box.
She asked one question.
Could this be adding to how tired I am
the next day?
The pharmacist said it could for some
people and suggested Joyce bring it up
with her doctor.
Joyce wrote it in the notebook under the
afternoon lines.
That evening, Ansel sat down at Joyce's
kitchen table with a ruler and a pencil.
For 40 years, Ansel kept logbooks for
railroad signals, and he can't look at a
notebook without wanting to make
columns.
Ansel drew a timetable across two pages.
One column for the time of day, one for
each pill, one for Joyce's tiredness
number.
"Now you can see if the trains run
together," Ansel said, tapping the page.
Joyce said it looked like a train
schedule, and Ansel took that as a
compliment.
Two weeks of columns showed something.
On the mornings after the bedtime
allergy pill, Joyce's first number was a
four.
On the few nights she skipped it because
her nose was clear, her morning number
was a two. It didn't prove anything,
but it was the kind of pattern a doctor
can actually use.
At her next visit, Joyce laid Ansel's
timetable on the exam table.
Her doctor read it twice and talked with
her about other ways to handle the
furnace sneezes.
They made that change together in the
exam room.
Joyce's question at the pharmacy counter
works for every pill you take,
prescription or not, and every vitamin.
Just don't stop or change any medicine
on your own.
Many of them are well worth taking, and
your doctor may have a better fit if one
is wearing you down.
By early December, Joyce had her first
B12 shots behind her,
but she'd found a new favorite place to
spend the day,
the armchair by her front window.
Number three is sitting more because
you're tired. [music]
The lake path was icy that December, and
the wind came straight [music] off the
frozen water.
Joyce stopped walking altogether.
"I'll walk when I have the energy,"
Joyce told Marion on the phone.
It sounds sensible.
Rest when you're tired.
But too little exercise is one of the
everyday habits that can make you feel
tired, and regular exercise can help
boost your energy.
The Aging Institute has a line for
exactly what Joyce said.
Many older adults feel less fatigue
during and after physical activity.
Joyce had already asked her doctor
whether walking was safe while the shots
did their work. Her doctor said yes, and
to start easy.
That question matters. If you have a
heart or lung condition, or your
tiredness hasn't been checked yet, ask
your doctor what kind of activity is
right for you first.
So Marion made a plan, the way Marion
plans everything.
One good answer to bad weather is to
walk indoors at a mall or a big store.
So Marion drove Joyce to the shopping
mall in the next town, where the walkers
go before the stores open.
Marion checked the spiral notebook
first.
Joyce's best hour was late morning,
around 11:00.
It helps to plan activity for the part
of the day when you feel most energetic.
So the walks went at 11:00.
The first morning, the mall was warm and
nearly empty. A few walkers in sneakers
went by in pairs, swinging their arms.
Joyce zipped her teal windbreaker
anyway, out of habit, and pushed her
white visor up on her forehead.
Marion made her start slowly for the
first few minutes at an easy stroll.
Warming up gives your heart rate and
breathing a chance to rise gradually,
and slowing down at the end lets them
settle.
That first day, Joyce and Marion walked
for 10 minutes past the closed shoe
store and the fountain, and sat down.
A 10-minute walk three times a week is a
fine first goal.
Put yours in your own best hour, and
treat it as a starting point, not a
test.
Then they built up slowly over the next
few weeks.
10 minutes became 15.
15 became one full lap of the upper
level. Joyce wrote every walk in her
notebook.
On the days the mall was closed, Joyce
walked laps of her own hallway during
the TV news.
Even small amounts of activity through
the day count.
On Saturdays, Ansel came along.
He walked a few steps behind the two of
them carrying everybody's coats and
timed the laps on his railroad pocket
"7 minutes flat," Ansel announced each
time as if he were calling out a train
schedule.
By the week before Christmas, Joyce's
afternoon numbers had dropped from five
to three.
The shots were helping her blood.
The walks were helping the rest of her.
Think back right now. What's one thing
you used to look forward to every week
that you've quietly let go?
Keep it in mind because number two is
about exactly that.
Joyce's legs were coming [music] back.
But on Friday afternoons, the mahjong
table in her dining room stayed folded
against the wall.
Number two is missing the low mood that
looks like tiredness.
For 11 years, Joyce had hosted Friday
mahjong for four women from church.
The clatter of tiles was the loudest
sound in her quiet yellow house by the
boat landing.
In December, Joyce canceled three
Fridays in a row. Each time she said the
same thing.
"I'm just too tired."
But Marion had seen Joyce walk 15
minutes at the mall that same week.
And Marion spent 40 years as a choir
director. She knows the sound of a voice
that has gone flat.
So at the mall fountain, Marion asked
straight out.
"Joyce, do you miss mahjong?"
Joyce watched the coins at the bottom of
the fountain for a long time.
"I don't miss it," Joyce said.
"That's the trouble. I don't really care
about much of anything lately.
Marion didn't try to fix it right there.
She stayed on the bench by the fountain
beside Joyce until the mall lights came
up for the day.
Depression in older adults can be hard
to recognize.
For some people, sadness isn't the main
symptom at all.
Instead, they may feel numb or lose
interest in things they used to enjoy or
just feel tired.
It hides well.
Fatigue, a smaller appetite, and trouble
sleeping can also come from getting
older or from a physical illness.
So, early depression may be ignored or
mistaken for something else.
The Aging Institute is direct about it.
Depression is a common problem among
older adults, but it isn't a normal part
of aging.
If several signs last more than 2 weeks,
talk with your doctor.
The risk factors read like Joyce's
autumn. Sleep problems, social
isolation, and loneliness. Too little
physical activity.
None of them necessarily causes
depression.
But that autumn, Joyce had drifted
toward two of them. Fewer walks and
fewer Fridays with friends.
At her follow-up visit in early January,
Joyce said it out loud, holding the
notebook in both hands.
I've lost interest in things I used to
love. Mahjong, my books, even.
If you felt down or stopped enjoying
things for 2 weeks or more, say it at
your next visit in plain words like
hers.
Joyce had expected her doctor to tell
her it was the winter or her age.
Her doctor took it seriously instead.
Low B12 can itself bring mood changes,
including depression. So, they'd watch
Joyce's mood together over the next few
weeks while the shots worked.
If it didn't lift, there was talk
therapy, and there were other
treatments.
For most people, depression gets better
with treatment.
And it can't get treated if nobody says
the words.
That Friday, Joyce unfolded the mahjong
table. Only Marion came, and Marion is
terrible at mahjong. She mixed up the
dragons and the winds, and asked twice
which tiles were the flowers. Joyce
laughed out loud for the first time
since October.
The next Friday, the church women came
back. Joyce set out the tiles and a
plate of rice crackers, and the clatter
filled the yellow house again.
If tiredness ever comes with thoughts of
harming yourself, don't wait for a
visit. Call or text 988, the suicide and
crisis lifeline, any hour of the day or
night.
By the middle of January, Joyce was
walking the whole lake loop again. She
thought the tiredness was finally behind
her. That's why she nearly missed the
morning it came back different.
Number one is [music] waiting it out
when the tiredness comes with other
warning signs.
It was that gray Tuesday in January,
about [music] 25°,
with the lake path freshly plowed. Joyce
and Marion passed the boat landing, and
Joyce slowed.
This tiredness was heavy, like walking
through deep snow.
Then came the squeezing across Joyce's
upper back, as if someone had pulled a
rope tight around her. She was short of
breath.
Under the white visor, her forehead was
wet with a cold sweat, and her stomach
felt sick.
Joyce sat down hard on the halfway
bench.
"It's my blood again," Joyce said.
"The doctor said it would take a while."
Then she added, "Or that heartburn."
The American Heart Association warns
about this exact moment.
Women often chalk up heart attack
symptoms to less serious things, like
acid reflux, the flu, or normal aging.
Joyce had all three explanations ready:
her age, her blood, and her heartburn.
Each one had been true at some point
that fall. None of them explained a back
squeezed like a rope.
A heart attack happens when the blood
flow that brings oxygen to the heart
muscle is badly reduced or cut off.
In Ansel's railroad terms, it's a
blocked line.
The boxcars can't reach the station at
all.
The most common heart attack symptom in
women and men is chest pain or
discomfort.
But women may also have symptoms people
don't link as often with a heart attack.
Shortness of breath. An upset stomach.
Pain in the shoulder, back, or arm.
An unusual tiredness and weakness.
Chest pain doesn't always come.
In that study of 515 women, more than
four in 10 had no chest pain at all
during the heart attack itself.
Some heart attacks are sudden and
intense.
Others start slowly with mild pain or
discomfort.
The advice is the same either way. Even
if you're not sure it's a heart attack,
get checked out.
Marion looked at Joyce's wet forehead
and her hand pressed to her back.
"Joyce, that's new." Marion said.
"Your blood never did that to your
back." Marion took out her phone and
called 911 right there on the bench.
Marion didn't try to walk Joyce back to
the car.
Calling 911 is almost always the fastest
way to get life-saving treatment.
The crew can start treatment when they
arrive. People with chest pain who
arrive by ambulance may also get faster
treatment at the hospital.
Then Marion called Ansel. Ansel drove
his truck to the lot by the boat landing
and stood at the trailhead waving both
arms so the ambulance would find the
right path.
The ambulance came down the plowed path
11 minutes later.
Marion sat with Joyce on the bench the
whole time holding her mitten, the
spiral notebook still in Joyce's
windbreaker pocket.
Later, Marion said the hardest part was
the few seconds she almost believed
Joyce.
Joyce had been right about being tired
for months.
She just wasn't right about this.
At the hospital, the heart team
confirmed a heart attack. They opened
the blocked artery that same morning.
Joyce went home 4 days later.
Before she left, Joyce asked a question.
Had her tiredness back in October been
her heart all along?
Nobody could say. Her low B12 was real,
and the shots had helped.
Even the researchers behind that seven
in 10 number wrote that it's unknown
whether early symptoms like that predict
a heart attack.
What everyone agreed on was the bench.
New warning signs on top of the
tiredness meant call, and Marion called.
In February, Joyce started cardiac rehab
at the hospital, a medically supervised
exercise program three mornings a week.
Marion drove. Ansel brought the thermos.
Joyce wrote every rehab session in the
same spiral notebook right after the
mall walks.
By April, the ice had pulled away from
the shore, and Joyce was walking the
lake loop again one marker at a time.
The first time she reached the halfway
bench, Joyce tapped its backrest with
her mitten and kept going.
If you've been tired for several weeks
with no relief, make an appointment and
bring your diary. Call your doctor right
away if the tiredness comes with
confusion or dizziness or blurred
vision. The same goes for little or no
urine or new swelling and weight gain.
For thoughts of harming yourself, call
or text 988 any hour.
Call 911 for chest pressure or pain or
discomfort in your arms, back, neck,
jaw, or stomach.
Call for shortness of breath, too,
especially with a cold sweat, nausea,
light-headedness, or unusual tiredness.
None of this can tell you what's behind
your own tiredness.
You and your own doctor, together, can
start to find it.
Tonight, make a deal with [music] the
person you walk with or live with.
If either of you says, "I'm just tired."
while short of breath, in a cold sweat,
or with pressure [music] in the chest,
back, jaw, or arms, the other one calls
911
No arguing. No waiting to see. Most
tired days are just tired days, and
you'll probably [music] never need it.
Then tell me in the comments,
would you have called 911 from that
bench?
>> [music]
>> Yes or no?
And send this to the friend who keeps
saying it's just their age.
In May, halfway around [music] the lake,
two walking partners sit on a bench in
the sun, and nobody is waiting for
anybody.
>> [music]

records.title: How to Drink Water After 60: 6 Mistakes, and #1 Looks Like Memory
records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
After sixty, your sense of thirst can get quieter, and the first sign you're running low on water often doesn't feel like thirst at all. When researchers checked the blood of two hundred people 65 and older admitted to the hospital as emergencies, about 37 out of every 100 were already dehydrated.

This video counts down six everyday water mistakes after 60: waiting until you're thirsty, saving your drinks for the evening, counting only plain water, cutting back to avoid the bathroom, drinking far too much "to be safe", and number one, missing the signs of dehydration because they look like age, or like a slipping memory. Keep count as we go. At the end, you'll know exactly what to do with your number, which signs need a call to your doctor this week, and which mean calling 911.

If your doctor has given you a fluid limit for your heart or kidneys, that limit comes first.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — Not thirsty after 60? Why that matters
1:23 — Mistake 6: Waiting until you're thirsty
4:51 — Mistake 5: Saving your drinks for the evening
6:16 — Mistake 4: Counting only plain water
9:16 — Mistake 3: Cutting back to avoid the bathroom
12:47 — Mistake 2: Drinking far too much, just to be safe
16:01 — Mistake 1: Signs that look like age or memory
23:34 — What to do with your count

If this helped, a like and a subscribe help the next video reach more people.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
The people in this video are illustrative examples. This channel shares general health education from published research. It is not medical advice — talk to your own doctor before changing medication, diet or exercise.

📚 SOURCES & REFERENCES
1. Phillips et al. 1984, N Engl J Med — Reduced thirst after water deprivation in healthy elderly men
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6472364/
2. El-Sharkawy et al. 2015, Age Ageing — Hydration and outcome in older patients admitted to hospital (HOOP)
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4621229/

https://www.nationalacademies.org/news/2004/02/report-sets-dietary-intake-levels-for-water-salt-and-potassium-to-maintain-health-and-reduce-chronic-disease-risk
4. National Academies Press 2005 — Dietary Reference Intakes for Water (summary)
https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/10925/chapter/2
5. MedlinePlus — Water in diet
https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002471.htm
6. MedlinePlus — Dehydration
https://medlineplus.gov/dehydration.html

https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm
8. MedlinePlus — Low blood sodium
https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000394.htm
9. MedlinePlus — Urination, excessive amount at night
https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm
10. Cleveland Clinic 2023 — The connection between age and dehydration
https://health.clevelandclinic.org/drink-up-dehydration-is-an-often-overlooked-health-risk-for-seniors/
11. Hix et al. 2011, Semin Nephrol — Diuretic-associated hyponatremia
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22099512/

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25924806/

https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/bladder-infection-uti-in-adults/symptoms-causes

After 60, your body handles water
differently, and the first morning often
doesn't feel like thirst at all. Maybe
you get through a whole morning on one
cup of coffee and never once think about
a drink. Maybe you skip the iced tea
before [music] church so you won't need
the restroom. Or you stand up from your
recliner and the room takes a second to
[music] settle. Most people shrug
moments like these off as getting older.

body is running low. [music] And it can
go further than you'd think. When
researchers checked the blood of 200
people 65 and older as they were
admitted to the hospital as emergencies,
about 37 out of every hundred were
already dehydrated when they came
through the door. Today, six mistakes

sign family's blame on a slipping memory

exactly what to do with your number. The
good news is that most of these mistakes
are easy to fix, and the fixes cost
nothing. Some of the water you need is
already in your kitchen in the soup pot
and the fruit bowl.
Number six is waiting until you're
thirsty. To see how easily this happens,
picture a woman [music] we'll call
Delphine Budro. She's 71 and for 30
years she ran the cafeteria at an
elementary school in Baton Rouge,
Louisiana.
On the side table by her recliner sits a
big plastic tumbler with a straw. Her
daughter Karen bought it for her. Most
afternoons it's still mostly full. The
ice long since melted. I'm just not a
thirsty person. Deline says she means it
as a plain fact about herself like being
left-handed.
Her mornings start with two cups of
coffee on the back porch with her
husband Royce. After that, she drinks
when she notices she's thirsty, which
she'll tell you is hardly ever. She fed
600 kids a day for 30 years and hardly
ever sat down to a glass of water
herself. For most of your life, thirst
was a reliable alarm. You got thirsty,
you drank, and that was the end of it.
After 60, that alarm can get quieter.
Experts at the National Library of
Medicine say some people lose their
sense of thirst as they age, so they
don't drink enough. A small study in the
New England Journal of Medicine showed
how big that gap can be. Researchers
kept seven healthy men in their late 60s

young men. At the end, the older men's
blood had grown more concentrated than
the young men's. Yet, they felt less

A lot of people get to supper, realize

Do most of your drinking in the morning

[music] rides in the cup holder all day

It can backfire.
Think back to the last time you were out

real drink before you left the house?
Keep that answer in mind. Nay. Bladder
experts say you can ask your doctor

tract. The fix is to move the drink

Do you skip drinks before church or a

Number two is drinking far too much just

For most healthy people, the extra

dehydrated may seem confused or cranky,

your blood pressure drops as you stand

enough is one of the known causes. In
older adults, a fall from that kind of

why don't people just notice? Because
the usual home checks don't work well at
this age. A large review of studies in
people 65 and older found that no single
sign was reliable on its own. That
included the color of your urine and
even feeling thirsty.

constipation are still worth paying
attention to. But the dependable answer

the signs themselves than the timing. A
change that shows up during a hot spell,

before anyone decides it's just age.
Deline's fog had come on slowly over a
week and a half of heat, and in between
she was still mostly herself. Sudden is

a racing pulse with fast breathing in
the heat, or someone who keeps getting

Saturdays, she drinks well at breakfast
and Royce stops at the gas station
halfway there. At the ballpark, she sips

empty. once in a while with Royce's
thumb in the frame. Two weeks [music]
later, Deline's blood work was back in

time. By then, she was back at Tuesday
Bridge, and by her own account, winning.

water. Memory trouble has a lot of
causes, and that's exactly why Deline's
family was right to get her checked
instead of guessing. If you or someone
you love has had a stretch of feeling
foggier or more worn out than usual,
start with one question. How much have

when you stand or a foggy, wiped out

Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

records.text:
CDC statisticians counted more than 2,200 food-choking deaths among Americans 65 and older in four years, a higher rate than at any other age. Yet the warning signs start weeks before an emergency, right at the dinner table. When 81-year-old Agnes stopped breathing in the middle of a bite of Sunday pot roast on Birch Lane, Ansel and Marion realized they had missed three full weeks of small, quiet clues.

In this episode of our Birch Lane story series, we follow 74-year-old Ansel, 72-year-old Marion, and their neighbor Agnes through the six everyday dinner-table mistakes that raise choking risk after 70. From rushing through meals and talking with a full mouth to swallowing dry pills like alendronate, potassium, and vitamin C without enough water, small shifts in how your voice box and throat work as you age can turn an ordinary supper into a crisis. We also look at how clicking dentures, dry-mouth medications, and that quiet little cough during meals signal it is time to ask for a swallow evaluation—plus the exact ten-second response that saves a life when someone is choking at the table or alone in their own kitchen.

that she couldn't breathe.
If you're over 70, you know the small
version of that [music] moment. A bite
goes down the wrong way, your eyes
water, and you cough until it clears.
CDC statisticians counted [music] over
2,200 food choking deaths in Americans
65 and older in 4 years, a higher rate
than at any other age.
Six dinner table mistakes [music] raise
that risk after 70, and each one has a
simple fix.
The last one [music] isn't a habit at
all. It's the next 10 seconds and what
Agnes would do alone in her own kitchen.
Try this in your chair. Rest two fingers
on the front of your throat and swallow.
Feel that bump rise and drop. That's
your voice box shutting your airway.
For that instant, your breathing stops.
If the person across your table started
choking tonight, would you know where to
put your hands? Yes or no?
One word in the comments, and keep your
answer handy for number one.
Ansel Brooks, 74, spent 40 years keeping
railroad signals working.
Marion, 72, directed the church choir
for 30.
They live on Birch Lane in a small
Minnesota lake town. Agnes, the widow
two doors down, eats Sunday dinner with
them almost every week.
But that Sunday wasn't the first
warning.
Marion counted three weeks of them.
Number six is talking, laughing, and
hurrying with a mouthful of food.
Three Sundays earlier, it was roast
chicken and mashed potatoes.
Ansel, in the mustard yellow tie he
still wears every day, was telling the
one about the blizzard of 1991.
A signal froze a crossing, and he fought
it with a thermos of coffee. Ansel
explains everything with his hands. So,
he told it with his fork, which drew
circles in the air.
Agnes is tiny with white hair and a bun
and thick round glasses, and her cookie
tin sat by her plate.
Agnes laughed so hard she had to hold
her napkin over her mouth with a bite of
chicken still in it.
Agnes coughed, waved her hand, and
laughed some more.
Marion had a habit of her own.
For 30 years, Marion ate lunch in the 15
minutes between choir rehearsals.
That Sunday, she finished her plate
before Ansel's story even reached the
thermos.
You felt the reason a minute ago with
your fingers on your throat. Swallowing
needs your airway shut.
Talking and laughing need it open
because both of them run on air. Laugh
with food in your mouth, and your throat
gets two orders at the same time.
Most of the time, a cough sorts it out.
But federal health guides list eating
too fast and not chewing food well among
the causes of choking in adults.
They also warn against talking or
laughing with food in your mouth. Their
swallowing advice puts it in one line.
Don't talk and swallow at the same time.
Alcohol is on that list, too. The same
guides say even a small amount affects
your awareness, and they advise against
drinking too much before or during a
meal.
Ansel has one glass of red wine with
Sunday dinner, and sometimes a second
one when the story is good.
Marion fixed it the way she used to fix
a rushed hymn.
"Breathe at the rests," Marion said. "In
the choir, you only take a breath where
the music stops. At the table, you only
talk where the chewing stops."
So, Ansel tried it. Chew, swallow, then
talk. It turned out Ansel couldn't tell
a story and hold a fork anyway because
the blizzard takes both hands. So, his
fork went down on the plate whenever a
story started.
Marion made a rule for herself, too.
Fork down between bites, and no second
helping until the kitchen clock says 20
minutes.
Agnes promised she would laugh after she
swallowed, and then Agnes laughed at
herself for promising.
Tonight at supper, set your fork down
between bites, and finish each bite
before you speak or laugh.
If you have wine with dinner, keep it to
one glass, and sip it between bites,
never with a mouthful. You don't have to
eat in silence. The conversation just
goes in the rests.
Number five is the big bite of tough
meat or dry bread.
On the Tuesday after that chicken
dinner, Ansel made himself a ham
sandwich on a crusty roll.
Ansel took a big bite while telling
Marion about the town council meeting.
Halfway through a sentence, a piece went
down the wrong way.
Ansel coughed hard, red in the face, one
hand flat on the kitchen table.
"I'm fine." Ansel said between coughs,
which is exactly what everyone says.
Marion was already out of her chair,
ready to pound him on the back.
Then Marion stopped herself because
Ansel was coughing loudly, and he was
talking.
That was the right call.
The Red Cross says that if a choking
person can cough, cry, or speak,
encourage them to keep coughing. Keep
watching them. Don't leave them alone,
and be ready to act if things change. A
strong cough means air is still getting
through, and the cough is the best tool
they have.
So, Marion stood beside Ansel with a
hand on his shoulder and said, "Keep
coughing."
After about half a minute, the piece of
roll came up. Ansel drank some water and
pretended the whole thing hadn't
happened.
Tough meat and crusty bread take the
most chewing of anything on the table.
And a federal fact sheet on swallowing
names the danger plainly.
Food pieces that are too large to
swallow can enter the throat and block
the passage of air.
The fix is to make the pieces small
before they ever reach your mouth.
Health guides say to cut large pieces of
food into easily chewable sizes and to
chew thoroughly.
The government's aging institute adds
advice for anyone learning to eat with
dentures. Cut your food into small
pieces and chew slowly using both sides
of your mouth.
Marion cut the rest of Ansel's sandwich
into quarters. Ansel said nobody had cut
his sandwich since the second grade. He
ate all four quarters anyway, slowly.
At supper that night, Ansel cut his
whole pork chop into small pieces first,
the way you line up the cars before you
couple them.
It took him an extra minute. Marion
noticed he talked less with his mouth
full, too, because there was hardly ever
a big mouthful to talk around.
That night, Marion opened the Red Cross
page on choking on the kitchen tablet.
Ansel and Marion read the steps for a
choking adult together.
Then they practiced only the hand
positions on each other, slowly, with no
squeeze at all. Real thrusts are only
for real choking.
Ansel found the right spot on Marion on
his second try, and he announced it like
a signal coming back online.
Marion said if he squeezed, he'd be
scrubbing the roasting pan for a month.
Neither of them knew how soon that
practice would matter.
Tonight, before your first bite of meat,
cut the whole portion into small pieces,
smaller than you think you need.
Cut sandwiches into quarters.
When a bite goes down wrong, the cough
is usually your body doing its job.
Smaller pieces give it much less work to
do.
Number four [music] is a loose denture
and a dry mouth.
Two Sundays before the pot roast, Marion
made ham and scalloped [music] potatoes.
Across the table, Marion heard a small
click every time Agnes chewed.
Agnes' upper denture was slipping.
Agnes chewed only on her left side and
not for long.
Then Agnes swallowed and went straight
on with her next sentence. Marion
noticed her take a sip of water after
almost every bite.
When Marion asked, Agnes laughed.
Agnes has had the same dentures since
the year her husband retired.
They'd been loose for a while, so she
just used more of the paste. "My mouth's
like cotton anyway," Agnes said.
Teeth that don't meet well can't grind
food down.
The government's aging institute
explains why old dentures stop fitting.
As your gums change shape over time,
dentures may need to be adjusted or
replaced. Your dentist should be the one
to do it.
There's a second catch. With dentures,
it can be harder to notice bones or hard
bits in your food. So a piece that
needed more chewing can slip past
without warning.
Then there was the cotton mouth.
Saliva softens food and makes it easier
to swallow.
A federal fact sheet on dry mouth says
that without enough of it, chewing and
swallowing get harder. Dentures may not
fit as well in a dry mouth, and they can
rub sore spots.
That same fact sheet says dry mouth
isn't a part of aging itself,
but many older adults take medicines
that dry out the mouth, and taking more
than one can make it worse.
It names medicines for high blood
pressure, depression, and bladder
control.
Agnes takes a blood pressure pill and a
pill for her bladder.
Agnes had never once connected either
one to her mouth.
Marion wrote two lines on the back of a
grocery receipt and slid it across the
table to Agnes.
"Call the dentist about the upper plate.
Ask the pharmacist whether either pill
could be drying out your mouth." Agnes
tucked the receipt into her cookie tin
and said she'd get to it next month.
In the meantime, the fact sheet's
simplest tip costs nothing.
Sip water or sugarless drinks often,
especially during meals, to make chewing
and swallowing easier.
Sugarless gum or sugarless hard candy
can get saliva flowing. Coffee and
alcohol both dry the mouth out.
Think about your own teeth or your own
dentures for a moment.
When did a dentist last check how they
fit?
If you have to stop and think about
which year, keep that year in mind.
Tonight, put a full glass of water at
your place for supper. Take a sip before
the first bite and more sips between
bites after you've swallowed. If your
dentures click or slip, call your
dentist this week. If your mouth always
feels dry, ask your pharmacist whether
any of your medicines could be the
reason.
Never stop one on your own.
A dry mouth and a loose denture are two
of the most fixable problems on this
list.
Number three is eating, drinking, or
taking pills while you're leaning back.
The Monday after that ham dinner, the
Vikings played at night.
Ansel ate his supper on a TV tray in his
recliner, tipped halfway back. By the
second quarter, Ansel was eating popcorn
with his chin pointed at the ceiling.
Marion watched him from the couch.
Marion didn't say a word until Ansel
coughed on a kernel.
Gravity helps every swallow you take.
When you lean far back, food and drink
travel through your throat at an awkward
angle. The same goes for breakfast in
bed or a cookie on the pillow before
sleep. For people with swallowing
trouble, health guides are direct. Sit
up as straight as possible when you eat
and stay upright for 30 to 45 minutes
afterward.
So, Marion reached over and pulled the
lever on Ansel's recliner.
Ansel finished his popcorn sitting up
straight like a man in a church pew and
complained through the whole third
quarter.
Then came bedtime.
Ansel takes one vitamin C tablet every
night, a big chalky one.
For years, Ansel has taken it the same
way. He's already lying in bed. He takes
one small sip from the glass on the
nightstand, and then he lies flat.
That Monday, the tablet didn't go all
the way down.
Ansel could feel it, high behind his
breastbone, sitting there like a freight
car on a siding.
Ansel sat up, drank the rest of the
glass, and the tablet moved on.
A pill that stalls on the way down can
irritate the tube that carries food to
your stomach.
Health guides say certain medicines can
inflame that tube if you take them
without plenty of water.
Their list includes some
bone-strengthening pills, the
antibiotics doxycycline and
tetracycline, potassium pills, and
vitamin C.
Ansel's vitamin was right there on the
list. The advice is short. Take your
pills with plenty of water, and don't
lie down right after.
Some labels spell it out.
The bone pill alendronate, sold as
Fosamax, says to swallow it with a full
glass of plain water, 6 to 8 oz.
Then you stay sitting or standing
upright for at least 30 minutes.
If pills are hard to swallow, the FDA
says to ask your doctor, nurse, or
pharmacist for ideas.
There may be a liquid version you could
use, but don't break, crush, or chew a
tablet without asking first, because
some pills aren't meant to be crushed.
So, the vitamin C moved to the kitchen
table.
Ansel now takes it after supper, sitting
up with a full glass of water, and then
he does the dishes.
Ansel says it's the first vitamin that
ever got him to wash a pan.
Tonight, take your evening pills sitting
up at the table with a full glass of
water, and stay upright for a while
afterward.
If you eat in a recliner, bring it all
the way up before the first bite.
Most pills go down without any trouble,
and this habit costs you nothing but a
glass of water.
Number two [music] is the little cough
at the table that nobody mentions.
Marion spent 30 years listening to
voices. Marion can hear a cold coming on
in an alto from across the choir loft.
Over those three Sundays, she kept
hearing something in Agnes' voice.
After a sip of coffee, Agnes' voice came
out wet, almost gurgly.
Then Agnes cleared her throat, and she
cleared it after nearly every sip.
At the church coffee hour, Agnes coughed
through her bowl of soup and blamed the
pepper.
Once Marion asked,
there was more.
Agnes said that some days a bite felt
like it stuck in her chest.
In the winter before, Agnes had
pneumonia, which she still calls that
bug.
The public pages of the Speech and
Hearing Association list the signs of a
swallowing problem.
They include coughing during or right
after eating or drinking.
They include clearing your throat often
after meals and a wet or gurgly voice.
The list goes on with food that feels
stuck in your throat or chest, needing
extra time to chew or swallow, and
losing weight.
A swallowing problem has a medical name,
dysphagia.
The government's Institute for Hearing
and Swallowing says it happens most
often in older adults.
That little cough matters for a reason.
When food or liquid slips into the
airway, coughing or throat clearing
sometimes can't get it all back out.
What stays behind can reach the lungs,
where bacteria grow. The result is a
lung infection called aspiration
pneumonia.
The CDC researchers from the start of
this story also looked at what else
showed up with food choking deaths in
older people.
Three conditions stood out: dementia,
Parkinson's disease, and pneumonitis, a
kind of lung inflammation.
The good news is that a swallow can be
checked.
If your swallowing changes slowly or
suddenly, that same institute says to
see your doctor.
Your doctor may send you to an ear,
nose, and throat doctor and to a speech
language pathologist, a specialist in
swallowing.
One test is a video x-ray taken while
you swallow food and drinks mixed with
barium. The team can watch exactly where
everything goes. Another uses a thin
tube with a light on the end passed
through the nose to watch your throat.
Then the specialist changes what needs
changing, like the size of your bites,
the texture of your food, or how you
hold your head.
One common move is a chin tuck, which
the therapist teaches to the people it
helps.
Marion brought it up on Saturday on the
front porch when Agnes dropped off a tin
of molasses cookies.
Agnes waved her hand.
"Everybody coughs, dear." Agnes said.
She'd mention it at her checkup in the
spring.
Marion let it go for one more day.
Marion understood why Agnes waved it
off.
Agnes has lived alone for 6 years and
she's proud of every meal she still
cooks for herself.
Admitting a cough at the table felt, to
Agnes, like the first step toward giving
up the food she loves. Marion knew that
wasn't how it works, but she also knew
Agnes well enough not to push on a
Saturday.
Tonight at supper, listen to yourself or
to the person across from you.
Notice any cough, throat clearing, or
wet voice during the meal and write it
on the calendar.
If it happens often, take that calendar
to your doctor and ask about a swallow
evaluation. That test isn't something
you pass or fail.
It's a map of your own swallow and it
shows exactly what to change.
Number one is [music] waiting or
freezing when someone can't breathe.
Back to that [music] Sunday at 5:06.
The pot roast had been in the oven since
church.
Ansel was telling Agnes about the moose
that stood on the tracks and wouldn't
budge for the evening freight. His fork
rested on his plate, the way Ansel had
practiced.
Agnes laughed.
Agnes had a big bite of pot roast in her
mouth, a piece she hadn't cut small. Her
upper plate was loose and her mouth was
dry from the long afternoon.
Then Agnes stopped laughing. She put
both hands to her throat. No cough came
out and no words. Agnes made only a
thin, high squeak and then no sound at
all.
These are the signs that same Red Cross
page lists for a blocked airway.
A weak cough or no cough at all, a
high-pitched squeak or no sound, not
being able to speak and hands at the
throat.
The skin may look red at first, then
turn pale or bluish.
Ansel was already on his feet.
Agnes, are you choking?
Agnes nodded. This was the difference
Ansel's sandwich had taught them.
Agnes couldn't cough or speak, so
waiting would not help.
Marion picked up the kitchen phone,
called 911 and put it on speaker.
Ansel helped Agnes up out of her chair
and stepped to her side, slightly behind
her.
Ansel put one arm across her chest and
bent her forward at the waist.
With the heel of his other hand, he gave
her five firm, separate blows between
the shoulder blades.
The piece didn't come out.
So Ansel stood Agnes up straight and
moved in behind her.
Agnes is tiny, so Ansel bent his knees.
He found her navel with two fingers.
Then he made a fist with his other hand.
He set the thumb side against her, just
above the navel and well below the
breastbone. He covered the fist with his
first hand.
Ansel pulled in and up, hard and quick,
five separate times.
Each thrust pushes a burst of air up out
of the lungs, like a cough someone else
makes for you.
On the fourth thrust, the piece of pot
roast shot out onto the tablecloth.
Agnes coughed, gasped, and breathed.
Then Agnes cried, and Marion held her
while the dispatcher on the speakerphone
said the ambulance was 2 minutes away.
Ansel sat down hard in his own chair.
His hands were shaking, the same hands
that had practiced on Marion at the
kitchen counter. The whole thing, from
the first squeak to the first breath,
took less time than it takes to read the
steps.
That sequence is newer than the one many
of us learned. In 2025, the American
Heart Association recommended
alternating five back blows and five
abdominal thrusts for a conscious adult
who is choking. You keep going until the
object comes out or the person stops
responding. Its earlier guidelines
didn't include choking advice for adults
at all.
If the first round doesn't work, keep
going, five and five. If the person
becomes unresponsive, the Red Cross says
to lower them to a firm, flat surface
and begin CPR. Make sure someone has
called 911.
If the person is too large to reach
around or pregnant, give thrusts to the
chest instead.
If they're in a wheelchair, you may need
to kneel behind it.
And one thing to avoid,
don't force open the mouth of a
conscious person to grab the food.
The Red Cross says never to sweep a
finger inside unless you can actually
see the object.
If you said no at the start, you have
plenty of company.
Three weeks earlier, Ansel would have
said no, too.
In a study of 141 choking deaths,
someone else was there in more than
eight out of 10. Most of the time, the
rescue is already sitting at the table.
The paramedics checked Agnes right there
in the dining room chair.
They took her to the emergency room
anyway, and that was the right thing to
do.
Health guides say that after an object
is cleared, the person should see a
provider because complications can
happen.
Those guides also list what to watch for
in the days after.
A cough that won't go away, a fever,
trouble swallowing or speaking,
shortness of breath, or wheezing means
call a provider right away.
Ansel and Marion drove to the hospital
and brought Agnes home by 10:00 that
night, sore across her ribs and very
embarrassed.
On her front step, Agnes said, "Ansel
Brooks, you found my belly button faster
than my doctor ever has."
Ansel said he'd already forgotten where
it was.
On Tuesday, [music]
Agnes asked the question that had kept
her up two nights.
Agnes eats most of her meals alone.
What happens when [music] nobody's at
the table?
So, Ansel and Marion walked two doors
down with the tablet. The same Red Cross
page has an answer.
If you're choking and alone, call 911 on
a landline or a cell phone with GPS. The
Red Cross says that even if you can't
speak, the open line will bring help.
Then give yourself abdominal thrusts
with your own hands, fist above your
navel, just as you would for someone
else.
Or bend over and press your belly hard
against something firm, like the back of
a sturdy chair or a railing.
Stay away from anything with a sharp
edge or corner, and be careful with a
railing that's up high.
Ansel went through every chair in
Agnes's kitchen.
Ansel picked the oak one with the solid,
rounded back and set it at the end of
her table, one step from her seat.
Agnes leaned over it gently, only to
learn the position. Then Agnes moved her
cordless phone from the hallway to the
kitchen table, next to the salt and
pepper.
Agnes made one more change on her own.
The toughest meats, the roasts and the
steaks, she now saves for Sundays at a
table with other people around it.
On her own, she cooks the softer things
and she cuts them small.
Reading the steps is a start.
If you'd like to practice on a mannequin
with someone watching your hands, the
Red Cross and other groups teach short
first aid classes.
Ansel and Marion signed up for one at
the community center the next month.
Tonight, find the spot on yourself. Make
a fist and rest the thumb side just
above your navel, well below your
breastbone, with no pressure.
Then pick the sturdiest chair in your
kitchen and keep your phone on the table
when you eat. You'll probably never need
any of it.
Learning it takes about 10 minutes and
it stays with you.
Agnes called her own doctor that
Wednesday before Marion could even ask.
Her doctor sent Agnes for a swallow
study.
A speech therapist watched the X-ray and
taught Agnes to take smaller bites, sip
slowly, and tuck her chin when she
drinks. Her dentist relined the upper
plate and it doesn't click anymore.
And her pharmacist went over both pills
with her doctor.
The next Sunday, Agnes was back at the
Brooks table with her cookie tin.
Agnes cut her pot roast into small
pieces before the first bite and kept a
glass of water by her plate.
When Ansel told the moose story again,
Agnes waited, swallowed, and then she
laughed.
Do you cough or clear your throat during
meals, feel food stick, hear a wet voice
after drinking, or lose weight without
trying?
Call your doctor this week and ask about
a swallow evaluation.
After any choking that needed back blows
or thrusts, see a doctor. In the days
after, call right away for a cough,
fever, wheezing, or trouble breathing.
Call 911 when someone can't cough,
speak, or breathe. Start five back blows
and five thrusts while someone else
makes the call.
None of this [music] is a diagnosis.
Your own doctor and dentist know your
swallow, your teeth, and your pills, and
every step here belongs [music] in that
conversation.
Tonight, cut your supper small, set your
fork down between bites, and find the
spot just above your navel where a fist
would go.
Then tell [music] me in the comments,
now that you've watched Ansel, would you
know where your hands go? Yes or no? And
send [music] this to the person who sits
across from you at Sunday dinner.
On Birch Lane, the pot roast comes
[music] to the table already cut small.
Two doors down, a sturdy oak chair waits
at the end of Agnes's kitchen table with
the phone beside her plate.

records.title: Over 60? You Don't Need 10,000 Steps A Day — Walk This Many Instead
records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.
