subtitles.plaintext:
11:15 in the morning.
You open your eyes and the ceiling
[music] is the wrong color.
Someone is saying your name and you know
the voice and you cannot place [music]
it. Your mouth is dry and there is a
tube taped to the back of your left
hand. Your glasses are in a plastic bag
on a [music] shelf you cannot see. Case
reports from recovery rooms describe
that exact minute over and over and in
adults [music] past 65 it has a name.
Postoperative delirium.
A sudden shifting confusion [music] that
arrives in the first hours or days after
surgery. And for some people
>> [music]
>> it does not fully leave.
Here's what happens inside an older
brain. First syringe to your own kitchen
and the one thing to ask for before you
sign.
One question first.
Have you been under general anesthesia
since you turned 60? Yes or no?
Hold on to your answer because it
changes what the second half of this
means for you. Tell me in the comments.
Just the one word.
Most people walk into surgery worrying
about the heart, [music] the incision,
the blood clot. The brain is the organ
nobody brings up at the pre-op [music]
visit and it is the one most likely to
come home different.
Anesthesiologists have been describing
[music] this for decades. In 2018 the
British Journal of Anesthesia published
a consensus statement from
anesthesiologists [music]
and brain researchers.
They had sat down to put names on what
they had been seeing for decades.
The decline in older adults after
surgery had been documented so
consistently that it needed a shared
vocabulary. Three names came out of that
room.
You will meet all three. And one group
of those researchers who scanned the
brains of adults over 70 before surgery
holds the second patient story.
Frank is 74. [music]
He is a retired electrician in Dayton,
Ohio.
He walks a mile [music] most mornings.
He takes a blood pressure pill, a
statin, and a sleep aid his wife Jean
picks up at the pharmacy.
His right hip has been grinding for 3
years and he is finally getting it
replaced.
He has told three people this week that
he is not worried. He is worried about
missing the Reds opener.
Jean has packed a crossword book and a
sweater for the chair beside his bed.
Tuesday, check in at 5:45 in the
morning. Surgery at 7:15.
At the check-in desk, a nurse hands him
a clear plastic bag and asks for his
glasses, his hearing aid, and his upper
denture.
He drops all three in.
He feels the difference right away.
Without the glasses, the room is a wash
of white and gray.
Without the hearing aid, her questions
reach him a beat late and twice he
answers the wrong one.
She asks his date of birth and he tells
her his home address. She asks it again,
slower, leaning in, and this time he
gets it right.
He laughs it off. So does she. The bag
goes on a shelf behind the nurses'
station.
He will not see it again for 11 hours.
On this subject, the research hands you
one specific thing to say out loud.
Before you sign the consent form, ask
the hospital a plain question.
Do you run a delirium prevention
protocol for patients over 65 and will I
be on it? Some hospitals run one. Many
do not, which is exactly why you have to
ask.
Many of them call it the hospital elder
life program, HELP for short.
It is a checklist of low-tech things the
nursing staff does differently when they
know a brain is at risk. It costs
nothing to ask. Almost nobody asks
because almost nobody has heard the word
delirium until they are living inside
it.
What you are watching is education, not
medical advice, and every decision about
your own operation belongs with your own
surgeon and anesthesiologist.
Keep that question in your pocket and we
will open the checklist item by item.
First, walk through what it is
protecting you from one step at a time
starting with the syringe.
Step one is induction, 7:20 in the
morning. Frank is on the table, a clear
mask [music] over his nose, and the
anesthesiologist tells him to think of
somewhere warm. The first drug is
usually propofol, a milky white liquid
pushed into the vein, and Frank is gone
[music] in about 40 seconds.
If you have been under, you may remember
the count.
You get to three, maybe four, and then
there is nothing. [music]
No dream, no sense of time passing at
all.
What it does is turn up the brain's main
braking chemical, a messenger called
GABA. It turns it up until the
conversations between brain regions that
make you you go quiet. Memory stops
recording. Pain signals still arrive in
the body, but there is no one home to
receive them.
In a 40-year-old brain, that is a wide,
safe margin.
The drugs clear, the conversation
restarts, and by lunchtime he is asking
for a sandwich.
At 74, the margin is thinner for reasons
you can count. Fewer neurons,
fewer connections between the ones that
remain.
A liver and a pair of kidneys that clear
the drugs more slowly, so the same dose
sits in the system longer. Think of a
full tank and a quarter tank on the same
drive. Both cars get there.
One of them has no room for a detour.
That is why a good anesthesiologist
doses by age and not just by weight.
There is a second thing happening at the
same time and it is the part the older
brain feels most. Every blood vessel in
your brain is wrapped in a lining of
cells that decides what gets from the
blood into the brain tissue. Doctors
call it the blood brain barrier. Picture
a window screen. When it is new, the
mesh is tight and only air gets through.
After years in the weather, a few
threads have gone and it lets in what it
used to keep out. Holding that lining
together are small support cells called
pericytes. In aged mice given a common
anesthetic gas plus a bone surgery,
researchers found the pericytes were
lost. The barrier leaked in the memory
center of the brain. Inflammatory
chemicals got through and the mice did
worse on memory tasks afterward. Mice
are not people,
but the pattern fits what is seen on the
ward.
An older barrier is already more porous
than a young one and the combination of
anesthesia and surgery pries it open
further. The anesthetic is the door.
What walks through it does the damage.
And 80 ft from the table, Frank's
glasses and hearing aid are still
sitting in the bag.
Step two is the surgery itself.
8:05
The surgeon makes a 9-in incision and
saws through the top of Frank's thigh
bone. Surgery, however necessary, is a
controlled injury and the body answers
injury the only way it knows, with
inflammation.
You know this response from a sprained
ankle.
It swells, it heats, it throbs, and the
swelling is the body sending in its
cleanup crew. Now imagine that crew sent
to a thigh bone and the alarm bell rung
loud enough to reach the head.
Chemical alarm signals called cytokines
pour into the blood.
In a younger body, that alarm stays
mostly local and quiet within a day. In
an older body where baseline
inflammation already runs higher, the
alarm is louder and lasts longer.
Those cytokines reach a barrier that is
already leaking.
On the far side of it, the brain's own
immune cells wake up and start clearing
what they think is debris. Some of that
debris is connection.
This is why the gas is not the whole
story. Researchers compared older hip
fracture patients given a spinal, awake
from the waist down, with patients given
general anesthesia.
In two large trials, the two groups came
out about the same and neither approach
showed a clear advantage for the brain.
Frank got a general. His neighbor down
the street got a spinal for the same
hip.
That is not what separated them. Awake
or asleep is worth discussing for other
reasons, pain control among them.
But it will not by itself keep your
memory intact. The injury, the
inflammation, and the days after the
operation carry more weight than the
drug that put you under.
Step three is the window. 11:15 in the
morning, Frank is [music] in recovery.
Groggy and slow and entirely normal for
a man who had his hip replaced two hours
ago. By 3:00 in the afternoon, he is on
the ward and Jean is in the chair beside
him. He asks what time it is. She tells
him. 4 minutes later he asks again. Jean
notices he keeps smoothing the same fold
in the blanket. He asks whether the dog
has been fed. They have not had a dog in
6 years.
She tells herself it is the pain
medicine. A nurse says that is normal
after anesthesia and for a few hours it
is.
Delirium does not look like the movies.
It comes and goes across a single day.
So, the person who was lucid at lunch is
lost at supper and lucid again at
breakfast. Attention is what fails
first. Think of a radio drifting off the
station, in and out, with music for 10
seconds and static for 30.
The Mayo Clinic lists the pieces
plainly, reduced awareness of where you
are. Trouble focusing on a question or
following a sentence. Thinking that
wanders and does not come back. Sleep
turned upside down, awake all night and
asleep all day. And either agitation or
its quiet opposite.
That quiet opposite is the one that gets
missed.
There are two faces to delirium. The
loud one, where the patient pulls at
lines and tries to climb [music] out of
bed, gets a nurse at the bedside within
a minute. The quiet one, where the
patient is drowsy, [music]
withdrawn, agreeable, and answers every
question with a yes, gets written
[music] in the chart as resting
comfortably.
The quiet patient looks like [music] a
good patient.
They do not press the call button. They
do not complain.
They thank everyone and remember none of
it.
The quiet form is the more common of the
two in older adults, and it is the one
most likely to be sent home undiagnosed.
Before you go in, give the person who
will sit beside you one test to run.
Have them ask you to say the months of
the year backward, starting with
December.
Have them ask you what day it is and
where you are. Tell them to watch
whether you can hold the question in
mind long enough to answer it.
If you did that easily at breakfast and
cannot do it at dinner, you have
drifted. Tell them to give the nurse the
exact words you got wrong. That detail
is what gets written down.
Frank gets the loud one. 2:40 in the
morning on Wednesday.
He is convinced [music] he is in his
garage and the furnace has gone out. He
pulls the tape off his hand and [music]
gets the IV halfway out.
He tells the night nurse that Gene is
his brother Dennis, who died in 1998.
Look at what is around him in [music]
that minute. The room is half dark.
There is a clock on the wall he cannot
read because his glasses are in a
plastic bag behind the nurses' station.
The voices around him are underwater
because his hearing aid is in the same
bag. Gene went home at 9:00 to feed the
cat and sleep. The chair beside him is
empty. The one voice in the building he
would have trusted is 12 miles away.
Every tool his brain uses to figure out
where it is has been taken away at the
exact hour it needed the most. Picture
your own nightstand right now. If
someone woke you at 2:40 in the morning
in a room you did not know, with your
glasses and your hearing aid in a bag
down the hall, how much of that room
could you make out?
Hold that picture.
The window usually opens on the first
day after surgery, peaks around the
second, and for most people closes
within a few days.
The consensus you heard about earlier
split what happens after that into three
stages.
Postoperative delirium is the acute
confusion in those first days. Delayed
neurocognitive recovery is the fog that
lingers after the delirium lifts out to
about 30 days.
Those are the weeks when you cannot hold
a phone number in your head or follow
the thread of a book. In that stage, you
can still dress yourself and make the
coffee. But you set the cup down and
cannot find it. You start a sentence
about the grandchildren and lose the end
of it. People say you seem tired. And
postoperative neurocognitive disorder is
the decline that is still measurable up
to a year later.
Most people stay in the first stage or
never enter it at all.
The point of the naming was that a
measurable number do not.
If you said yes to the question at the
start, think about your own first week
home.
Could you follow a television program?
Did you reread the same page? Did a
family member say you seemed off? And
did you put it down to the pain [music]
pills?
That week has a name now.
How common is it? Honest answer, it
depends enormously [music] on the
surgery and the patient. After a short
outpatient procedure in a fit
70-year-old, confusion afterward is
uncommon. After major [music] surgery,
it is a different story.
A hip fracture, heart surgery, a long
abdominal operation.
In the oldest and frailest patients,
estimates run as high as one in three
waking confused. The range is that wide
because the operation is only half the
equation. The other half is the brain
that walked in.
Think about your own bathroom. How many
prescription and over-the-counter
medications are in the cabinet or on the
counter right now? Include the sleep aid
and the allergy pill. Get a rough number
in your head.
It comes back in a few minutes, and it
will matter more than you expect.
Why Frank and not his neighbor? Same
age, same hip, same surgeon, who went
home on day three asking about the Reds
game.
The word researchers use is reserve.
Delirium is a stress test, and what it
tests is how much spare capacity a brain
had before the first syringe. The
neighbor had been swimming three
mornings a week for a decade. He walked
in with a bigger tank.
In a study of cancer patients 65 and
older heading into surgery, researchers
measured two things beforehand. Frailty,
meaning grip strength, walking speed,
unintended weight loss, how much help a
person needed with daily tasks, and a
short screen of memory and attention.
Then they watched who became delirious
afterward using a standardized bedside
check called the confusion assessment
method. Both measures carried weight.
Both of those can be measured in a
10-minute pre-op appointment, and in
most hospitals, neither one is, unless
you ask.
Now the part that explains Carol.
In 2020, the Journal of Alzheimer's
Disease published results from a cohort
called Sages, adults 70 and older.
None of them had dementia. All of them
were having elective surgery, and they
had their brain scanned before the
operation. Some of those scans showed
thinning in the brain regions
Alzheimer's disease touches first, a
pattern called cortical atrophy.
This was in people who were still sharp
in daily life.
Those who had that pattern and then
developed delirium after surgery may be
at increased risk. The risk is long-term
cognitive decline in the years that
followed.
It does not say anesthesia causes
Alzheimer's.
It suggests that for some people,
delirium is the moment a quiet,
invisible vulnerability becomes visible
and maybe the push that speeds it up.
For you, that means a delirium episode
is never just a bad night. It is
information, and it belongs in your
medical record and in front of your
primary care doctor.
Carol is 79, knee replacement in March.
She had the quiet kind. She slept most
of the second day and answered yes to
everything. She was discharged on day
three with a note that said tolerated
the procedure well. In June, she was
reading the same paragraph three times.
In August, she stopped doing the
crossword she had done for 40 years. Her
daughter noticed something else first.
Carol used to beat everyone to the
answer on the evening game show. Now she
sat with the remote in her lap and did
not reach for it.
When her daughter asked, Carol said she
was fine. The same way she had said yes
to everything on the ward. Her doctor
told her she was 79. Nobody drew a line
from the knee to the crossword because
nobody had written the word delirium
anywhere because nobody had looked. By
the consensus names, Carol is in the
territory of post-operative
neurocognitive disorder. The right
response to that is a proper cognitive
assessment, a hearing test, a medication
review, and a check for depression and
poor sleep.
Those last two can imitate decline and
are treatable.
Some people in Carol's position recover
slowly over the following year. Some
plateau.
The ones who do worst are the ones
nobody evaluates.
There is a billing code for the hip.
There is a billing code for the knee.
There is no billing code for the 45
minutes it takes to protect the brain
attached to them.
That is why the protecting [music] falls
to you.
Five things to put in place before you
go under. Counting down to the one that
protects [music] you most.
Number five is the plastic bag. Your
glasses, your hearing aids, and your
dentures are not comfort items.
They are the instruments your brain uses
to know where it is. Write on the pre-op
form that you want them returned in the
first hour of recovery.
Say it out loud to the pre-op nurse and
say it again to the recovery nurse.
Send a labeled case with whoever is
waiting for you. Pack that [music] case
yourself. Write your name on it in
letters you could read without your
glasses. Hand it to your person, not to
the desk. Give them one job. Put the
glasses [music] on your face before
anyone asks how you feel. Sensory
impairment, uncorrected vision and
hearing, is one of the named risk
factors [music] that prevention programs
target directly. That is precisely
because it is the easiest one to fix.
Frank's hearing aid cost $4,000.
It's been his worst night in a bag 80 ft
from his bed.
Number four is the number in your head
from a few minutes ago, the medications.
Certain pills make delirium more likely,
and most of them are quiet, ordinary
things. Sleep aids that contain
diphenhydramine, which is the PM in
nighttime pain relievers, and the active
ingredient in most drugstore sleep
pills. Older antihistamines,
some bladder control pills, some older
antidepressants,
benzodiazepines,
the family that includes lorazepam and
diazepam. Many of these work by blocking
acetylcholine, which happens to be the
brain's main attention chemical.
Delirium is a failure of attention. So,
you are walking into a stress test of
attention with the attention system
already partly switched off. Add the
opioids you will genuinely need for pain
afterward, and the load climbs again.
In the 2 weeks before surgery, put every
bottle, including the over-the-counter
ones, in a bag.
Bring it to the pre-op visit or to your
pharmacist, and ask one question.
Which of these raise my risk of
confusion after surgery, and what can be
done about them before the date? Do not
stop anything on your own, because
stopping some of these abruptly is its
own hazard.
Ask too about a pain plan after surgery
that leans on scheduled acetaminophen
and nerve blocks, so that less opioid is
needed.
Jean does this later, after the fact.
She lines the bottles up on the kitchen
table, six of them, two from the
drugstore shelf. One is the pink one for
sleep. She reads the small print for the
first time in 6 years.
Frank's sleep aid was diphenhydramine.
He had taken it every night for 6 years.
Nobody at the check-in desk asked.
Number three is reserve, and you can
build it in the weeks you are waiting
for the surgery date. Walk every day
because the muscle you carry in is the
muscle you recover on. Sarcopenia, the
slow loss of muscle with age, is half of
what frailty means. Put protein on the
plate at every meal.
Eggs or yogurt at breakfast, not toast
alone. Drink water on a schedule because
dehydration on its own can tip an older
brain into confusion, and most people
arrive at surgery dry. Keep a glass by
the sink and finish it each time you
walk past. Be honest about alcohol
because three or more drinks a night
means withdrawal on day two, and
withdrawal looks exactly like delirium.
Tell the anesthesiologist the real
number, not the polite one. Keep a
steady sleep and wake time, and do one
thing in your living room this week.
Sit in a sturdy chair, cross your arms
over your chest, and stand up and sit
down five times as fast as you safely
can. Count out loud. Notice whether you
need to uncross your arms and push off.
If it takes you more than about 15
seconds, bring that up at the pre-op
visit. It is one of the [music] simplest
frailty measures there is.
Then, ask for the other half, a short
memory and attention screen [music]
before surgery, so there is a baseline
on paper.
If something is [music] different
afterward, somebody can prove it.
Number two [music] is the conversation
with the anesthesiologist.
In most hospitals, you will meet them
for about 6 minutes on the morning of
surgery.
6 minutes is enough [music] if you know
what to ask. Write the questions on the
back of a card the night before.
You will be cold in a paper gown and the
minutes go fast. Ask whether they
monitor the depth of anesthesia with
EEG. That is a brainwave monitor on the
forehead. It lets them keep you as light
as is safe instead of deeper than you
need. Researchers pooled the trials of
this in older adults. The results have
not all pointed the same direction.
Some showed fewer cases of delirium and
some showed no difference. So, it is not
a guarantee, but it is a reasonable
thing to ask for and many
anesthesiologists use it as a matter of
routine.
Ask whether the calming shot given right
before surgery, often a benzodiazepine,
can be skipped or reduced in your case.
It is commonly avoided in older patients
for exactly this reason. You already
know a spinal is not a shield for the

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

If you're over 60 and eat peanut butter most days, six things are happening on your plate, and only some of them are good news. This video counts down six of them: the real size of your spoonful, the protein you think you're getting, what peanut butter does and doesn't do for your heart, what's actually in the jar, how it goes down when your mouth is dry, and the one that shows up hours later at a different meal.

Keep count as we go. At the end, your number tells you whether peanut butter is working for you or against you. You almost never have to give it up: for each one there's a simple swap or a better time of day. We also check the viral claim that peanut butter cuts Alzheimer's risk by 80% against what the research actually found.

records.title: Millions Over 60 Check Blood Pressure Wrong — It Can Hide Stroke Risk
records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
One-arm home blood pressure checks can hide a stroke warning. A 10-point gap between your arms is the number seniors never see. At 7:15 every morning the cuff goes on the same arm, the number looks fine, and the louder reading your heart actually lives with never makes it onto the page.

Most home monitors are used on one arm for years, and nobody ever says which arm. This episode explains the inter-arm blood pressure difference in plain language: why the two arms can read differently, why a systolic gap of 10 mmHg or more is the threshold researchers have linked to stroke, heart attack and early death, and how to check both arms correctly in one sitting. You will also meet Charles, a composite patient whose "normal" one thirty-six hid a narrowed artery for a decade, and count down the five home blood pressure mistakes — cuff size, the thirty minutes before the reading, and the one at the bottom of the list that never trips an alarm.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — The 7:15 reading that lies to your body
1:13 — Both arms, one sitting, the ten-point rule
1:50 — Charles and eleven years on the left arm
5:06 — Why one arm runs quieter than the other
10:48 — What a ten-point gap predicts
11:57 — Five home mistakes, counting down to the worst
12:08 — Glenn's cuff: eleven points that were never his
14:07 — The thirty minutes that inflate your number
19:40 — The last mistake hides for a decade
25:20 — Walking the chain back to the kitchen table
26:16 — What to do tonight, by urgency

If this check is new to you, subscribe and turn on notifications — the next episode in the stroke series builds on it, and the comment section is where the "which arm came up higher" answers land.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Charles, Glenn and every other person named in this episode are composites drawn from published case patterns, not real patients. A gap between your arms is a reason to be seen, not a diagnosis — bring both numbers to your own doctor, who knows your history, before changing any medication or treatment. If you notice face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech, sudden vision loss or the worst headache of your life, call 911 immediately.

🤖 AI NOTE
The illustrations and voice in this video were produced with AI assistance. Dr. Ansel is a drawn character, not a real physician, and nobody on this channel is a licensed physician.

📚 SOURCES & REFERENCES

2. Zhou M, et al. (2016) Clinical and experimental hypertension (New York, N.Y. : 1993) — The inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference and risk of cardiovascular mortality: A meta-analysis of cohort studies.
   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028...
3. Clark CE, et al. (2021) Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979) — Associations Between Systolic Interarm Differences in Blood Pressure and Cardiovascular Disease Outcomes and Mortality: Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis, Development and Validation of a Prognostic Algorithm: The INTERPRESS-IPD Collaboration.
   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33342...

   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17670...
5. An X, et al. (2022) Frontiers in cardiovascular medicine — Evaluation of the role of combining inter-arm systolic pressure difference and derivatives of pulse volume recording in detecting subclavian artery stenosis.
   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36186...
6. Kranenburg G, et al. (2017) International journal of cardiology — Inter-arm systolic blood pressure differences, relations with future vascular events and mortality in patients with and without manifest vascular disease.
   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28641...

Then he starts a conversation about a
second pill he does not need.
If the number you kept in mind earlier

change this week.
It will do more for the honesty of your

Number two is trusting a single reading.
Peggy is 74, and one evening after a
hard phone call with her sister, she
took her pressure to settle herself.
168 systolic over 92 diastolic. She felt
her chest tighten just reading it. Her
face went warm. She could hear her own

She had her hand on her car keys before

Blood pressure moves minute to minute.
One reading is a snapshot of one moment

unless it comes with symptoms, and a
single low number is not permission to
skip a dose.
Number one is for Charles's left arm.

down.

Write them in two columns. Right on one

right to the average of the left. If the

If the left arm gave you 126 and 130,
that averages 128. The difference is 14.
That difference in points is your
interarm gap.

simply use the arm that read higher for

That arm is the one closest to what your
heart feels.

records.channelDescription:
Health stories for adults over 65, told through one small lake town.

On Birch Lane in Minnesota, Ansel and Marion Brooks and their neighbors live through the moments that matter after 65: the 3 a.m. trip to the bathroom, the bedroom that's too cold, the flu that won't let go, the new pill on the counter, the step you didn't see.

Each episode follows one of them through an everyday situation and turns published research into plain steps: the warning signs worth a call today, a simple check you can do at home, and the questions to bring to your own doctor or pharmacist.

Topics: falls and balance, sleep, heart and stroke warning signs, bladder and bowels, eyesight, medicines, surgery and tests, and winter safety.

Ansel, Marion and the Birch Lane neighbors are fictional characters. Stories are narrated with an AI voice and the pictures are AI-generated. Nobody on this channel is a doctor, and nothing here is medical advice. Talk with your doctor before changing any medicine.

records.text:
Six days after the midterms, Trump found a new reason he lost, offered the White House press secretary job to the head of the UFC, and then said he was only kidding. Jimmy Kimmel, Seth Meyers and Jimmy Fallon kept the receipts, and we kept count of the excuses. He gets to six.

Along the way: the White House puts out a second official statement about Jimmy Kimmel (this one goes after his brain), Ted Cruz finds grief at a Best Buy, there turn out to be two Dana Whites, and the real one gives his answer in front of the cameras inside the White House. Plus bad messaging, the 60 Minutes question about what history will say, and a State of the Union with a jackhammer.

What will excuse number seven be? Give us your best guess in the comments, and subscribe for the next one.

Chapters:
0:00 "I was kidding"
0:51 Six Days Late
2:42 Grief Counseling
4:12 White House vs. Kimmel: Round Two
5:55 Raccoon In A Duffel Bag
9:30 The Wrong Dana White
12:41 His Own Press Secretary
14:22 60 Minutes, Round Two

Sources:
• Jimmy Kimmel Live! (ABC): monologue of Nov. 9, 2026
• Late Night with Seth Meyers (NBC): Nov. 9, 2026
• The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon (NBC): Nov. 9, 2026
• President Trump's posts and the White House statement on Jimmy Kimmel, as read on Jimmy Kimmel Live
• 60 Minutes (CBS): interview with President Trump by Ross Douthat, as played on the shows above
• Photos: official presidential portrait (public domain); Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

Independent commentary and criticism. Not affiliated with ABC, NBC, CBS, any show, campaign or party. Short clips are used for commentary, criticism and news reporting under fair use.
